0.title: 1 Chronicles — Seek His Presence
0.overview:
First Chronicles is not a duplicate of Samuel and Kings: it is a sermon preached to a broken people, returned from exile, standing in the rubble of Jerusalem and asking whether God's promises have failed. The answer the Chronicler gives across twenty-nine chapters is thunderous: No. The throne of David still stands in the purposes of God, and the remnant, those who returned, are still his people.

The book divides in two. Chapters 1–9, the genealogies, are not padding but an argument: Israel's story is set inside the story of all humanity, traced from Adam, and Matthew and Luke draw on these lines to present Jesus as son of David, son of Abraham and son of Adam (Matthew 1:1–17; Luke 3:23–38). The reader belongs to a line that stretches back to the first man and forward to the eternal King. Chapters 10–29 give us David, not chiefly David the soldier or David the sinner, but the man who organized Israel's worship, carried the ark with joy, and prepared for the temple.

Who wrote Chronicles? The writer is unnamed; Jewish tradition named Ezra, and the last verses of 2 Chronicles are the first of Ezra. It was written after the exile, for a people back in the land, which is why it centres on the temple, the true worship of God, and David’s line, the hope of the promise.

Why does it leave out David’s sin with Bathsheba, and much of Solomon’s fall? Not to hide them: the readers had Samuel and Kings. Chronicles retells the story for a new purpose, to show the returned exiles what God had promised David and his house, and how worship pleasing to God was established. It does record sins that served that purpose, such as David’s census (21:1).

Can its numbers be trusted? Some are much larger than in Samuel and Kings. Numbers were easily miscopied in Hebrew manuscripts, and the word for “thousand” may sometimes mean a unit or clan rather than a thousand individuals. This commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error, and takes these as problems of copying or counting, not mistakes of the author; some cases remain unresolved, and none touches what the books teach.

The book's governing phrase, "seek the LORD," "seek his presence" (16:11; 22:19; 28:9), is the writer's pastoral word to every discouraged believer: when the temple has burned and the family is scattered, God is still there and his covenant is still sure. And we seek him only because he first came near: the God who called Israel his own now dwells by his Spirit in those who are Christ's.

Above all, 1 Chronicles looks ahead to the greater David and the true temple. David may not build the house; his son, a man of rest, will (22:8–10). Yet the promise reaches past Solomon: I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (17:13), words Hebrews 1:5 applies to Jesus. He spoke of his own body as the temple (John 2:19–21), and his is the throne established for ever (Luke 1:32–33). First Chronicles is the gospel in outline.

1.overview:
The book begins where the Bible begins, with the first man, and takes fifty-four verses to reach the edge of Israel: Adam to Noah, the nations, the line through Shem to Abraham, Abraham's other sons, Isaac's two sons, and the kings and chiefs of Edom.

Read as a bare list it is lifeless; read as the answer to a question it is not. The first readers lived in a province of Persia with no king, a small temple and a burnt city, asking whether they were still the people of God at all. The Chronicler (the unnamed writer of the book) answers by opening the register at Adam and letting the line run unbroken through everything that had happened to them.
1.theology:
Two doctrines are carried by the shape of the chapter. The first is that election, God's choosing of one line to carry his promise, narrows without leaving the others with nothing: the brothers outside the line are named and given real futures. God's choice of one has never meant abandoning the rest.

The second is providence, God's ruling of events, at work over centuries. Edom reigns while Israel waits, and a genealogy is the least dramatic form providence takes and one of the most convincing: nobody in it knew what he was part of.
1.examples:
Fifty-four verses of names are the last thing a modern reader wants, and they were the first thing the first readers needed, because a name in a register is a fact that does not depend on how a man feels about himself. A believer who cannot see what his life has amounted to is in the position of one of Joktan's thirteen sons in verse 22: no story attached, no deed recorded, and set down in the book of God all the same.

The record is still being kept, and the names in it now are written where nothing can burn them: the Lamb's book of life (Revelation 21:27), which is the register this one was always leading to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ten names carry creation to the flood (vv. 1-4); the world spreads out in the sons of Japheth and Ham (vv. 5-16); the line narrows through Shem to Eber and forks at Peleg and Joktan (vv. 17-23), and walks on to Abram, that is, Abraham (v. 27). Only two men get a note of character, Nimrod (v. 10) and Peleg (v. 19), and both point at Babel.
verseByVerse.theology: Beginning at Adam rather than at Abraham is a theological decision. Israel is not an alternative to the nations but a branch of the one human family, which is why the list can run forward to a Gospel preached to every nation. Paul carries the line to its end: Adam was a type, a pattern set in advance, of the one who was to come (Romans 5:14), and Christ is the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45), head of a new humanity gathered from every nation.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, a believer whose world has shrunk can still say whose he is. The exiles' identity was given by God, not granted by Persia, and the same holds in Christ: a Christian's standing rests on the God who called him out of darkness (1 Peter 2:9–10), not on what he owns or controls.

verseByVerse.quote: Adam, Seth, Enosh; Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared; Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech; Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nine chapters of names stand between the reader and the first story in this book, and they begin with no sentence at all, only a name, and then another.

Picture the man who first read it, in Jerusalem, perhaps four generations after the return. His temple is smaller than the one his great-grandfather wept over. There is no king, no army, no border he could defend, and Persia decides what happens in his city.

The question underneath a life like that is whether his people are still anybody. And the answer he is handed is a list, and it does not begin at Abraham, or at Sinai, or at the throne he no longer has. It begins at the first man God made.

Everything that could be taken from that community had been taken except the register: an empire can burn a palace, but it cannot make a man not be his father's son.

Which is why Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy, and Luke runs the line back to the son of Adam, the son of God (Luke 3:38). The chain that starts here did not stop at the exile.

The ten names from the first man to the flood have no verbs and no deeds attached, and the God who has kept the record since then has not lost one of them.

Do these genealogies have gaps? Some biblical lists skip generations (Matthew 1:8 passes over three kings between Joram and Uzziah), and Luke includes a Cainan found in the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, but missing from the Hebrew list (Luke 3:36), so the names cannot be added up to an exact date for creation; but they trace one real line from Adam to Abraham. Gaps of a few generations do not stretch that line across vast ages, and with the six ordinary days of Genesis 1 it points, in this commentary’s view, to a young creation, though faithful Christians who hold an old earth read the gaps more widely.
verseByVerse.note: Chronicles was written after the exile, probably in the 400s BC, to show the returned community that they still belong to God’s story. It begins with Adam to place Israel within all humanity. In most printed Hebrew Bibles it is the last book.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim. The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan. The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. Cush fathered Nimrod. He was the first on earth to be a mighty man. Egypt fathered Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim (from whom the Philistines came), and Caphtorim. Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn and Heth, and the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the line narrows it widens. Forty-odd names cover the whole known world, and the Philistines are named inside a parenthesis (v. 12) as though four centuries of Israel's grief were a footnote.

A small people surrounded by larger ones is always under pressure to define itself against them. The Chronicler will not allow it. Before Israel is a nation at all, it is a branch. The families in these twelve verses are not the enemy; they are relatives.

One man is given a sentence of his own: Nimrod, the first mighty man (v. 10), whose kingdom in Genesis begins at Babel and takes in Babylon (Genesis 10:8–10). The reader's people had walked home from there, and the Chronicler adds nothing.

That restraint is itself the argument: Babel is given one verse, and the line that runs to David nine chapters.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram. And the sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech. Arpachshad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber. To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg (for in his days the earth was divided), and his brother's name was Joktan. Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pace changes with Shem. Japheth's descendants were handed a paragraph and dropped; Shem's are walked one generation at a time.

Eber's two sons are the fork in the road. Peleg carries the line; Joktan is given thirteen sons and is never heard of again. Of Peleg it is said in his days the earth was divided (v. 19); this is usually taken to mean the scattering at Babel, and the name itself means division.

The Chronicler is establishing a pattern: of two brothers, the one with the longer list drops out of the story. Scripture does this again and again, and numbers never decide it: Ishmael will have twelve princes and Esau kings before Jacob has a tent.
verseByVerse.note: “Peleg” means “division” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah; Eber, Peleg, Reu; Serug, Nahor, Terah; Abram, that is, Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten more names complete a symmetry, ten from Adam to Noah and ten from Shem to Abraham, without once stopping to tell a story.

Then the line halts on a change of name: Abram, that is, Abraham (v. 27). The Chronicler assumes his reader knows the call out of Ur, the covenant, the son given when the body was as good as dead, and retells none of it. He sets the two names side by side and lets the second do the work: exalted father becomes father of a multitude, a name given to a man of ninety-nine whose wife had never borne a child.

God changes what a man is called, and then spends centuries making the name true.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–42 — The Brothers Named and Set Aside
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abraham's sons who are not the heir are honoured first: Ishmael's twelve princes (vv. 29-31), then Keturah's and Midian's sons (vv. 32-33). Only then come Isaac's sons, Esau and Israel (v. 34), and Esau's line and the Horite clans of Seir (vv. 35-42).
verseByVerse.theology: God gave Ishmael princes because he had promised to (Genesis 17:20), and Esau a kingdom. Being passed over for the line of promise did not mean being forgotten.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone who feels defined by past failures: the record God keeps of his people is the name his grace gave them, not the tally of their struggles, and in Christ that is true of every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael. These are their genealogies: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth, and Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael. The sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine: she bore Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the descendants of Keturah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the pattern that governs the rest of the chapter. Abraham's sons are named in the order of birth, and then the Chronicler takes the son who is not the heir and gives him his full honours first. Ishmael's twelve princes are set down by name, a promise kept and not a slight. Keturah's six sons follow, and Midian's five after them.

More than twenty men, each of whom became a people, are given six verses before the text returns to the one it is following: the brothers are given their due before the line narrows to Isaac.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham fathered Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He writes Israel, not Jacob. The Chronicler steps over the bought birthright, the stolen blessing, the years with Laban and the night of wrestling at the ford, and writes the new name in as though it had always been there. Jacob wrestled until daybreak for it. Here it takes one word.

A genealogy compresses everything a man suffered into the name he ends up with, and that name is the one God gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, Kenaz, and of Timna, Amalek. The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. The sons of Lotan: Hori and Hemam; and Lotan's sister was Timna. The sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. The son of Anah: Dishon. The sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eight verses cover Esau's descendants and the Horite clans of Seir, the people already in the land Esau settled; the Chronicler is finishing with the side branches.

One name carries a history. Timna appears as the mother of Amalek (v. 36; a concubine, Genesis 36:12) and as Lotan's sister (v. 39). Amalek cut down the stragglers on the way out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 25:17–18), and Saul was ordered to destroy it and spared it. When the genealogies end and the first story begins, it is Saul's death, and the reason given is a command he did not keep (10:13).

Nothing in a list like this is dead weight: the names lay out the reasons the story afterwards goes the way it goes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eight kings of Edom are named, each with a city and a successor (vv. 43-50), then eleven chiefs (vv. 51-54), and the roll is dated by one clause: before any king reigned over the people of Israel (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: God's delays are not defeats. The verse is written by a man who knows the throne came; it dates Edom's kings before Israel's, and so admits that Israel had to wait.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the oldest ache in the life of faith, and Scripture never pretends it away: the people not waiting on God appear to be doing better, for a long time. Asaph could not resolve it until he went into the sanctuary (Psalm 73:16–17).

verseByVerse.quote: These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the people of Israel: Bela the son of Beor, the name of his city being Dinhabah. Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place. Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place. Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place, the name of his city being Avith. Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place. Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigned in his place. Shaul died, and Baal-hanan, the son of Achbor, reigned in his place. Baal-hanan died, and Hadad reigned in his place, the name of his city being Pai; and his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read verse 43 with the eyes of a man who has no king. Eight kings follow, each with a city, a working succession for generations in the country of the brother who sold his birthright for soup.

The Chronicler neither softens it nor explains it. He records that the family outside the promise was governed, settled and crowned while the family inside it was still a family of shepherds waiting on a promise.

And the man writing that clause knows the throne came, and knows the King it pointed to: Edom's crowns were real, but the promise to Jacob's line was the one with a future (Genesis 35:11).

verseByVerse.quote: And Hadad died. The chiefs of Edom were: chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel, and Iram; these are the chiefs of Edom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kings give way to eleven chiefs, and then Edom is finished. It will return only as an enemy or as a conquered province.

Fifty-four verses have established one thing: God keeps a record of everyone. Nations, brothers, elder sons and men with crowns are all named, and none of them is the main line.

When the record narrows, it will narrow to Israel, then Judah, then Jesse, then a boy nobody thought to call in from the sheep. The God who took the trouble to write down every chief of Edom was working the whole time on that single line, and at the end of it stands a Son whose genealogy Matthew opens with the two names the Chronicler has just used: the son of David, the son of Abraham.

2.title: The Sons of Israel: Jacob's Family and Judah's Line
2.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun,<sup>2</sup>Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.<sup>3</sup>The sons of Judah: Er, Onan and Shelah; these three Bath-shua the Canaanite bore to him. Now Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the sight of the LORD, and he put him to death.<sup>4</sup>His daughter-in-law Tamar also bore him Perez and Zerah. Judah had five sons in all.<sup>5</sup>The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul.<sup>6</sup>The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara, five in all.<sup>7</sup>The son of Carmi: Achan, the troubler of Israel, who broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing;<sup>8</sup>and Ethan's son was Azariah.<sup>9</sup>The sons of Hezron that were born to him: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai.<sup>10</sup>Ram fathered Amminadab, and Amminadab fathered Nahshon, prince of the sons of Judah.<sup>11</sup>Nahshon fathered Salmon, Salmon fathered Boaz,<sup>12</sup>Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse.<sup>13</sup>Jesse fathered Eliab his firstborn, Abinadab the second, Shimea the third,<sup>14</sup>Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth,<sup>15</sup>Ozem the sixth, David the seventh.<sup>16</sup>And their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. The sons of Zeruiah: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, three.<sup>17</sup>Abigail bore Amasa, and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite.<sup>18</sup>Caleb the son of Hezron fathered children by his wife Azubah, and by Jerioth; and these were her sons: Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.<sup>19</sup>When Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur.<sup>20</sup>Hur fathered Uri, and Uri fathered Bezalel.<sup>21</sup>Afterward Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, whom he married when he was sixty years old, and she bore him Segub.<sup>22</sup>And Segub fathered Jair, who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead.<sup>23</sup>But Geshur and Aram took from them Havvoth-jair, Kenath, and its villages, sixty towns. All these were descendants of Machir, the father of Gilead.<sup>24</sup>After the death of Hezron, Caleb went in to Ephrathah, the wife of Hezron his father, and she bore him Ashhur, the father of Tekoa.<sup>25</sup>The sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron: Ram, his firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah.<sup>26</sup>Jerahmeel also had another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam.<sup>27</sup>The sons of Ram, the firstborn of Jerahmeel: Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.<sup>28</sup>The sons of Onam: Shammai and Jada. The sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur.<sup>29</sup>The name of Abishur's wife was Abihail, and she bore him Ahban and Molid.<sup>30</sup>The sons of Nadab: Seled and Appaim; and Seled died childless.<sup>31</sup>The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The son of Sheshan: Ahlai.<sup>32</sup>The sons of Jada, Shammai's brother: Jether and Jonathan; and Jether died childless.<sup>33</sup>The sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. These were the descendants of Jerahmeel.<sup>34</sup>Now Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, but Sheshan had an Egyptian slave whose name was Jarha.<sup>35</sup>So Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha his slave, and she bore him Attai.<sup>36</sup>Attai fathered Nathan, and Nathan fathered Zabad.<sup>37</sup>Zabad fathered Ephlal, and Ephlal fathered Obed.<sup>38</sup>Obed fathered Jehu, and Jehu fathered Azariah.<sup>39</sup>Azariah fathered Helez, and Helez fathered Eleasah.<sup>40</sup>Eleasah fathered Sismai, and Sismai fathered Shallum.<sup>41</sup>Shallum fathered Jekamiah, and Jekamiah fathered Elishama.<sup>42</sup>The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel: Mareshah his firstborn, who fathered Ziph. The son of Mareshah: Hebron.<sup>43</sup>The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem and Shema.<sup>44</sup>Shema fathered Raham, the father of Jorkeam; and Rekem fathered Shammai.<sup>45</sup>The son of Shammai: Maon; and Maon fathered Beth-zur.<sup>46</sup>Ephah also, Caleb's concubine, bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez; and Haran fathered Gazez.<sup>47</sup>The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph.<sup>48</sup>Maacah, Caleb's concubine, bore Sheber and Tirhanah.<sup>49</sup>She also bore Shaaph the father of Madmannah, Sheva the father of Machbenah and the father of Gibea; and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah.<sup>50</sup>These were the descendants of Caleb. The sons of Hur the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim,<sup>51</sup>Salma, the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph the father of Beth-gader.<sup>52</sup>Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim had other sons: Haroeh, half of the Menuhoth.<sup>53</sup>And the clans of Kiriath-jearim: the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; from these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites.<sup>54</sup>The sons of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab and half of the Manahathites, the Zorites.<sup>55</sup>The clans also of the scribes who lived at Jabez: the Tirathites, the Shimeathites and the Sucathites. These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.
2.overview:
The twelve tribes are named and eleven are dropped (vv. 1-2), because this book follows Judah. Then the royal genealogy: Judah's disastrous first family, Achan, the silent generations to Jesse, and David, last of his brothers (vv. 3-17). The rest works outward through Hezron's other households (vv. 18-41) and closes on the towns of Judah, Bethlehem among them, and the Kenite scribes (vv. 42-55).

It reads like a filing cabinet and works like an argument. Every objection a returning exile might raise about his own fitness has already been answered by somebody in this list.
2.theology:
The chapter puts the book's main claim inside a name (see v. 7): the exile is explained not as bad luck or Babylonian strength but as Israel breaking faith with God, and the explanation is set down before the story starts.

Against that runs God's persistence in using unworthy people. Grace is not a late New Testament softening of an earlier severity; it is in the oldest documents Israel had.
2.examples:
The register is not a list of achievements: one man is in it because he stole and was stoned (v. 7). A believer who reads his own life as a ledger of what he has produced is reading the wrong document.

And the chapter is quietly walking towards a village. Bethlehem is filed in verse 51 between two others, with no star over it: God was a thousand years from finishing and had already written down the address.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Line to David, and What Is in It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The twelve sons of Israel are named (vv. 1-2) and the Chronicler follows Judah. The line begins badly: a Canaanite wife, a firstborn put to death for wickedness, an heir by a daughter-in-law (vv. 3-4), and Achan, the troubler of Israel (v. 7). Then the quiet names from Ram to Jesse (vv. 10-12), and Jesse's sons, David last, with his two sisters (vv. 13-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler does not clean this line, and Matthew keeps Tamar in it on purpose, because the Son at the end of it came for sinners (Matthew 9:13).
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, a believer who thinks his family history disqualifies him has not read this genealogy properly. It is the royal line of the Son of God, with a dead man in verse 3 and a stoning in verse 7.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve names are given, and then eleven are set aside for Judah, fourth in birth order and neither the eldest nor the favourite.

The Chronicler will explain himself three chapters on (Reuben forfeited the birthright and the ruler came from Judah, 5:1-2); here he simply does it. Being first in a family has never yet decided anything in this book. Jacob had said the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and the New Testament draws the line to its end: it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah (Hebrews 7:14).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Judah: Er, Onan and Shelah; these three Bath-shua the Canaanite bore to him. Now Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the sight of the LORD, and he put him to death. His daughter-in-law Tamar also bore him Perez and Zerah. Judah had five sons in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verses into the royal genealogy and there is already a corpse: Judah's firstborn, put to death by the LORD. It was not a battle or an illness but a sentence. And the mother of those sons is Bath-shua the Canaanite, from the people Abraham's family had refused to marry into (Genesis 24:3; 28:1).

Then the line goes on through Tamar, Judah’s widowed daughter-in-law. Judah had promised her his youngest son and did not give him, so she veiled herself, sat by the road, and conceived by Judah himself. Genesis does not praise the deception, but it records Judah's verdict: She is more righteous than I (Genesis 38:26). Perez, born of that night, carries the royal line.

The Chronicler could have started at verse 5. He writes all this into the opening lines of the family that produces the Messiah, with no apology, and Matthew will do the same, putting Tamar in his first paragraph (Matthew 1:3). The line is not clean, and the Son of God, born at the end of it, did not come into a clean family.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul. The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara, five in all. The son of Carmi: Achan, the troubler of Israel, who broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing; and Ethan's son was Azariah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among four verses of names, one lands like a bomb: Achan, the troubler of Israel (v. 7). He is in the register because he belongs to the family, and the Chronicler will not remove him; but he does something more deliberate than that. The phrase broke faith translates a verb that 1 Chronicles uses at just four points in its twenty-nine chapters, and the four together are its whole account of what went wrong in Israel's history: Achan here; the tribes across the Jordan who broke faith with the God of their fathers (5:25); Judah carried to Babylon because of their breach of faith (9:1); and Saul, whose obituary reads So Saul died for his breach of faith (10:13).

A thief at Jericho, then two and a half tribes, then the whole nation, and last of all one man, the king. The Chronicler has put the main claim of his book inside a list of names and never states it outright.
verseByVerse.note: Achan is the man whose theft of devoted things at Jericho troubled Israel (Joshua 7). The devoted thing was plunder placed under the ban (Hebrew herem), given wholly to God and not to be taken.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Hezron that were born to him: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai. Ram fathered Amminadab, and Amminadab fathered Nahshon, prince of the sons of Judah. Nahshon fathered Salmon, Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four verses give seven names, and nothing except who their fathers were. Nahshon is called prince of the sons of Judah; the rest are given nothing.

These are the centuries between the promise and the throne, handled in about twenty-five words. Nahshon led Judah's camp through the wilderness, Salmon lived through the conquest, Boaz settled a matter at the gate about a foreign widow. The register keeps the fact and drops the story.

And it drops one story in particular. Boaz is here; Ruth is not, though without her there is no David. Matthew will put her back (Matthew 1:5).

God's work in a family is carried by generations who are given no lines to speak, and the God who required none of them to be remarkable brought his own Son out of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesse fathered Eliab his firstborn, Abinadab the second, Shimea the third, Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth, Ozem the sixth, David the seventh. And their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. The sons of Zeruiah: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, three. Abigail bore Amasa, and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesse's sons are counted off, David the seventh. But 1 Samuel says Jesse had eight sons (1 Samuel 17:12), and has seven pass before Samuel before the youngest is fetched from the sheep (1 Samuel 16:11).

The likeliest answer is that one son died without children. A genealogy records descent, and a man who leaves no descendants leaves no entry; this chapter notes two such men (vv. 30, 32). The Chronicler is not contradicting Samuel; he is doing a different job with the same family.

Then verse 16 quietly explains a great deal. Zeruiah and Abigail are David's sisters, so Joab, Abishai, Asahel and Amasa are the king's nephews. The hardest men in David's reign, the ones he could neither control nor dismiss, were family.

Abigail is “daughter of Nahash” in 2 Samuel 17:25 and Jesse’s daughter here: most likely Nahash was her mother’s first husband, or another name. Jether was an Israelite living among Ishmaelites, or of Ishmaelite descent.
verseByVerse.note: Zeruiah's sons Joab and Abishai were David's commanders; Amasa, Abigail's son, led Absalom's army (2 Sam. 17:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–41 — Hezron's Other Houses, and an Egyptian Slave
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The text works through Hezron's other sons: Caleb's line to Bezalel, who built the tabernacle (v. 20); Jair's twenty-three cities, lost to Geshur and Aram (vv. 21-23); Jerahmeel's line, where two men died childless (vv. 30, 32); and Sheshan, who gives his daughter to his Egyptian slave Jarha, and thirteen generations come of it (vv. 34-41).
verseByVerse.theology: The wall between Israel and the nations was never as high as Israel tried to make it (see vv. 34-41), and Christ in the end broke it down (Ephesians 2:14).
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone without children, verses 30 and 32 are tender. In a world where a man lived on through his sons, the register still kept Seled and Jether. God's care for a person never depended on descendants: he promises the childless who hold fast to him a name better than sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Caleb the son of Hezron fathered children by his wife Azubah, and by Jerioth; and these were her sons: Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon. When Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur. Hur fathered Uri, and Uri fathered Bezalel. Afterward Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, whom he married when he was sixty years old, and she bore him Segub. And Segub fathered Jair, who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead. But Geshur and Aram took from them Havvoth-jair, Kenath, and its villages, sixty towns. All these were descendants of Machir, the father of Gilead. After the death of Hezron, Caleb went in to Ephrathah, the wife of Hezron his father, and she bore him Ashhur, the father of Tekoa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Away from the royal line, three generations down from Caleb, sits a name the reader of Exodus knows: Bezalel (v. 20).

Bezalel is the first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and he was filled in order to work gold and cut stone for the tabernacle. He belongs to the tribe the temple builder will come from, and the Chronicler files him here without remark.

Around him is ordinary loss. Hezron's grandson holds twenty-three towns in Gilead, and then Geshur and Aram take them (v. 23). It is an inheritance won and lost, and no one says whether it was deserved.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron: Ram, his firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah. Jerahmeel also had another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam. The sons of Ram, the firstborn of Jerahmeel: Maaz, Jamin, and Eker. The sons of Onam: Shammai and Jada. The sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur. The name of Abishur's wife was Abihail, and she bore him Ahban and Molid. The sons of Nadab: Seled and Appaim; and Seled died childless. The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The son of Sheshan: Ahlai. The sons of Jada, Shammai's brother: Jether and Jonathan; and Jether died childless. The sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. These were the descendants of Jerahmeel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerahmeel, Hezron's firstborn, is traced carefully for nine verses, and then the line simply stops, with no king, no prophet and no city. Twice the register pauses on the same fact: Seled died childless (v. 30), Jether died childless (v. 32). In a document whose entire purpose is descent, two men are written down precisely because their lines ended.

A genealogy could have passed over them in silence. Instead their names were written. God's record of a man is not a record of his usefulness, nor of what he leaves behind.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, but Sheshan had an Egyptian slave whose name was Jarha. So Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha his slave, and she bore him Attai. Attai fathered Nathan, and Nathan fathered Zabad. Zabad fathered Ephlal, and Ephlal fathered Obed. Obed fathered Jehu, and Jehu fathered Azariah. Azariah fathered Helez, and Helez fathered Eleasah. Eleasah fathered Sismai, and Sismai fathered Shallum. Shallum fathered Jekamiah, and Jekamiah fathered Elishama.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows now Sheshan had no sons, only daughters is one of the strangest paragraphs in the genealogies. Sheshan gives his daughter to his Egyptian slave Jarha, and the son of that marriage begins a line the Chronicler traces for thirteen generations, more patiently than he traces most of Judah.

A man of Judah with no heir gives a foreigner, from the nation that once enslaved Israel, his daughter and his future. Israel spent much of its history arguing about who was properly inside. Its own family papers say a slave out of Egypt married into the royal tribe and his children were counted. The door was never as narrow as the doorkeepers wanted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 42–55 — Caleb, Bethlehem, and the Scribes at Jabez
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Caleb's descendants are traced through towns (vv. 42-49), with his daughter Achsah (v. 49). Hur's line gives Kiriath-jearim and Salma, the father of Bethlehem (v. 51). The chapter closes on the scribes at Jabez, who are Kenites (v. 55).
verseByVerse.theology: Providence lays its groundwork where nobody is watching. The chief priests would one day quote Micah's word about this little town to Herod (Matthew 2:4–6).
verseByVerse.examples: Some of the people who preserved Israel's records were outsiders (v. 55): God's book has always been kept by those he brought in.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel: Mareshah his firstborn, who fathered Ziph. The son of Mareshah: Hebron. The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem and Shema. Shema fathered Raham, the father of Jorkeam; and Rekem fathered Shammai. The son of Shammai: Maon; and Maon fathered Beth-zur. Ephah also, Caleb's concubine, bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez; and Haran fathered Gazez. The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph. Maacah, Caleb's concubine, bore Sheber and Tirhanah. She also bore Shaaph the father of Madmannah, Sheva the father of Machbenah and the father of Gibea; and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah. These were the descendants of Caleb. The sons of Hur the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caleb's descendants are given as towns as much as people: Ziph, Hebron, Maon, Beth-zur and the rest. This is a survey as much as a genealogy, who holds what and by what right.

To a community that had just come home to a land other people had been farming for seventy years, that was not old history; it was the title deed to the farm. A returning family could put a finger on a verse and say: this ridge, these terraces.

And at the end, one daughter, Achsah (v. 49), who, given a field in the Negeb, asked her father for the springs as well, and got them. She is remembered for asking for water in a dry place, which is not the worst thing to be remembered for.

verseByVerse.quote: Salma, the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph the father of Beth-gader. Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim had other sons: Haroeh, half of the Menuhoth. And the clans of Kiriath-jearim: the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; from these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites. The sons of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab and half of the Manahathites, the Zorites. The clans also of the scribes who lived at Jabez: the Tirathites, the Shimeathites and the Sucathites. These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hur's line runs out into the villages of Judah, and one of them stops the eye. Salma, the father of Bethlehem (v. 51).

That is all, and the list moves on to Beth-gader. Bethlehem enters the record as an entry in a survey, small enough that Micah will call it too little to be among the clans of Judah before promising that the ruler comes out of it (Micah 5:2).

The scribes at Jabez were Kenites, the people of Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, not Israelites at all. Some of the men who kept the records of the covenant nation had come in from outside it.

So the chapter that began with a Canaanite mother ends with foreign scribes, and between them stand an executed son, a thief, an Egyptian slave and a town too small to count. This is the line God chose, and kept, and came down into. He was never looking for material he could be proud of; he was making something in which he would be glorified.

3.title: The House of David: The Covenant Line Continues
3.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron: the firstborn, Amnon, by Ahinoam the Jezreelite; the second, Daniel, by Abigail the Carmelite,<sup>2</sup>the third, Absalom, whose mother was Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth, Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith;<sup>3</sup>the fifth, Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth, Ithream, by his wife Eglah;<sup>4</sup>six were born to him in Hebron, where he reigned for seven years and six months. And he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>These were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon, four by Bath-shua, the daughter of Ammiel;<sup>6</sup>then Ibhar, Elishama, Eliphelet,<sup>7</sup>Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,<sup>8</sup>Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine.<sup>9</sup>All these were David's sons, besides the sons of the concubines, and Tamar was their sister.<sup>10</sup>The son of Solomon was Rehoboam, Abijah his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son,<sup>11</sup>Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son,<sup>12</sup>Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son,<sup>13</sup>Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son,<sup>14</sup>Amon his son, Josiah his son.<sup>15</sup>The sons of Josiah: Johanan the firstborn, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, the fourth Shallum.<sup>16</sup>The descendants of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son;<sup>17</sup>and the sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son,<sup>18</sup>Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah;<sup>19</sup>and the sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei; and the sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah, and Shelomith was their sister;<sup>20</sup>and Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed, five.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah, his son Rephaiah, his son Arnan, his son Obadiah, his son Shecaniah.<sup>22</sup>The son of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. And the sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat, six.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam, three.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani, seven.
3.overview:
David's family is set out in three movements: the sons born at Hebron and Jerusalem, closing on his daughter Tamar (vv. 1-9); the throne handed from Solomon to Josiah in one unvarying formula (vv. 10-14); and the collapse and what came after it, Jeconiah the captive, Zerubbabel, and further generations of a royal house with no crown (vv. 15-24).

The chapter's weight is in its last verses, and they are the easiest to skim. A king list that keeps being written after the kingdom has fallen is not an administrative record but a community refusing to believe that God has given up on his promise.
3.theology:
God’s covenant with David was a promise with no conditions attached, but the way it worked out in history was painful. This chapter shows an unbroken succession through men who in many cases deserved to end it, and then the throne is lost and still the family line does not break. God does not always keep his word by preventing disaster; he keeps it through disaster, which is harder to watch and much harder to doubt afterwards.

The omissions matter too. Uriah is not in verse 5, and Manasseh's reign is not in verse 13. A genealogy answers one question: not what the fathers deserved, but whether the promise survived them.
3.examples:
Anani, the last man named here, ends the Old Testament's record of the house of David, and he did nothing anyone wrote down. Faithfulness in a family very often looks like that: someone in a bad century keeps the records, teaches the children, and never learns what it was for.

Every clerk who copied these names was working on the genealogy of Jesus of Nazareth, and not one of them knew it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six sons are born at Hebron, each named with his mother (vv. 1-3), and thirteen more at Jerusalem (vv. 5-8), the reign split across the two cities (v. 4). Four Jerusalem sons are by Bath-shua, Solomon the last of them (v. 5). The roll closes with a line that has no business in a list of sons: and Tamar was their sister (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: A register can be merciful in a way a narrative cannot: it tells the truth about who existed without retelling what they did.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone wronged within a family, it matters that God's record names Tamar and does not file her under her abuser: the Lord sees what was done (Psalm 10:14), and the abused should seek safety and help at once.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron: the firstborn, Amnon, by Ahinoam the Jezreelite; the second, Daniel, by Abigail the Carmelite, the third, Absalom, whose mother was Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth, Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth, Ithream, by his wife Eglah; six were born to him in Hebron, where he reigned for seven years and six months. And he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six sons and six mothers are given with a clerk's care, and three of the names are the reason David's old age was a misery. Amnon the firstborn raped his half-sister; Absalom killed him for it, seized the kingdom and died in a tree; Adonijah crowned himself while his father was still breathing. None of that is said. The register gives the names and moves on to the years of the reign.

The mothers are named because in a royal house a prince’s standing depended on who his mother was. Maacah, Absalom's mother, was a foreign princess, the daughter of the king of Geshur, which is where Absalom went when he had to run.

Some of David’s sons have two names in Scripture: Daniel is Chileab (2 Samuel 3:3), and Bath-shua is Bathsheba, with her father’s name in two forms.

verseByVerse.quote: These were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon, four by Bath-shua, the daughter of Ammiel; then Ibhar, Elishama, Eliphelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine. All these were David's sons, besides the sons of the concubines, and Tamar was their sister.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirteen sons in Jerusalem, and the first four are by Bath-shua, the daughter of Ammiel. That is Bathsheba, and Solomon is the fourth of her four.

The Chronicler says nothing of the rooftop, Uriah’s murder, Nathan’s rebuke or the child who died. He records a marriage that produced four sons, one of whom built the temple, and leaves the crime out of the register.

Matthew will not. At the same point in the line he leaves out the woman's name and writes that David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah (Matthew 1:6). One writer keeps the family's record; the other keeps the family's conscience, and Scripture gives both.

Then the last line: and Tamar was their sister. She is named after nineteen brothers, and what was done to her is left to another book. Here she is simply counted, which is more than her family managed at the time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — Fifteen Kings in Five Verses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Rehoboam to Josiah the throne is handed on in one formula, fifteen reigns in five verses with no assessment (vv. 10-14). Then Josiah's four sons (v. 15), and the collapse to Jeconiah his son (v. 16), the king who went to Babylon.
verseByVerse.theology: Everything Kings spends chapters weighing is compressed here into succession alone, to establish the one fact the exiles needed: the line held.
verseByVerse.examples: The worst king Judah ever had is a name in the middle of verse 13, with nothing said about him. Yet Chronicles alone will record that he humbled himself in captivity and God heard him (2 Chronicles 33:12–13): the line held, and so did mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: The son of Solomon was Rehoboam, Abijah his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son, Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son, Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son, Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son, Amon his son, Josiah his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five verses cover fifteen kings without one word of judgment on any of them. Elsewhere these reigns are weighed at length; here the formula never varies, and Asa the reformer and Ahaz who burned his children get the same three words.

To a man reading this in a ruined city, the question was not which ancestors had been admirable but whether the chain had held from Solomon to the burning of Jerusalem, and this list answers without adjectives: it did. God's faithfulness to a promise is not measured by the quality of the people it passes through; if it were, it would have stopped at verse 11.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Josiah: Johanan the firstborn, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, the fourth Shallum. The descendants of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son;
verseByVerse.commentary:
With Josiah's four sons the succession goes wrong immediately. Johanan the firstborn never reigns, and Judah burns through four kings in twenty-three years, three of them brothers.

Josiah was the best king since David (2 Kings 23:25), and these are his sons. A good father cannot guarantee the generation after him, and a grieving parent need not read that as his own failure.

Jeremiah said none of Jeconiah’s offspring would sit on David’s throne (Jeremiah 22:30). Jesus is Jeconiah’s heir through Joseph, his legal father (Matthew 1:11–12, 16), but, born of a virgin, not Joseph’s physical son, and Luke traces his descent through Nathan, another son of David (Luke 3:31). Luke also names a Shealtiel and a Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27); whether they are the same men is debated, and some think the branches joined by marriage or adoption. Either way, the throne passed to a Son of David in a way that kept God’s word on every side.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Line That Keeps Going After the Throne Is Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeconiah is given a title rather than a kingdom, the captive (v. 17), and the register carries on: Shealtiel, Pedaiah, Zerubbabel who rebuilt the temple (v. 19), and further generations of men who never ruled anything, down to Anani (vv. 21-24).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise to David did not depend on his descendants holding office. Keeping this list for generations after the throne was gone was an act of faith in a covenant.
verseByVerse.examples: When God's promises seem to have gone quiet, remember this line: it does not end in a blaze but trails off into names nobody remembers, and it stays alive there.

verseByVerse.quote: and the sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah; and the sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei; and the sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah, and Shelomith was their sister; and Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed, five.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The captive is a title now. He was eighteen when he surrendered Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:8; most Hebrew copies of 2 Chronicles 36:9 read eight, probably a copying slip), spent thirty-seven years in a Babylonian prison, and the register of the house of David identifies him by his captivity.

Yet the line does not stop. Zerubbabel came home with the first company and laid the foundation of the second temple while old men who remembered the first wept out loud.

Here Zerubbabel is the son of Pedaiah; Ezra, Haggai and Matthew call him the son of Shealtiel. A likely explanation is the law for exactly this case (Deuteronomy 25:5–6): Shealtiel died without a son, his brother raised up an heir to his name, and Zerubbabel was legally the one man's son and biologically the other's.
verseByVerse.note: Jeconiah is Jehoiachin. Zerubbabel was a leader of the first return from exile (Ezra 2:2; 3:2).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah, his son Rephaiah, his son Arnan, his son Obadiah, his son Shecaniah. The son of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. And the sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat, six. The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam, three. The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani, seven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Zerubbabel the register keeps writing, down to seven brothers, the last of whom is Anani. Generations past the last event the Old Testament records, somebody was still keeping the papers of the house of David. (The Hebrew of verse 21 is hard to follow, and the Greek Old Testament reads it as one line of fathers and sons, so counts after Zerubbabel range from about six generations to eleven.)

There was no throne, no army, a Persian governor in the citadel, and one reason not to let the record lapse: God had said of David's son I will establish his throne forever (17:12), and men who could see no evidence of it went on writing down the names.

They were right to. Four centuries later a young woman in Nazareth was told that God would give her son the throne of his father David (Luke 1:32), and Matthew opened his Gospel by running this list forward until it arrived at Joseph, a carpenter, the husband of Mary. The clerks who kept this chapter going in the dark were keeping the family line of the King.

4.title: Judah and Simeon: Names Preserved, Prayers Answered
4.text: <sup>1</sup>The sons of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal.<sup>2</sup>Reaiah the son of Shobal fathered Jahath, and Jahath fathered Ahumai and Lahad. These were the clans of the Zorathites.<sup>3</sup>These were the sons of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash; and the name of their sister was Hazzelelponi,<sup>4</sup>and Penuel fathered Gedor, and Ezer fathered Hushah. These were the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, the father of Bethlehem.<sup>5</sup>Ashhur, the father of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Naarah;<sup>6</sup>Naarah bore him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Helah: Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan.<sup>8</sup>Koz fathered Anub, Zobebah, and the clans of Aharhel, the son of Harum.<sup>9</sup>Jabez was more honorable than his brothers; and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, "Because I bore him in pain."<sup>10</sup>Jabez called upon the God of Israel, saying, "Oh that you would bless me and enlarge my border, and that your hand might be with me, and that you would keep me from harm so that it might not bring me pain!" And God granted what he asked.<sup>11</sup>Chelub, the brother of Shuhah, fathered Mehir, who fathered Eshton.<sup>12</sup>Eshton fathered Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, the father of Ir-nahash. These are the men of Recah.<sup>13</sup>The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah; and the sons of Othniel: Hathath and Meonothai.<sup>14</sup>Meonothai fathered Ophrah; and Seraiah fathered Joab, the father of Ge-harashim, so-called because they were craftsmen.<sup>15</sup>The sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh: Iru, Elah, and Naam; and the son of Elah: Kenaz.<sup>16</sup>The sons of Jehallelel: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel.<sup>17</sup>The sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. These are the sons of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered married; and she conceived and bore Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa.<sup>18</sup>And his Judahite wife bore Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah.<sup>19</sup>The sons of the wife of Hodiah, the sister of Naham, were the fathers of Keilah the Garmite and Eshtemoa the Maacathite.<sup>20</sup>The sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-hanan, and Tilon. The sons of Ishi: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Shelah the son of Judah: Er the father of Lecah, Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the clans of the house of linen workers at Beth-ashbea;<sup>22</sup>and Jokim, and the men of Cozeba, and Joash, and Saraph, who ruled in Moab and returned to Lehem (now the records are ancient).<sup>23</sup>These were the potters who were inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah. They lived there in the king's service.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, Shaul;<sup>25</sup>Shallum was his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son.<sup>26</sup>The sons of Mishma: Hammuel his son, Zaccur his son, Shimei his son.<sup>27</sup>Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters; but his brothers did not have many children, nor did all their clan multiply like the men of Judah.<sup>28</sup>They lived in Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual,<sup>29</sup>Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad,<sup>30</sup>Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag,<sup>31</sup>Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susim, Beth-biri, and Shaaraim. These were their cities until David reigned.<sup>32</sup>And their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan, five cities,<sup>33</sup>along with all their villages that were around these cities as far as Baal. These were their settlements, and they kept a genealogical record.<sup>34</sup>Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah the son of Amaziah,<sup>35</sup>Joel, Jehu the son of Joshibiah, son of Seraiah, son of Asiel,<sup>36</sup>Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah,<sup>37</sup>Ziza the son of Shiphi, son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah—<sup>38</sup>these mentioned by name were princes in their clans, and their fathers' houses increased greatly.<sup>39</sup>They journeyed to the entrance of Gedor, to the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks,<sup>40</sup>where they found rich, good pasture, and the land was very broad, quiet, and peaceful, for the former inhabitants there belonged to Ham.<sup>41</sup>These, registered by name, came in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and destroyed their tents and the Meunites who were found there, and marked them for destruction to this day, and settled in their place, because there was pasture there for their flocks.<sup>42</sup>And some of them, five hundred men of the Simeonites, went to Mount Seir, having as their leaders Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi.<sup>43</sup>And they defeated the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped, and they have lived there to this day.
4.overview:
The chapter runs Judah a second time by clans rather than by kings (vv. 1-23), and then gives Simeon his own short record (vv. 24-43). In the middle of Judah's clans the list halts for two verses on a man called Jabez, who prays and is answered (vv. 9-10), the first prayer in nine chapters of names.

Around him are people the narrative books never mention: an Egyptian princess (v. 17), linen workers and potters (vv. 21-23), a fading tribe that kept its records anyway (v. 33), and five hundred men who finished a war Saul had abandoned (vv. 42-43).
4.theology:
Jabez is the centre of the chapter’s teaching and easily mishandled in two ways: his prayer is neither a formula (see vv. 9-10) nor an oddity to be embarrassed by. God is presented as the rest of Scripture presents him, able to be asked and pleased to answer.

The second theme is providence working through decline. Simeon shrinks and is absorbed, and yet its princes' houses increase and its men complete an unfinished command of God.
4.examples:
A reader who was handed the Jabez prayer as a method and found that his own borders did not move has been badly served. Jabez asked for a specific thing out of a specific pain, and rested it all on that your hand might be with me. A prayer built on that clause can survive not getting what it asked for. A prayer that rests on getting more land cannot.

And the man whose name sounded like pain, who asked to be kept from it, belongs to the tribe of one who was named before birth as the one who would save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). He asked his Father in a garden whether the cup could pass, and it did not. He bore the pain, and because he did, everyone who is his can pray with Jabez's confidence that God's hand is with them: the Father who did not spare his own Son will not withhold what is truly good (Romans 8:32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Judah's Clans, and the Prayer of Jabez
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah's line is worked through a second time, sideways, by clans and households (vv. 1-8), with Hur again the father of Bethlehem (v. 4). Then the list stops dead for two verses: a man named for his mother's pain prays one sentence, and God granted what he asked (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer breaks into the record. This is the first prayer in nine chapters of names, and one of only two answered prayers in them; the other is in the next chapter (5:20).
verseByVerse.examples: If you carry a name, a past or a wound that someone else gave you, Jabez shows what to do with it: take it to God. He asks not for escape from the name but for blessing inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal. Reaiah the son of Shobal fathered Jahath, and Jahath fathered Ahumai and Lahad. These were the clans of the Zorathites. These were the sons of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash; and the name of their sister was Hazzelelponi, and Penuel fathered Gedor, and Ezer fathered Hushah. These were the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, the father of Bethlehem. Ashhur, the father of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Naarah; Naarah bore him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah. The sons of Helah: Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan. Koz fathered Anub, Zobebah, and the clans of Aharhel, the son of Harum.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah is traced again from a different angle, sideways across the tribe, clan by clan and town by town. Bethlehem surfaces again (v. 4), still a village belonging to Hur. And a sister is named in verse 3, Hazzelelponi, with nothing recorded about her but that somebody knew her name.

This is what most of a nation's history looks like from the inside: households, villages, a trade, a well, and far more people than ever reach the narrative books.

verseByVerse.quote: Jabez was more honorable than his brothers; and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, "Because I bore him in pain." Jabez called upon the God of Israel, saying, "Oh that you would bless me and enlarge my border, and that your hand might be with me, and that you would keep me from harm so that it might not bring me pain!" And God granted what he asked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After nine chapters of names, the list stops and a man speaks. He is introduced by his mother's suffering. Whatever happened at that birth, his mother named the child after it, and he carried a name that sounded like the word for pain every time anyone called him to dinner.

What he does with it is the point. He makes four requests, and the last answers his own name: keep me from pain.

The middle two are the substance. Enlarge my border sits in a chapter of land allocations; it is a farmer asking for ground. That your hand might be with me is what the request rests on, and it makes the other three safe to pray.

This prayer has been sold as a technique, and the chapter refuses that reading: around Jabez are dozens of men given no enlargement, and the register does not suggest they failed to say the words. What is recorded is that a man in pain asked the God of Israel for something specific, and the God of Israel is the kind of God who can be asked. Nor is it a promise of being spared pain or given property: Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed and was given grace instead (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and that too was an answer.

And God granted what he asked: the God of nine chapters of silent record-keeping had been listening the whole time.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew the name Jabez transposes two letters of the word for pain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–23 — Craftsmen, Potters, and Pharaoh's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The clans run on through Othniel the judge (v. 13), a valley of craftsmen (v. 14), and Caleb (v. 15). Mered marries Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh (v. 17), and the section closes with linen workers and royal potters (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: God's family has always been less tidy than its members would like, and that is good news for outsiders.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, ordinary work done well is part of God's record. Clans of Judah are remembered for linen and clay rather than battles (vv. 21-23).

verseByVerse.quote: Chelub, the brother of Shuhah, fathered Mehir, who fathered Eshton. Eshton fathered Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, the father of Ir-nahash. These are the men of Recah. The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah; and the sons of Othniel: Hathath and Meonothai. Meonothai fathered Ophrah; and Seraiah fathered Joab, the father of Ge-harashim, so-called because they were craftsmen. The sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh: Iru, Elah, and Naam; and the son of Elah: Kenaz. The sons of Jehallelel: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel. The sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. These are the sons of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered married; and she conceived and bore Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa. And his Judahite wife bore Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. The sons of the wife of Hodiah, the sister of Naham, were the fathers of Keilah the Garmite and Eshtemoa the Maacathite. The sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-hanan, and Tilon. The sons of Ishi: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two names stand out. Othniel is here (v. 13), Israel's first judge, who married Achsah, the woman who asked for springs (2:49). And a valley is named for its trade, because they were craftsmen (v. 14).

Then comes a marriage with no explanation. Mered's wife Bithiah is the daughter of Pharaoh (v. 17), given a Hebrew name that appears to mean daughter of the LORD. Like the Egyptian slave of 2:34-35, she is written into the family of the Messiah, and the Chronicler never stops to justify it. He will not let the record be tidier than the family was.
verseByVerse.note: “Ge-harashim” means “valley of craftsmen” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Shelah the son of Judah: Er the father of Lecah, Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the clans of the house of linen workers at Beth-ashbea; and Jokim, and the men of Cozeba, and Joash, and Saraph, who ruled in Moab and returned to Lehem (now the records are ancient). These were the potters who were inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah. They lived there in the king's service.
verseByVerse.commentary: Weavers and potters working for the crown are written into the genealogy of the royal tribe alongside princes and judges, and the register does not rank them below the princes or below Jabez. A way of reading Scripture that treats one as important and the other as filler is not the Chronicler's.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–43 — Simeon: The Tribe That Shrank
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Simeon's genealogy is short: its clans did not multiply like Judah's (v. 27), and its towns are dated until David reigned (v. 31). Then two expeditions: to Gedor for pasture in Hezekiah's day (vv. 34-41), and to Mount Seir against the last of the Amalekites (vv. 42-43).
verseByVerse.theology: The same judgment can fall on two people and God may do different things with each. Jacob's words scattered Simeon and Levi alike (see vv. 24-27).
verseByVerse.examples: A believer in a dwindling congregation or a family that seems to be fading can take heart from Simeon. The decline is written down honestly, but it is not the last word: a tribe going down is not a tribe God has finished using.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, Shaul; Shallum was his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son. The sons of Mishma: Hammuel his son, Zaccur his son, Shimei his son. Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters; but his brothers did not have many children, nor did all their clan multiply like the men of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon's genealogy is short, and verse 27 gives the reason out loud, that their clan did not multiply like the men of Judah: a hard sentence to have in your family papers. One man has sixteen sons and six daughters, and even he cannot lift the average. The tribe is fading while the record is kept, and the record says so.

Jacob had said it would be like this, for their violence at Shechem (Genesis 49:5–7). Levi was scattered into the priesthood and given the LORD himself as an inheritance; Simeon was scattered into Judah and slowly disappeared.

verseByVerse.quote: They lived in Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad, Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susim, Beth-biri, and Shaaraim. These were their cities until David reigned. And their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan, five cities, along with all their villages that were around these cities as far as Baal. These were their settlements, and they kept a genealogical record.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until David reigned: after that these were no longer Simeon's towns. They lay inside Judah's territory, and in the end the tribe was absorbed by the neighbour it lived among.

The last thing said about them is that they kept a genealogical record (v. 33): a shrinking tribe went on writing down who its people were, which is why they are in this chapter at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah the son of Amaziah, Joel, Jehu the son of Joshibiah, son of Seraiah, son of Asiel, Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah, Ziza the son of Shiphi, son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah— these mentioned by name were princes in their clans, and their fathers' houses increased greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirteen princes are named, and the reason for naming them is at the end: these mentioned by name were princes in their clans, and their fathers' houses increased greatly.

So there was increase in a tribe that did not increase. The Chronicler will not let the general statement hide the families that did grow, the same care he showed the men who died childless in chapter 2.

verseByVerse.quote: They journeyed to the entrance of Gedor, to the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks, where they found rich, good pasture, and the land was very broad, quiet, and peaceful, for the former inhabitants there belonged to Ham. These, registered by name, came in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and destroyed their tents and the Meunites who were found there, and marked them for destruction to this day, and settled in their place, because there was pasture there for their flocks. And some of them, five hundred men of the Simeonites, went to Mount Seir, having as their leaders Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi. And they defeated the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped, and they have lived there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two expeditions close the chapter, men from a tribe with too little land going out to find some. One party came back with grazing land in Hezekiah's reign. The other came back having destroyed the last of a people Saul was told to destroy, the remnant of the Amalekites.

That clause finishes something: Amalek entered this book as a name (1:36); Saul was ordered to destroy it and spared its king and the best of the sheep (1 Samuel 15). Generations later five hundred men of the smallest tribe finish the job, with no song and no prophet present.

God's purposes do not lapse when the man commissioned to carry them out refuses. They are handed on, quietly, to people nobody remembers, and completed.

The Simeonites struck the Amalekites, whom God had placed under judgment for attacking the faint and weary at the back of Israel's column (Exodus 17:14; Deuteronomy 25:17–19; 1 Samuel 15:2), and seized pastureland. Chronicles records what happened; it is no pattern for taking land or for violence today. That judgment belonged to Israel's unique calling under the old covenant; the church's warfare is not against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12), and its King conquers by the gospel.

5.title: Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh: Faithfulness and Failure East of the Jordan
5.text: <sup>1</sup>The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel, so that he could not be enrolled as the oldest son;<sup>2</sup>though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph),<sup>3</sup>the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.<sup>4</sup>The sons of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son,<sup>5</sup>Micah his son, Reaiah his son, Baal his son,<sup>6</sup>Beerah his son, whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile; he was a chief of the Reubenites.<sup>7</sup>And his kinsmen by their clans, when the genealogy of their generations was recorded: the chief, Jeiel, and Zechariah,<sup>8</sup>and Bela the son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel, who lived in Aroer, as far as Nebo and Baal-meon.<sup>9</sup>He also lived to the east as far as the entrance of the desert this side of the Euphrates, because their livestock had multiplied in the land of Gilead.<sup>10</sup>And in the days of Saul they waged war against the Hagrites, who fell into their hand. And they lived in their tents throughout all the region east of Gilead.<sup>11</sup>The sons of Gad lived over against them in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah:<sup>12</sup>Joel the chief, Shapham the second, Janai, and Shaphat in Bashan.<sup>13</sup>And their kinsmen according to their fathers' houses: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia and Eber, seven.<sup>14</sup>These were the sons of Abihail the son of Huri, son of Jaroah, son of Gilead, son of Michael, son of Jeshishai, son of Jahdo, son of Buz.<sup>15</sup>Ahi the son of Abdiel, son of Guni, was chief in their fathers' houses,<sup>16</sup>and they lived in Gilead, in Bashan and in its towns, and in all the pasturelands of Sharon to their limits.<sup>17</sup>All of these were recorded in genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel.<sup>18</sup>The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had valiant men who carried shield and sword, and drew the bow, expert in war, 44,760, able to go to war.<sup>19</sup>They waged war against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab.<sup>20</sup>And when they prevailed over them, the Hagrites and all who were with them were given into their hands, for they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him.<sup>21</sup>They carried off their livestock: 50,000 of their camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys, and 100,000 men alive.<sup>22</sup>For many fell, because the war was of God. And they lived in their place until the exile.<sup>23</sup>The members of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They were very numerous from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon.<sup>24</sup>These were the heads of their fathers' houses: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty warriors, famous men, heads of their fathers' houses.<sup>25</sup>But they broke faith with the God of their fathers, and whored after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them.<sup>26</sup>So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, the spirit of Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, and he took them into exile, namely, the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and brought them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river Gozan, to this day.
5.overview:
The two and a half tribes east of the Jordan: Reuben, with the reason the firstborn's birthright went elsewhere (vv. 1-10); Gad, surveyed in the eighth century (vv. 11-17); their victory over the Hagrites (vv. 18-22); and half-Manasseh, ending in idolatry and deportation (vv. 23-26).

The chapter turns on a reversal: a prayer answered in battle (v. 20), then the same people breaking faith with the God who answered it (v. 25). Between the two lies the book's account of why a nation with such a history ended up in exile.
5.theology:
Verse 20 shows prayer and skill working together, and the Chronicler feels no tension between them. Human skill is not a rival to God’s action; it is one of the ways God acts.

Verse 26 says the same about judgment. God stirred up a pagan king, the king did what pagan kings do, and the exile was both Assyrian policy and divine act. The book will need this when it explains why Jerusalem fell: not that God lost, but that God was acting in judgment.
5.examples:
Read verse 20 beside verse 25. A man can look back on a time he cried out and was heard and treat the memory as proof that he stands well with God. These tribes had such a memory, and it did not keep their descendants faithful.

What holds is not the memory of an answered prayer but the God who answered it, and he was as present in the deportation as in the victory. That is the comfort for anyone whose own record has broken down: God's faithfulness, not ours, is what keeps his people, and the way back for those who have wandered is the confession he has always heard (Psalm 32:5). The tribes carried into Assyria did not stop being his: their names are in this chapter, written in Jerusalem centuries after their nation had ceased to exist. And the northern tribes were never wholly lost: when the infant Christ was brought to the temple, Anna, a prophetess of the tribe of Asher, was there to give thanks and speak of him (Luke 2:36–38).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens by explaining why Reuben, the firstborn, lost the birthright (vv. 1-2), then traces his clans east of the Jordan, down to a chief carried away by Tiglath-pileser (vv. 3-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The birthright, the double portion and the throne are separated here. Reuben lost all of it by one act; Joseph received the inheritance and Judah the crown, and neither was the eldest. Putting the eldest son first is the world's way of ordering a family, and God overrules it in nearly every generation of this book.
verseByVerse.examples: A single night's sin cost Reuben's descendants a status they never recovered, though the register still names him first.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel, so that he could not be enrolled as the oldest son; though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph),
verseByVerse.commentary:
These two verses answer a question the book raised three chapters ago.

Why does a genealogy of Israel start with Judah, who was fourth? Because Reuben, who was first, defiled his father's couch (he slept with his father's concubine), and his birthright went to the sons of Joseph. And yet, the Chronicler adds, the birthright and the crown did not travel together: though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph.

So the double portion went to one brother and the throne to another, and the eldest got neither. Nothing in this family has ever been decided by the order of birth.
