Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Judah and Joseph over Reuben, David over seven brothers: by now God's passing over the obvious man is not a surprise but a signature. The chief who came from Judah was David, and at the end of the line stands the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David (Revelation 5:5).
verseByVerse.note: The firstborn’s rights were split: the double portion went to Joseph, the leadership to Judah.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. The sons of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son, Micah his son, Reaiah his son, Baal his son, Beerah his son, whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile; he was a chief of the Reubenites. And his kinsmen by their clans, when the genealogy of their generations was recorded: the chief, Jeiel, and Zechariah, and Bela the son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel, who lived in Aroer, as far as Nebo and Baal-meon. He also lived to the east as far as the entrance of the desert this side of the Euphrates, because their livestock had multiplied in the land of Gilead. And in the days of Saul they waged war against the Hagrites, who fell into their hand. And they lived in their tents throughout all the region east of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben spread east into Gilead because its livestock multiplied: good grazing on the wrong side of the river, chosen back in Numbers when Reuben and Gad asked not to cross over.

It was a reasonable request, and it put them first in the path of anything coming from the north. Verse 6 records the result almost in passing, a chief carried into exile by Assyria, and the empire that ended the northern tribes enters this book inside a list of fathers and sons.

A decision about pasture, taken for sound reasons by men who meant no harm, set the geography that centuries later decided who went into captivity first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The War That Was of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gad's clans are set beside Reuben's in Bashan and Gilead (vv. 11-17). Then the fighting strength of the two and a half tribes, 44,760 men expert in war, and a campaign against the Hagrites won because they cried out to God in the battle; the reason is given flatly: the war was of God (vv. 18-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 20 puts prayer in the right order: they cried out, and he granted it because they trusted. Trust is the reason, crying out the act; neither numbers nor expertise is offered as the explanation.
verseByVerse.examples: Someone good at their work can pray in the middle of it as earnestly as anyone; expertise does not make prayer unnecessary.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Gad lived over against them in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah: Joel the chief, Shapham the second, Janai, and Shaphat in Bashan. And their kinsmen according to their fathers' houses: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia and Eber, seven. These were the sons of Abihail the son of Huri, son of Jaroah, son of Gilead, son of Michael, son of Jeshishai, son of Jahdo, son of Buz. Ahi the son of Abdiel, son of Guni, was chief in their fathers' houses, and they lived in Gilead, in Bashan and in its towns, and in all the pasturelands of Sharon to their limits. All of these were recorded in genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The record of Gad was compiled under Jotham and Jeroboam (v. 17).

That administrative note is quietly remarkable. Someone surveyed the tribes east of the Jordan in the eighth century BC, the document outlived those tribes, and a scribe in Jerusalem still had it three hundred years later, after his own city had burned.

verseByVerse.quote: The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had valiant men who carried shield and sword, and drew the bow, expert in war, 44,760, able to go to war. They waged war against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. And when they prevailed over them, the Hagrites and all who were with them were given into their hands, for they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him. They carried off their livestock: 50,000 of their camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys, and 100,000 men alive. For many fell, because the war was of God. And they lived in their place until the exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The battle is described twice, once in terms of the army and once in terms of God, and the two accounts do not compete. The crying out happens in the battle itself, not the night before or at a shrine, by men who were themselves expert.

The plunder is counted like an inventory, and the explanation is five words long: the war was of God.

Does that make any war a holy war? No. This was the covenant nation defending the land God had given it, and the Chronicler records that God gave the victory. No nation today stands in Israel's place, and Christ's people fight with the gospel and prayer (Ephesians 6:12–18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — And Then They Broke Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Half-Manasseh is numerous and famous (v. 24). Then the sentence the chapter has been walking towards: they broke faith (v. 25), and the tribes east of the Jordan went into exile first (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler's verb returns. Achan broke faith and Israel lost a battle; these tribes lost a territory; Judah will lose the temple (9:1); Saul lost a kingdom (10:13). One word carries the book's account of why things went wrong.
verseByVerse.examples: Assyria is not the subject of verse 26. God is. The king who deported them was stirred up by the God they had left, a more frightening reading of the news than the political one.

verseByVerse.quote: The members of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They were very numerous from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon. These were the heads of their fathers' houses: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty warriors, famous men, heads of their fathers' houses. But they broke faith with the God of their fathers, and whored after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them. So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, the spirit of Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, and he took them into exile, namely, the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and brought them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river Gozan, to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Half-Manasseh is numerous and famous, and the chapter has gone well since verse 18. Then one word, But, turns it over.

The sting is the last clause: they took up the worship of nations that were no longer there, nations God had removed for that very worship.

Set verse 25 against verse 20 and the chapter's real subject appears. The men who cried out to God in the battle and were heard have, generations later, become the people worshipping the gods of the nations round them. An answered prayer is no guarantee of faithfulness. It settles nothing about the next generation, or about the next decade of the same generation.

So the tribes who had asked for the land east of the river were the first to lose it. Assyria is not the actor but the tool: the God who granted their plea in verse 20 is the God who moved Assyria in verse 26. He was not less faithful in the judgment than he had been in the victory.
verseByVerse.note: Pul is another name for Tiglath-pileser III.

pasturelands,<sup>81</sup>Heshbon with its pasturelands, and Jazer with its pasturelands.
6.overview:
The longest chapter in the book does three things. It runs the high-priestly line from Aaron to the man who went to Babylon (vv. 1-15). It traces the three Levite clans and, within them, the singers David appointed, Heman, Asaph and Ethan (vv. 16-48). And it maps the forty-eight towns given to a tribe with no land (vv. 49-81), with one verse stating what the tribe existed to do: make atonement for Israel (v. 49).

Two things are buried in it: Samuel’s line runs back to the rebel Korah, and Samuel’s grandson Heman is the chief musician (vv. 22-33); and the landless tribe holds all six cities of refuge (vv. 57, 67).
6.theology:
Two offices stand on equal footing. Priests offered blood, singers offered song; both were appointed, both had to prove descent, both are recorded with the same care. Israel's worship was never a service with music added.

Underneath the whole tribe lies verse 49: atonement is why Levi exists, and it was work that no offering ever finished.
6.examples:
Korah's descendants are the pastoral centre of this chapter (vv. 22-33). Nobody chooses his ancestor, and the children of a rebel became a prophet's family and the singers of the house he had tried to storm. No family history puts a person beyond God's mercy.

Every name in this chapter served a system that pointed beyond itself. The priests stood daily at the altar because no sacrifice could take away sins; Christ, a priest for ever, offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:23–27). The singers sang before an ark; the church sings to the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The High Priests, Down to the Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The line runs from Levi through Kohath and Amram to Aaron, Moses, and Miriam (v. 3), then follows Aaron's third son Eleazar, because the first two died before the LORD, through Phinehas and Zadok (v. 8) for twenty-two generations. It ends with Jehozadak going into exile by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The priesthood was handed from father to son, not chosen as a career, and the line is unbroken from Sinai to Babylon. The list stops at the deportation without comment, but a line that goes into exile has not ended (see v. 15).
verseByVerse.examples: A family record that keeps Nadab and Abihu in it is honest: the register does not tidy away the members whose story ended badly.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. The children of Amram: Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of Levi's three sons the chapter follows the middle one, and of Amram's children it follows Aaron and lets Moses go.

That is startling editing. The man who brought Israel out of Egypt is named once, between his brother and sister, and the line this book needs runs through the priest, not the prophet. (In Hebrew Bibles verses 1–15 are numbered 5:27–41.)

Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorised fire and died before the altar. The register names them with no word about it, lists them because they were born, and passes on to Eleazar because the priesthood did.

verseByVerse.quote: Eleazar fathered Phinehas, Phinehas fathered Abishua, Abishua fathered Bukki, Bukki fathered Uzzi, Uzzi fathered Zerahiah, Zerahiah fathered Meraioth, Meraioth fathered Amariah, Amariah fathered Ahitub, Ahitub fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Ahimaaz,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten generations, and two of the names have large stories behind them.

Phinehas drove a spear through an Israelite and a Midianite woman in the middle of a plague and was given a covenant of perpetual priesthood (Numbers 25:7–13). His zeal for God’s honour ended a plague of judgment. It belonged to Israel under the old covenant and is never a licence for private violence. Zadok went out with David when Absalom took the city and carried the ark back at David's command, and his house held the high priesthood until the time of the Maccabees, in the second century BC.

Neither story is told. The list records only who held the office and handed it on. What a man did in it belongs to the narrative books.

verseByVerse.quote: Ahimaaz fathered Azariah, Azariah fathered Johanan, and Johanan fathered Azariah (it was he who served as priest in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem). Azariah fathered Amariah, Amariah fathered Ahitub, Ahitub fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Shallum, Shallum fathered Hilkiah, Hilkiah fathered Azariah, Azariah fathered Seraiah, Seraiah fathered Jehozadak; and Jehozadak went into exile when the LORD sent Judah and Jerusalem into exile by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-two generations, and then the sentence the list has been travelling towards. The LORD sent Judah into exile; Nebuchadnezzar was only the hand he used. Israel’s own priestly records describe the most powerful man in the world as an instrument. The Chronicler will not let his readers think of Babylon as a defeat that God suffered.

And then the list simply stops. No return, no restoration, no comment, though the men reading it knew perfectly well that Jehozadak's son Jeshua had come home with the first company and stood in the new courts. The line is left ending in captivity, and the readers are expected to supply the rest from memory, because they themselves, back in the land, are what happened next.

The list is not a complete roll. It leaves out Eli’s house, descended from Aaron’s youngest son Ithamar, and men such as Jehoiada; it traces Zadok's line, the line that came home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The three Levite clans are traced, with Korah and Samuel inside Kohath's branch (vv. 16-30). Then David's singers, with pedigrees as careful as any priest's: Heman in the centre, Samuel's grandson (v. 33); Asaph on his right (v. 39); Ethan on his left (v. 44); and the rest of the Levites for the service of the tabernacle (v. 48).
verseByVerse.theology: Music in Israel's worship is not an atmosphere or a preference. It is an office, with a charter from the king, a place in the building and a genealogy behind it.
verseByVerse.examples: Those who lead a church's singing today hold no hereditary office, but the principle stands: leading praise is a service to God and his people, not a performance, offered in response to the God who has already come near. It is rightly done with preparation and order (1 Corinthians 14:40), and with the word of Christ dwelling richly in those who sing (Colossians 3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Levi: Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. And these are the names of the sons of Gershom: Libni and Shimei. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their fathers. Of Gershom: Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son, Joah his son, Iddo his son, Zerah his son, Jeatherai his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The three clans again in more detail, because the priests were only one family inside Levi. The rest of the tribe were the Levites who served alongside them.

Gershom's and Merari's descendants have no office attached and no story told. These are the men who carried frames and curtains across a desert and then kept the doors and stores of a temple for four hundred years.

The register gives them the same treatment as the high priests. In the tribe that existed to serve near God, there was no second class.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Kohath: Amminadab his son, Korah his son, Assir his son, Elkanah his son, Ebiasaph his son, Assir his son, Tahath his son, Uriel his son, Uzziah his son, and Shaul his son. The sons of Elkanah: Amasai and Ahimoth, Elkanah his son, Zophai his son, Nahath his son, Eliab his son, Jeroham his son, Elkanah his son. The sons of Samuel: Joel his firstborn, the second Abijah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Kohath's branch stands a name that ought to stop the reader: Korah his son (v. 22).

Korah led the rebellion against Moses and Aaron, and the ground opened under him. Numbers records the earth closing over his household and then adds, ten chapters later, But the sons of Korah did not die (Numbers 26:11).

This is what became of them. The line runs on until it reaches the sons of Samuel (v. 28).

Samuel, the child who heard his name called in the dark at Shiloh and anointed Israel's first two kings, descends from the man who tried to seize the priesthood by force. Was Samuel a Levite or an Ephraimite? 1 Samuel 1:1 calls his father an Ephrathite of the hill country of Ephraim, which describes where the family lived; Levites lived among the other tribes, as the end of this chapter shows. This chapter tells where the family came from.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Merari: Mahli, Libni his son, Shimei his son, Uzzah his son, Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, and Asaiah his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Merari's line closes the section: seven names, no comment.

One is a name the reader will meet again. An Uzzah put out his hand to steady the ark on a new cart and died beside it (13:9–10). That Uzzah is probably not this man, but this list belongs to the tribe God charged with carrying the sanctuary: the Merarites its frames, the Kohathites the ark on poles (Numbers 4:15, 31). Chapter 13 is about what happens when it is carried the wrong way.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the men whom David put in charge of the service of song in the house of the LORD after the ark rested there. They ministered with song before the tabernacle of the tent of meeting until Solomon built the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they performed their service according to their order.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter changes subject, and a new office appears.

Song is a service, the word used of the sacrifices; it has an appointment from the king; and it begins after the ark rested there, a response to God's arrival, not a device for summoning him.

Verse 32 adds that they performed their service according to their order. Israel's praise was rostered, with a rota, a place to stand and a move from the tent to Solomon’s temple to manage, and none of that was thought to be in tension with its being worship.
verseByVerse.note: Heman, Asaph and Ethan (or Jeduthun) were the leading musicians; several psalms bear their names.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the men who served and their sons. Of the sons of the Kohathites: Heman the singer the son of Joel, son of Samuel, son of Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Eliel, son of Toah, son of Zuph, son of Elkanah, son of Mahath, son of Amasai, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Tahath, son of Assir, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief singer's pedigree runs back as far as the high priests' own: Heman the singer the son of Joel, son of Samuel, and therefore Korah's descendant.

The family whose father the earth swallowed for wanting a place at the altar was given, centuries later, a place in front of it with a harp. Eleven psalms carry the heading of the sons of Korah, the first of them the prayer of a soul panting after God as a deer pants for water (Psalm 42).

The register draws no attention to it. A reader who knows Numbers finds the mercy for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: and his brother Asaph, who stood on his right hand, namely, Asaph the son of Berechiah, son of Shimea, son of Michael, son of Baaseiah, son of Malchijah, son of Ethni, son of Zerah, son of Adaiah, son of Ethan, son of Zimmah, son of Shimei, son of Jahath, son of Gershom, son of Levi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asaph stood on his right hand, his line running through Gershom. The three chief singers came one from each clan, so no branch owned the music.

Asaph's name stands over twelve psalms, some of the bleakest in the book: one admits he almost stumbled from envying the wicked until he went into the sanctuary; another asks how long God will be angry with his people's prayers.

The man appointed over Israel's praise put his worst doubt into the hymn book, and Israel sang it for centuries. A man does not need to have every doubt settled before he leads God’s people in worship.

verseByVerse.quote: On the left hand were their brothers, the sons of Merari: Ethan the son of Kishi, son of Abdi, son of Malluch, son of Hashabiah, son of Amaziah, son of Hilkiah, son of Amzi, son of Bani, son of Shemer, son of Mahli, son of Mushi, son of Merari, son of Levi. And their brothers the Levites were appointed for all the service of the tabernacle of the house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ethan and the Merarites stood on the left hand: Kohath in the centre, Gershom right, Merari left.

Then verse 48, and the vast majority of the tribe: no names, no pedigrees, no instrument. One sentence covers thousands of men whose whole working lives were spent inside that building.

To be covered by that one sentence was no lesser gift. The service was the honour; being recorded was never the point of doing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–81 — Aaron's Altar, and Forty-Eight Towns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse states what the priests were for: to make atonement for Israel (v. 49). Aaron's line is repeated to Ahimaaz (vv. 50-53), and the chapter becomes a map: thirteen priestly towns out of Judah, Simeon and Benjamin (vv. 54-60), and the rest of Levi scattered across every tribe, forty-eight towns in all (vv. 61-81).
verseByVerse.theology: The one tribe with no territory held all six cities of refuge (vv. 57, 67): the tribe that served the altar of atonement also kept the shelters for the guilty.
verseByVerse.examples: Anathoth (v. 60) is a priestly town like any other. Centuries later Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, bought a field there with the Babylonian army outside the walls, as a sign that fields would be bought in this land again (Jeremiah 32:6–15).

verseByVerse.quote: But Aaron and his sons made offerings on the altar of burnt offering and on the altar of incense for all the work of the Most Holy Place, and to make atonement for Israel, according to all that Moses the servant of God had commanded. These are the sons of Aaron: Eleazar his son, Phinehas his son, Abishua his son, Bukki his son, Uzzi his son, Zerahiah his son, Meraioth his son, Amariah his son, Ahitub his son, Zadok his son, Ahimaaz his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After forty-eight verses of descent, one verse says what it was for: atonement. Everything else in the chapter, the towns, the singers, the twenty-two generations, exists around that one function: blood carried to an altar so that a guilty people could go on living beside a holy God. The Chronicler states it once, plainly, and goes back to the lists.

It took a whole tribe, a portable sanctuary, forty-eight towns and many centuries to keep that work going. And it was never finished, because the same offerings were made every morning and every evening for a thousand years, and every priest in this list died with the work still unfinished. The Son who ended it made one offering and sat down (Hebrews 10:11–12), and those who trust him stand before God on that finished work, not on their own.

verseByVerse.quote: These are their dwelling places according to their settlements within their borders: to the sons of Aaron of the clans of Kohathites, for theirs was the first lot, to them they gave Hebron in the land of Judah and its surrounding pasturelands, but the fields of the city and its villages they gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The map opens on Hebron, where Abraham buried Sarah and David reigned seven years.

Then a division that says a great deal in one verse. The priests were given the town and its pasturelands, but the fields and villages went to Caleb. Caleb had asked Joshua for that hill country at eighty-five, forty-five years after Moses promised it to him, on the ground that he had followed the LORD wholly. He got the farmland; the priests got the town and enough grass for their animals.

Nobody was cheated. The tribe that lived on the offerings needed no arable land, and the old soldier who had waited for a promise was not asked to give up his fields.

verseByVerse.quote: To the sons of Aaron they gave the cities of refuge: Hebron, Libnah with its pasturelands, Jattir, Eshtemoa with its pasturelands, Hilen with its pasturelands, Debir with its pasturelands, Ashan with its pasturelands, and Beth-shemesh with its pasturelands; and from the tribe of Benjamin, Gibeon, Geba with its pasturelands, Alemeth with its pasturelands, and Anathoth with its pasturelands. All their cities throughout their clans were thirteen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a phrase that changes what this list is: the cities of refuge.

A city of refuge was where a man who had killed somebody without meaning to could run and live. He fled to the gate, stated his case to the elders, and stayed inside the walls until the high priest died, safe from the avenger of blood, the dead man’s relative, who had the legal right to kill him outside. Six such towns were appointed in Israel, and the priests and Levites held all six.

So the tribe with no land of its own, whose office was atonement, was given custody of every place in the country where the killer could not be touched.

Many Christians have seen here a picture of Christ, and the New Testament gives them the language: believers are those who have fled for refuge to the hope set before them (Hebrews 6:18). The fugitive's freedom came by a high priest's death; the guilty sinner's comes by the death of the great High Priest, who lives for ever to keep those who have fled to him.

verseByVerse.quote: To the rest of the Kohathites were given by lot out of the clan of the tribe, out of the half-tribe, the half of Manasseh, ten cities. To the Gershomites according to their clans were allotted thirteen cities out of the tribes of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and Manasseh in Bashan. To the Merarites according to their clans were allotted twelve cities out of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun. So the people of Israel gave the Levites the cities with their pasturelands. They gave by lot out of the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin these cities that are mentioned by name.
verseByVerse.commentary: By lot. No tribe chose its Levites and no Levite his neighbours; the method that put a teaching family in every district took the decision out of everybody's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the clans of the sons of Kohath had cities of their territory out of the tribe of Ephraim. They were given the cities of refuge: Shechem with its pasturelands in the hill country of Ephraim, Gezer with its pasturelands, Jokmeam with its pasturelands, Beth-horon with its pasturelands, Aijalon with its pasturelands, Gath-rimmon with its pasturelands, and out of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Aner with its pasturelands, and Bileam with its pasturelands, for the rest of the clans of the Kohathites. To the Gershomites were given out of the clan of the half-tribe of Manasseh: Golan in Bashan with its pasturelands and Ashtaroth with its pasturelands;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The refuge formula returns with Shechem (v. 67), where Joshua gathered Israel to choose whom they would serve and Joseph's bones were buried, and Golan in Bashan (v. 71).

Every town here belonged to somebody else: Ephraim and Manasseh gave up settlements they had fought for, so the tribe with no inheritance could live among them.

verseByVerse.quote: and out of the tribe of Issachar: Kedesh with its pasturelands, Daberath with its pasturelands, Ramoth with its pasturelands, and Anem with its pasturelands; out of the tribe of Asher: Mashal with its pasturelands, Abdon with its pasturelands, Hukok with its pasturelands, and Rehob with its pasturelands; and out of the tribe of Naphtali: Kedesh in Galilee with its pasturelands, Hammon with its pasturelands, and Kiriathaim with its pasturelands. To the rest of the Merarites were allotted out of the tribe of Zebulun: Rimmono with its pasturelands, Tabor with its pasturelands, and beyond the Jordan at Jericho, on the east side of the Jordan, out of the tribe of Reuben: Bezer in the wilderness with its pasturelands, Jahzah with its pasturelands, Kedemoth with its pasturelands, and Mephaath with its pasturelands; and out of the tribe of Gad: Ramoth in Gilead with its pasturelands, Mahanaim with its pasturelands, Heshbon with its pasturelands, and Jazer with its pasturelands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last three cities of refuge are here: Kedesh (v. 76), Bezer (v. 78) and Ramoth in Gilead (v. 80). Forty-eight towns, none in Levi's own country, because Levi had none.

Every other tribe walked away from the division of the land holding a map: this valley, that ridge, the olive terraces, the well. Levi was handed no acres, no boundary stones, no deed. What he was given instead was a house in each of his brothers' territories, enough grass for the animals, and a promise that the LORD himself was his portion.

The arrangement was practical as well as theological: scatter the teaching tribe across every border and no family in Israel lives far from a man whose whole life is the law of God.

The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God.

7.title: The Northern Tribes: Every Name Counted

And the sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah, all five of them were chief men.<sup>4</sup>And along with them, by their generations, according to their fathers' houses, were units of the army for war, 36,000, for they had many wives and sons.<sup>5</sup>Their kinsmen belonging to all the clans of Issachar were in all 87,000 mighty warriors, enrolled by genealogy.<sup>6</sup>The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Jediael, three.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Bela: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, and Iri, five, heads of fathers' houses, mighty warriors. And the sons of Bilhan: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar.<sup>11</sup>All these were the sons of Jediael according to the heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, 17,200, able to go to war.<sup>12</sup>And Shuppim and Huppim were the sons of Ir, Hushim the son of Aher.<sup>13</sup>The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer and Shallum, the descendants of Bilhah.<sup>14</sup>The sons of Manasseh: Asriel, whom his Aramean concubine bore; she bore Machir the father of Gilead.<sup>15</sup>And Machir took a wife for Huppim and for Shuppim. The name of his sister was Maacah. And the name of the second was Zelophehad, and Zelophehad had daughters.<sup>16</sup>And Maacah the wife of Machir bore a son, and she called his name Peresh; and the name of his brother was Sheresh; and his sons were Ulam and Rakem.<sup>17</sup>The son of Ulam: Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh.<sup>18</sup>And his sister Hammolecheth bore Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah.<sup>19</sup>The sons of Shemida were Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, and Aniam.<sup>20</sup>The sons of Ephraim: Shuthelah, and Bered his son, Tahath his son, Eleadah his son, Tahath his son,<sup>21</sup>Zabad his son, Shuthelah his son, and Ezer and Elead, whom the men of Gath who were born in the land killed, because they came down to raid their livestock.<sup>22</sup>And Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brothers came to comfort him.<sup>23</sup>And Ephraim went in to his wife, and she conceived and bore a son. In these lived the sons of Joseph the son of Israel.<sup>30</sup>The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah.<sup>31</sup>The sons of Beriah: Heber, and Malchiel, who fathered Birzaith.<sup>32</sup>Heber fathered Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and their sister Shua.<sup>33</sup>The sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the sons of Japhlet.<sup>34</sup>The sons of Shemer his brother: Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram.<sup>35</sup>The sons of Helem his brother: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal.<sup>36</sup>The sons of Zophah: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah.<sup>37</sup>Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera.<sup>38</sup>The sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara.<sup>39</sup>The sons of Ulla: Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia.<sup>40</sup>All of these were men of Asher, heads of fathers' houses, approved, mighty warriors, chiefs of the princes. Their number enrolled by genealogies, for service in war, was 26,000 men.
7.overview:
Six tribes in forty verses, mostly muster rolls: Issachar (vv. 1-5), Benjamin in brief (vv. 6-12), Naphtali in one line (v. 13), Manasseh (vv. 14-19), Ephraim (vv. 20-29) and Asher (vv. 30-40). Dan and Zebulun never receive a genealogy at all.

In the middle the list breaks open into one of the genealogies' rare stretches of narrative: Ephraim loses two sons in a cattle raid, mourns many days, and names the next child after the disaster (vv. 21-23); and his daughter Sheerah builds three towns, including the fortress at the pass (v. 24).
7.theology:
The numbers record past greatness, not present strength. The point is continuity: the small community reading this book is the same people as those tribes, and it remained that people because its identity never depended on its numbers.

Against that stands an honest gap, two tribes missing and unexplained (see vv. 36-40). The completeness belongs to God's memory, not Israel's paperwork.
7.examples:
Ephraim is the pastoral centre of the chapter. A father buried two young men, grieved a long time while his brothers sat with him, and carried the loss into the next child's name, and nobody in the text hurries him or suggests a believer should be further along by now.

The loss stays a loss; later blessings do not explain it away. But the household that grief nearly ended went on to produce Sheerah and Joshua (vv. 24, 27), and what God does after a disaster in a family is rarely visible to the generation that suffered it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four tribes handled briskly: Issachar's 87,000 mighty warriors (vv. 1-5); Benjamin's 59,434 (vv. 6-12); Naphtali in a single verse (v. 13); and Manasseh, whose line runs through Machir to a man with no sons: Zelophehad had daughters (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: These are counts of fighting men, kept by a community with no army, a record of what the tribes once were.
verseByVerse.examples: Five sisters once asked Moses that their father's name not disappear for want of a son, and the law was changed for them (Numbers 27:1–11). Speaking up for the overlooked is not presumption.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four. The sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their fathers' houses, namely of Tola, mighty warriors of their generations, their number in the days of David being 22,600. The son of Uzzi: Izrahiah. And the sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah, all five of them were chief men. And along with them, by their generations, according to their fathers' houses, were units of the army for war, 36,000, for they had many wives and sons. Their kinsmen belonging to all the clans of Issachar were in all 87,000 mighty warriors, enrolled by genealogy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Issachar’s entry reads like an army list: houses, chiefs and 87,000 men enrolled by genealogy.

These numbers are not pride. The men holding this book could not have raised a thousand soldiers. Jerusalem was a small town in a Persian province with a wall it had needed help to rebuild. These figures are a record of what the tribes had been, written by people who were now something much smaller.

One way of remembering a great past poisons the present; another steadies it. The difference is whether the memory is of what we were or of what God did, and the Chronicler keeps the credit with God.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Jediael, three. The sons of Bela: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, and Iri, five, heads of fathers' houses, mighty warriors. And their enrollment by genealogies was 22,034. The sons of Becher: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth. All these were the sons of Becher. And their enrollment by genealogies, according to their generations, as heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, was 20,200. The son of Jediael: Bilhan. And the sons of Bilhan: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar. All these were the sons of Jediael according to the heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, 17,200, able to go to war. And Shuppim and Huppim were the sons of Ir, Hushim the son of Aher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin briefly, a placeholder before its own chapter.

It carries a shadow. Benjamin was reduced to six hundred men hiding at a rock after the civil war in Judges 20, and these numbers are its recovery. That tribe produced Israel's first king, and later a Pharisee from Tarsus who listed being of the tribe of Benjamin among the things he counted as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus (Philippians 3:5–8).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer and Shallum, the descendants of Bilhah. The sons of Manasseh: Asriel, whom his Aramean concubine bore; she bore Machir the father of Gilead. And Machir took a wife for Huppim and for Shuppim. The name of his sister was Maacah. And the name of the second was Zelophehad, and Zelophehad had daughters. And Maacah the wife of Machir bore a son, and she called his name Peresh; and the name of his brother was Sheresh; and his sons were Ulam and Rakem. The son of Ulam: Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh. And his sister Hammolecheth bore Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah. The sons of Shemida were Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, and Aniam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naphtali is named as descended from Bilhah, Rachel’s servant, without apology.

Then, inside Manasseh's line, a clause that stops the eye: Zelophehad had daughters. Those five women argued their case before Moses and the assembly, and God told Moses they were right.

Here the whole affair is a few words in a genealogy, which is the fate of most things that changed the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–29 — Ephraim: A Father Who Mourned, and a Daughter Who Built
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The list becomes a story: Ephraim's sons are killed raiding cattle at Gath, he mourns many days and is comforted, and names the next son Beriah (vv. 21-23). His daughter Sheerah builds the Beth-horons (v. 24). The section closes with Joshua at the end of Ephraim's line (v. 27) and the towns of Joseph's sons (vv. 28-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Scripture gives grief time and company. Ephraim's brothers sat with him, and the Son of God wept at a friend's tomb before he raised him (John 11:35), so no believer need be ashamed of mourning long.
verseByVerse.examples: Sheerah is one of very few people in nine chapters of genealogy credited with building anything (Shemed is another, 8:12), and her towns guarded the pass armies used for centuries.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Ephraim: Shuthelah, and Bered his son, Tahath his son, Eleadah his son, Tahath his son, Zabad his son, Shuthelah his son, and Ezer and Elead, whom the men of Gath who were born in the land killed, because they came down to raid their livestock. And Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brothers came to comfort him. And Ephraim went in to his wife, and she conceived and bore a son. And he called his name Beriah, because disaster had befallen his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without warning, the list becomes a story.

Two of Ephraim's sons were killed raiding cattle, and the next sentence is one of the few in these chapters with a heart in it.

Nothing is explained: not whether the raid was justified or the boys foolish. We are told how long the grief lasted, many days, and that other men came and sat with him.

Then he had another son, and named him Beriah, because disaster had befallen his house. A father who buries two children gives the next one a name that sounds like the word for disaster, and every time he called that boy in from the field he said the word out loud. Scripture does not tell him to stop, and does not treat it as a failure of faith. The register simply carries the name down the generations, so that the loss can still be read more than a thousand years later in a list that had no obligation to mention it at all.

How could Ephraim mourn sons killed at Gath? He lived in Egypt, and Gath is in Canaan. This raid likely happened while Israel was in Egypt, when Ephraim’s sons went up to Canaan, or “Ephraim” here means a later descendant of the tribe.
verseByVerse.note: “Beriah” sounds like the Hebrew for “disaster” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: His daughter was Sheerah, who built both Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah. Rephah was his son, Resheph his son, Telah his son, Tahan his son, Ladan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son, Nun his son, Joshua his son. Their possessions and settlements were Bethel and its towns, and to the east Naaran, and to the west Gezer and its towns, Shechem and its towns, and Ayyah and its towns; also in possession of the Manassites, Beth-shean and its towns, Taanach and its towns, Megiddo and its towns, Dor and its towns. In these lived the sons of Joseph the son of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hundreds of men in these chapters fathered somebody. Very few built something, and one of them is a woman who built three towns, one bearing her name.

Beth-horon is not a village on a hill. It is the pass, the road up from the coastal plain into the highlands, the route every invading army took. Joshua chased the five kings down it the day the sun stood still, and armies fought over it for centuries. A woman built towns on that ascent, and her name stayed on the map.

Three verses later the line reaches Joshua son of Nun: the family that lost two sons to a cattle raid also produced the man who took the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–40 — Asher, and the Two Tribes That Are Missing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asher's line is given with unusual care, down to their sister Serah (v. 30), closing on a muster of 26,000 (v. 40). It is the last chapter to cover several tribes at once.
verseByVerse.theology: Dan and Zebulun have no genealogy anywhere in 1 Chronicles. The register that insists God keeps track of everyone is itself silent about two tribes.
verseByVerse.examples: Some find a fragment of Dan in verse 12, since Genesis names Dan's son Hushim (Genesis 46:23), though the Hebrew is uncertain. Either way, the record has holes, and the God whose record it is does not.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah. The sons of Beriah: Heber, and Malchiel, who fathered Birzaith. Heber fathered Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and their sister Shua. The sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the sons of Japhlet. The sons of Shemer his brother: Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram. The sons of Helem his brother: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asher's register does something rare: it names a sister, Serah.

Serah is named in Genesis among the seventy who went into Egypt, and in the wilderness census, and nothing is recorded about her. Three documents centuries apart wrote her name and none explains why.

That is one of the quiet arguments these chapters make. A person can be in the book of God for no reason that anyone can reconstruct, and stay there, because it is God who wrote the name there, not the person. Jesus told his disciples that the thing to rejoice in was not their achievements but that their names were written in heaven (Luke 10:20).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Zophah: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah. Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera. The sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara. The sons of Ulla: Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia. All of these were men of Asher, heads of fathers' houses, approved, mighty warriors, chiefs of the princes. Their number enrolled by genealogies, for service in war, was 26,000 men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last multi-tribe register closes on a muster of twenty-six thousand.

And then the genealogies of the tribes are finished, and two of the twelve have not appeared. The Chronicler, who gave eighty-one verses to Levi and three chapters to Judah, does not account for the omission of Dan and Zebulun.

Whatever the reason (records lost, a scroll damaged, tribes that had ceased to be traceable), the effect on a returning exile from either tribe is not softened by the explanation. He opened the book and his family was not in it.

Set that beside the last roll of Israel in Scripture, twelve thousand sealed from every tribe, a picture many take to stand for the whole people of God (Revelation 7:4–8). Zebulun is named there; Dan is still absent, and Ephraim appears under Joseph.

So the two rolls do not match each other, and neither of them settles the matter. The names that finally count are written in the Lamb's book of life (Revelation 21:27), and no scroll in Jerusalem was ever the master copy.

8.title: Benjamin: The Tribe of Saul and the Background of David's Kingdom
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Benjamin fathered Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third,<sup>2</sup>Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth.<sup>3</sup>And Bela had sons: Addar, Gera, Abihud,<sup>4</sup>Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah,<sup>5</sup>Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram.<sup>6</sup>These are the sons of Ehud (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Geba, and they were carried into exile to Manahath):<sup>7</sup>Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera, that is, Heglam, who fathered Uzza and Ahihud.<sup>8</sup>And Shaharaim fathered sons in the country of Moab after he had sent away Hushim and Baara his wives.<sup>9</sup>He fathered sons by Hodesh his wife: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam,<sup>10</sup>Jeuz, Sachia, and Mirmah. These were his sons, heads of fathers' houses.<sup>11</sup>He also fathered sons by Hushim: Abitub and Elpaal.<sup>12</sup>The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, and Shemed, who built Ono and Lod with its towns,<sup>13</sup>and Beriah and Shema (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Aijalon, who caused the inhabitants of Gath to flee);<sup>14</sup>and Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth.<sup>15</sup>Zebadiah, Arad, Eder,<sup>16</sup>Michael, Ishpah, and Joha were sons of Beriah.<sup>17</sup>Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber,<sup>18</sup>Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab were the sons of Elpaal.<sup>19</sup>Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi,<sup>20</sup>Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel,<sup>21</sup>Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath were the sons of Shimei.<sup>22</sup>Ishpan, Eber, Eliel,<sup>23</sup>Abdon, Zichri, Hanan,<sup>24</sup>Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah,<sup>25</sup>Iphdeiah, and Penuel were the sons of Shashak.<sup>26</sup>Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah,<sup>27</sup>Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri were the sons of Jeroham.<sup>28</sup>These were the heads of fathers' houses, according to their generations, chief men. These lived in Jerusalem.<sup>29</sup>Jeiel the father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon, and the name of his wife was Maacah.<sup>30</sup>His firstborn son: Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab,<sup>31</sup>Gedor, Ahio, Zecher,<sup>32</sup>and Mikloth (he fathered Shimeah). Now these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen.<sup>33</sup>Ner was the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Eshbaal;<sup>34</sup>and the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal; and Merib-baal was the father of Micah.<sup>35</sup>The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz.<sup>36</sup>Ahaz fathered Jehoaddah, and Jehoaddah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri fathered Moza.<sup>37</sup>Moza fathered Binea; Raphah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son.<sup>38</sup>Azel had six sons, and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel.<sup>39</sup>The sons of Eshek his brother: Ulam his firstborn, Jeush the second, and Eliphelet the third.<sup>40</sup>The sons of Ulam were men who were mighty warriors, bowmen, having many sons and grandsons, 150. All these were Benjaminites.
8.overview:
Benjamin is given a chapter of his own: the early houses, an exile to Manahath and a divorce in Moab (vv. 1-14); lists of chiefs who lived in Jerusalem (vv. 15-28); and the family of Saul, from Jeiel of Gibeon through Kish to Saul, Jonathan and Eshbaal, and on for a dozen generations, ending in bowmen (vv. 29-40).

The placing is deliberate. The genealogies end on the house that lost the kingdom (the list is repeated at 9:35–44), and the very next verse is the battle in which it lost it.
8.theology:
The chapter shows how the Chronicler works. He writes Eshbaal and Merib-baal where the books of Samuel write Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth, most likely because his sources have them that way. A historian who leaves the name Baal in a king’s family is copying his documents faithfully, not tidying them.

And the theological weight is in the arrangement: Saul's genealogy closes the nine chapters, kept in the archive of the dynasty that replaced him. Rejection from an office is not erasure from the record.
8.examples:
Whole households here are remembered for nothing but an address: they lived in Jerusalem while it mattered. That is closer to most Christian lives than anything heroic.

And the last family in the genealogies is the one that failed publicly, written down carefully with its children and its skill with a bow. God keeps a family in his record even when its story is one of failure.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Benjamin's sons, an exile to Manahath (v. 6), a divorce and a new family in Moab (v. 8), and the heads of houses at Aijalon who put Gath to flight (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Benjamin produced the first king and stayed with Judah when the ten northern tribes broke away, so the returned community was essentially Judah, Benjamin and Levi.
verseByVerse.examples: A deportation, a man divorcing two wives and starting again in Moab: the register carries small domestic catastrophes without a syllable of judgment, and carries their children into the tribe of the first king.

verseByVerse.quote: Benjamin fathered Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third, Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth. And Bela had sons: Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah, Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram. These are the sons of Ehud (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Geba, and they were carried into exile to Manahath): Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera, that is, Heglam, who fathered Uzza and Ahihud.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only Judah and Levi also receive a chapter to themselves. These are not antiquarian notes about a vanished world; they are the family papers of the men reading the book.

And already in verse 6 there is an exile, at a time and for reasons nobody records. Deportation did not come from nowhere in 586 BC, when Jerusalem fell; it had been happening in smaller ways for a long time.

verseByVerse.quote: And Shaharaim fathered sons in the country of Moab after he had sent away Hushim and Baara his wives. He fathered sons by Hodesh his wife: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia, and Mirmah. These were his sons, heads of fathers' houses. He also fathered sons by Hushim: Abitub and Elpaal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verse here has a marriage in it, and the marriage has ended.

A man divorced two women, left the country and started a family somewhere else, and his children are in the official genealogy of the tribe of Israel's first king. The register records that these people exist and how they came to. Recording is not approving: Scripture's teaching on marriage stands elsewhere (Malachi 2:16; Matthew 19:3–9), and here the point is that the children of a broken home are counted.

A writer anxious for appearances would have left him out. Scripture does not guard its reputation that way. The genealogy of Judah, the Messiah’s tribe, already has a Canaanite wife, a deceived father-in-law and an Egyptian slave in it (chapter 2). Benjamin's line has a divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, and Shemed, who built Ono and Lod with its towns, and Beriah and Shema (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Aijalon, who caused the inhabitants of Gath to flee); and Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses here do something no other verse in Benjamin's list does.

First, a builder: Shemed built Ono and Lod. Both towns long outlive him. Ono is where Sanballat tried to lure Nehemiah down from the wall, and Nehemiah replied that he was doing a great work and could not come down (Nehemiah 6:2–3). Lod is Lydda, where Peter told a man bedridden eight years that Jesus Christ healed him (Acts 9:32–35).

Second, a reversal: Beriah and Shema caused the inhabitants of Gath to flee. In the previous chapter the men of Gath killed two of Ephraim's sons. The text draws no moral, but the city that took two sons from one tribe was put to flight by another, and both facts are kept in the same archive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — The Heads of Houses Who Lived in Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Long lists of Benjaminite chiefs, closing with the note that gives the section its point: These lived in Jerusalem (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Jerusalem sat on the border of Judah and Benjamin, and Benjaminites lived in it from the beginning. The record of who lived there mattered enormously to a generation trying to repopulate it.
verseByVerse.examples: A half-empty city needed ordinary families willing to move in (Nehemiah 11:1–2). Being where God's people need you can be a real service, even if it is all anyone remembers.

verseByVerse.quote: Zebadiah, Arad, Eder, Michael, Ishpah, and Joha were sons of Beriah. Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber, Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab were the sons of Elpaal. Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath were the sons of Shimei.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three houses in seven verses, and not one word about any of them: the genealogies at their barest, a family's claim to belong, preserved. Every name is somebody's grandfather, and somebody after the return from exile needed it written down.

verseByVerse.quote: Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah, Iphdeiah, and Penuel were the sons of Shashak. Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri were the sons of Jeroham. These were the heads of fathers' houses, according to their generations, chief men. These lived in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two more houses, and then the clause the section exists for.

Benjaminites had houses in the city from the start, and that mattered to the people holding this book, because Jerusalem after the return was half empty. Nehemiah had to cast lots to move one family in ten into the city, and the people blessed those who volunteered (Nehemiah 11:1–2).

These verses are the precedent: a written record that Benjamin had always lived there. Somebody arguing about a ruined street after the return could put his finger on verse 28 and say his family had held it before Babylon burned the city.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter turns to Gibeon and works down to Saul, Jonathan and Eshbaal (v. 33) and Jonathan's son Merib-baal (v. 34), then on for a dozen generations to Ulam's bowmen (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogies close on the family that failed, and the narrative's first report is Saul's death on Gilboa. Nine chapters are arranged so the story opens at a funeral.
verseByVerse.examples: Even the last names (v. 40) are remembered for a skill. A family's record includes its gifts as well as its failures.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeiel the father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon, and the name of his wife was Maacah. His firstborn son: Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zecher, and Mikloth (he fathered Shimeah). Now these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen. Ner was the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Eshbaal; and the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal; and Merib-baal was the father of Micah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line the book has been walking towards arrives quietly, through a man in Gibeon and his wife Maacah.

Two names need explaining for a reader who knows the books of Samuel. Eshbaal is 2 Samuel's Ish-bosheth, and Merib-baal is Mephibosheth, Jonathan's crippled son. Most scholars think the names were altered in Samuel: baal, which meant lord or master and was once used innocently, was replaced with bosheth, shame.

That substitution tells its own story about what happened to a word. In Saul's generation a man could name his son Eshbaal and mean nothing by it. By the time Samuel was copied, Baal meant the false god Elijah opposed on Mount Carmel, and the scribes probably would not write it as part of a man’s name.

The Chronicler keeps what are probably the original forms, writing what his older documents say.

Merib-baal is the lame son of Jonathan whom David sought out for Jonathan's sake and seated at the king's table for life (2 Samuel 9). Many Christians have seen there a picture of the gospel: the heir of a fallen house, unable to walk, brought to eat with the king for the sake of another. The greater Son of David does that for sinners.

Ner and Kish were both sons of Abiel (1 Samuel 9:1; 14:51); here Ner is named as the father of a Kish, most likely a second Kish in the family, or the list names a grandfather as father.
verseByVerse.note: Esh-baal and Merib-baal are probably the original names of Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz. Ahaz fathered Jehoaddah, and Jehoaddah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri fathered Moza. Moza fathered Binea; Raphah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son. Azel had six sons, and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel. The sons of Eshek his brother: Ulam his firstborn, Jeush the second, and Eliphelet the third. The sons of Ulam were men who were mighty warriors, bowmen, having many sons and grandsons, 150. All these were Benjaminites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul's family goes on for generation after generation, ending with Ulam's sons, mighty warriors, bowmen.

The archers of Gilboa wounded Saul, and his descendants are remembered for the bow. Nothing is made of it.

Here the list ends, though chapter 9 will repeat Saul's line. From Adam to a hundred and fifty Benjaminite archers, and the last family named is the house God rejected.

That arrangement is deliberate and merciful. A chronicler serving the house of David wrote Saul's line into the record of the kingdom that replaced it. God did not erase the family that failed; he kept their names in the book, and then told the truth about what happened.

9.title: The Returned Remnant and the Gatekeepers of the Holy
9.text: <sup>1</sup>So all Israel was recorded in genealogies, and these are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. And Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith.<sup>2</sup>Now the first to dwell again in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants.<sup>3</sup>And some of the people of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem:<sup>4</sup>Uthai the son of Ammihud, son of Omri, son of Imri, son of Bani, from the sons of Perez the son of Judah.<sup>5</sup>And of the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons.<sup>6</sup>Of the sons of Zerah: Jeuel and their kinsmen, 690.<sup>7</sup>Of the Benjaminites: Sallu the son of Meshullam, son of Hodaviah, son of Hassenuah,<sup>8</sup>Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, Elah the son of Uzzi, son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephatiah, son of Reuel, son of Ibnijah;<sup>9</sup>and their kinsmen according to their generations, 956. All these were heads of fathers' houses according to their fathers' houses.<sup>10</sup>Of the priests: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin,<sup>11</sup>and Azariah the son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the chief officer of the house of God;<sup>12</sup>and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah, and Maasai the son of Adiel, son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith, son of Immer;<sup>13</sup>besides their kinsmen, heads of their fathers' houses, 1,760, mighty men for the work of the service of the house of God.<sup>14</sup>Of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari;<sup>15</sup>and Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal and Mattaniah the son of Mica, son of Zichri, son of Asaph;<sup>16</sup>and Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, son of Elkanah, who lived in the villages of the Netophathites.<sup>17</sup>The gatekeepers were Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman, and their kinsmen (Shallum was the chief);<sup>18</sup>until then they were in the king's gate on the east side as the gatekeepers of the camps of the Levites.<sup>19</sup>Shallum the son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, and his kinsmen of his fathers' house, the Korahites, were in charge of the work of the service, keepers of the thresholds of the tent, as their fathers had been in charge of the camp of the LORD, keepers of the entrance.<sup>20</sup>And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the chief officer over them in time past; the LORD was with him.<sup>21</sup>Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was gatekeeper at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>22</sup>All these, who were chosen as gatekeepers at the thresholds, were 212. They were enrolled by genealogies in their villages. David and Samuel the seer established them in their office of trust.<sup>23</sup>So they and their sons were in charge of the gates of the house of the LORD, that is, the house of the tent, as guards.<sup>24</sup>The gatekeepers were on the four sides, east, west, north, and south.<sup>25</sup>And their kinsmen who were in their villages were obligated to come in every seven days, in turn, to be with these,<sup>26</sup>for the four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, were entrusted to be over the chambers and the treasures of the house of God.<sup>27</sup>And they lodged around the house of God, for on them lay the duty of watching, and they had charge of opening it every morning.<sup>28</sup>Some of them had charge of the utensils of service, for they were required to count them when they were brought in and taken out.<sup>29</sup>Others of them were appointed over the furniture and over all the holy utensils, also over the fine flour, the wine, the oil, the incense, and the spices.<sup>30</sup>Others, of the sons of the priests, prepared the mixing of the spices,<sup>31</sup>and Mattithiah, one of the Levites, the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, was entrusted with making the flat cakes.<sup>32</sup>Also some of their kinsmen of the Kohathites had charge of the showbread, to prepare it every Sabbath.<sup>33</sup>Now these, the singers, the heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, were in the chambers of the temple free from other service, for they were on duty day and night.<sup>34</sup>These were heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, according to their generations, leaders. These lived in Jerusalem.<sup>35</sup>In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon, Jeiel, and the name of his wife was Maacah,<sup>36</sup>and his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab,<sup>37</sup>Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth;<sup>38</sup>and Mikloth was the father of Shimeam; and these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen.<sup>39</sup>Ner fathered Kish, Kish fathered Saul, Saul fathered Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal.<sup>40</sup>And the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal fathered Micah.<sup>41</sup>The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz.<sup>42</sup>And Ahaz fathered Jarah, and Jarah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. And Zimri fathered Moza.<sup>43</sup>Moza fathered Binea, and Rephaiah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son.<sup>44</sup>Azel had six sons and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan; these were the sons of Azel.
9.overview:
The genealogies close with the sentence they were written to explain, Judah's exile because of their breach of faith (v. 1), and turn to the return: who came back, and to which streets (vv. 2-9). Most of the chapter is the temple staff, above all the gatekeepers, with their charter from David and Samuel, their rota, inventories, spices and baking (vv. 10-34). It ends by repeating Saul's genealogy (vv. 35-44), and the next verse is his death.

It is the most ordinary chapter of the nine, and the most telling: a community that had lost everything is described in terms of who unlocked the doors.
9.theology:
Verse 1 gives the reason for the exile, and the reason concerns God, not politics. The Chronicler knew how strong the empires were; he refuses to let them be the explanation.

Against the breach of faith stands the doorkeeping. The chapter’s answer to Israel’s unfaithfulness is not a reform programme but a rota: men enrolled by name, opening a building every morning, counting the vessels, baking the bread every Sabbath. And the rota exists only because God brought them back. Faithfulness in Scripture is far more often a duty performed at dawn, by people God has already taken back, than a decision made at a crisis.
9.examples:
The men in this chapter are remembered for opening a door, counting spoons, mixing spices and making flat cakes. It is the closest the Bible comes to describing a normal working life among the people of God, written with the same care as the covenant with David.

And the family at the centre is Korah's (v. 19). God’s mercy to a disgraced family was not to give it the priesthood Korah had grasped at but to give it something better to want.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Exile, and the First to Come Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse closes the genealogies and gives the reason for everything: Judah went into exile because of their breach of faith (v. 1). Then the resettlement of Israel, priests, Levites and temple servants (v. 2), and the households of Judah and Benjamin in Jerusalem, counted to the man (vv. 4-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler’s word for breaking faith is now used of a whole nation, which loses the city and the temple. The exile is explained by unfaithfulness to God’s covenant, not by Babylon’s power.
verseByVerse.examples: The returned are counted by household, as a community small enough to count is. A returning family could find itself in verse 8 and know it had a place.

verseByVerse.quote: So all Israel was recorded in genealogies, and these are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. And Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith. Now the first to dwell again in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants. And some of the people of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The genealogies end, and one clause says what all nine chapters were leading to.

The verb broke faith has run through the book since chapter 2. Achan broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing and Israel lost a battle; the eastern tribes broke faith and lost their land. Now the whole nation breaks faith and loses the city and the house of God.

What is not given as the reason is telling. Not Babylonian siege engineering, not the size of Nebuchadnezzar's army, not a failed alliance with Egypt, not the incompetence of Zedekiah. Every one of those was true and none of them is mentioned. The catastrophe is explained in six words as unfaithfulness to God, and the word at their centre is the one used of a single thief centuries earlier.

Then verse 2 turns the page: the exile is over, and the people are back in their own towns. They came home not because they had kept faith but because God kept his. The list runs closely parallel to Nehemiah 11, which suggests the Chronicler drew on the same records of the resettlement.

verseByVerse.quote: Uthai the son of Ammihud, son of Omri, son of Imri, son of Bani, from the sons of Perez the son of Judah. And of the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons. Of the sons of Zerah: Jeuel and their kinsmen, 690. Of the Benjaminites: Sallu the son of Meshullam, son of Hodaviah, son of Hassenuah, Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, Elah the son of Uzzi, son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephatiah, son of Reuel, son of Ibnijah; and their kinsmen according to their generations, 956. All these were heads of fathers' houses according to their fathers' houses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The householders of Judah and Benjamin in Jerusalem, named to the grandfather and totalled to the man.

A few thousand people in a half-ruined city are counted as carefully as the armies of eighty-seven thousand in the earlier chapters, because the counting was never a measure of strength.

A man reading verse 8 could find his own family in it. That is why the number is written down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–34 — The Men Who Kept the Doors
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The returned priests, 1,760 (v. 13), then the Levites, then 212 gatekeepers whom David and Samuel the seer established in their office (v. 22). Their duties: the four quarters, the watch, opening the house every morning (vv. 23-27), the utensils, spices, flat cakes and showbread (vv. 28-32), and the singers on duty day and night (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: A community with no king and no army is described by its priests, Levites, gatekeepers and singers: a God to worship, and men set apart to keep that worship going. The house came first because God's presence was the one thing they could not do without.
verseByVerse.examples: Mattithiah is named for making the flat cakes (v. 31). Whatever unseen work someone does for God's people, baking, counting or locking up, God does not overlook it.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the priests: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin, and Azariah the son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the chief officer of the house of God; and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah, and Maasai the son of Adiel, son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith, son of Immer; besides their kinsmen, heads of their fathers' houses, 1,760, mighty men for the work of the service of the house of God. Of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari; and Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal and Mattaniah the son of Mica, son of Zichri, son of Asaph; and Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, son of Elkanah, who lived in the villages of the Netophathites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The returned priests, their descent traced through Zadok and Ahitub, totalled as mighty men.

That is a soldier's phrase, used of men whose work was sacrifice and instruction.

Then the Levites, one living in the villages of the Netophathites near Bethlehem. The temple staff commuted in from the villages, as it always had.

verseByVerse.quote: The gatekeepers were Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman, and their kinsmen (Shallum was the chief); until then they were in the king's gate on the east side as the gatekeepers of the camps of the Levites. Shallum the son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, and his kinsmen of his fathers' house, the Korahites, were in charge of the work of the service, keepers of the thresholds of the tent, as their fathers had been in charge of the camp of the LORD, keepers of the entrance. And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the chief officer over them in time past; the LORD was with him. Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was gatekeeper at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first gatekeeper named carries the chapter's weight: Shallum, descended from Korah.

Korah: the man who stood up against Moses and Aaron with two hundred and fifty princes of the congregation, accused them of setting themselves above the LORD’s people, and went down alive into the earth for it. Numbers adds, almost in passing, that his sons did not die.

And here is what the family was doing centuries later. His descendants are keepers of the thresholds of the tent, the doorkeepers. The house their ancestor tried to storm, they now open in the morning and shut at night, as their fathers had been in charge of the camp of the LORD.

Eleven psalms carry their name. One says a day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere, and that its writer would rather stand at the door of the house of his God than dwell in the tents of wickedness (Psalm 84:10). For the men who wrote it, that was a job description.

God did not restore Korah's family to the altar. He gave them the doorway, and they made a song of it that Israel sang for a thousand years.

verseByVerse.quote: All these, who were chosen as gatekeepers at the thresholds, were 212. They were enrolled by genealogies in their villages. David and Samuel the seer established them in their office of trust. So they and their sons were in charge of the gates of the house of the LORD, that is, the house of the tent, as guards. The gatekeepers were on the four sides, east, west, north, and south. And their kinsmen who were in their villages were obligated to come in every seven days, in turn, to be with these, for the four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, were entrusted to be over the chambers and the treasures of the house of God. And they lodged around the house of God, for on them lay the duty of watching, and they had charge of opening it every morning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David and Samuel, a king and a prophet, jointly over a rota of doormen. The office is not improvised and it is not menial. It is a trust, established by the king who founded Israel's lasting dynasty and the prophet who anointed him.

The duties are wonderfully ordinary: four quarters, a week on and then back to the village, the chambers and treasures, and lodging around the house to watch and open it every morning.

Somebody had to get up early and unlock the temple. Every morning for four hundred years, in the rain and the cold and on the mornings when he did not feel like it, a man walked to a door and opened it so that Israel could come in and meet God. The Chronicler thought that worth recording by name.

Samuel died before David became king, so “David and Samuel the seer” probably means Samuel began organising the gatekeepers while David was young, and David completed it.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of them had charge of the utensils of service, for they were required to count them when they were brought in and taken out. Others of them were appointed over the furniture and over all the holy utensils, also over the fine flour, the wine, the oil, the incense, and the spices. Others, of the sons of the priests, prepared the mixing of the spices, and Mattithiah, one of the Levites, the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, was entrusted with making the flat cakes. Also some of their kinsmen of the Kohathites had charge of the showbread, to prepare it every Sabbath. Now these, the singers, the heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, were in the chambers of the temple free from other service, for they were on duty day and night. These were heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, according to their generations, leaders. These lived in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A stock-take, a spice recipe and a baking rota. In the house of God there was no line between sacred and domestic work.

And the singers, in verse 33, are free from other service because they were on duty day and night: a choir excused from carrying and counting because it was needed around the clock. In the temple's ordered life the praise did not stop, and somebody had to staff the night.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes by repeating, almost word for word, Saul's genealogy from the end of chapter 8 (vv. 35-44).
verseByVerse.theology: The repetition has a purpose: it hands the reader straight from the lists to the battle on Mount Gilboa.
verseByVerse.examples: The restored community, having just read of the return, is handed Saul's family again and then a funeral. It may not read its own history without first reading how a king was lost.

verseByVerse.quote: In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon, Jeiel, and the name of his wife was Maacah, and his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth; and Mikloth was the father of Shimeam; and these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen. Ner fathered Kish, Kish fathered Saul, Saul fathered Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal. And the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal fathered Micah. The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz. And Ahaz fathered Jarah, and Jarah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. And Zimri fathered Moza. Moza fathered Binea, and Rephaiah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son. Azel had six sons and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan; these were the sons of Azel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no transition, Saul's family again.

The repetition is not an accident of copying. It is a door being opened: nine chapters close on the household of the king who lost the kingdom, and the moment the list ends the narrative begins, with the men of Israel falling on Mount Gilboa.

The reader passes out of the genealogies straight into a funeral: before he is told anything about David, he is shown what happens to a king who does not seek the LORD.

So the genealogies end where they began, with a register and a God who keeps it: from Adam through a Canaanite wife, an Egyptian slave, a thief, a rebel's children and two vanished tribes, down to a few thousand people rebuilding a wall and a man unlocking a door at dawn. Not one name was lost. And at the end of the line, four centuries off, the Son who would say that he was the door (John 10:9).

10.title: The Death of Saul: Unfaithfulness and Its Wages
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.<sup>2</sup>And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul.<sup>3</sup>The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was wounded by the archers.<sup>4</sup>Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly.
