Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it.<sup>5</sup>And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died.<sup>6</sup>Thus Saul died; he and his three sons and all his house died together.<sup>7</sup>And when all the men of Israel who were in the valley saw that the army had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled, and the Philistines came and lived in them.<sup>8</sup>The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.<sup>9</sup>And they stripped him and took his head and his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to carry the good news to their idols and to the people.<sup>10</sup>And they put his armor in the temple of their gods and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.<sup>11</sup>But when all Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul,<sup>12</sup>all the valiant men arose and took away the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons, and brought them to Jabesh. And they buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days.<sup>13</sup>So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the LORD in that he did not keep the command of the LORD, and also consulted a medium, seeking guidance.<sup>14</sup>He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.
10.overview:
The narrative begins with a funeral. Israel is routed on Gilboa, Saul's sons are killed, and Saul, wounded and refused by his armour-bearer, falls on his own sword (vv. 1-7). The Philistines take his head and armour into their temples (vv. 8-10). The men of Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul had rescued at the start of his reign, come by night for the bodies (vv. 11-12). Then two verses of verdict: he broke faith, he did not seek the LORD, and the LORD gave the kingdom to David (vv. 13-14).

Everything the Chronicler wants his readers to understand about their history is in those last two verses, placed at the head of the story, before David appears.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The narrative opens in the middle of a defeat: Israel flees, Saul's sons fall, the archers find Saul, and refused by his armour-bearer he falls on his own sword (vv. 1-6). The men of the valley abandon their towns to the Philistines (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler assumes his reader knows the reign and tells only how it ended. A king introduced by his death is introduced as a warning.
verseByVerse.examples: The battle takes a few verses because the first readers knew it from 1 Samuel 31. What they are to take away is the reason, held back to the last two verses.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul. The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was wounded by the archers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul is not introduced; the narrative puts the reader on a hillside in a rout already lost.

The order matters: Israel flees, Saul is overtaken, the sons die, then the archers find him. A king called to go out before his people and fight their battles is the last man on a hill his army has abandoned, and the arrows arrive while he is alone.

One of the sons is Jonathan. He had long known the throne was not coming to him, and said so to David in a wood at Horesh while Saul was hunting David: You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you (1 Samuel 23:17). It never happened. He died on the hill his father had lost.

It is Jonathan's only mention in the book outside the genealogies. A man can love the right person, tell the truth about God's choice against his own interest, and still go down with the house he was born into.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it. And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter's one conversation is a request to be killed.

Saul is not asking to escape death but to control it. What he cannot bear is being taken alive, and the shame of what the Philistines will do to a captured king.

The armour-bearer refuses, for he feared greatly.

Then Saul falls on his own sword, and the armour-bearer, having refused to kill the king, kills himself. Being afraid to do a wrong thing is not the same as trusting God, and on Gilboa it saved nobody.

Saul's last decision as king is made without reference to God, which is exactly what verse 14 says of his life.

Is suicide a sin, and is it unforgivable? Taking one’s own life breaks the sixth commandment, a grave sin against the God who gives life (Exodus 20:13). But it is not the unforgivable sin; that is the settled rejection of Christ (Mark 3:28–29). A true believer who dies this way, in despair or illness of mind, is not cut off from the grace that saves sinners, for salvation rests on Christ’s work, not on the state of our last moment (Romans 8:38–39). Anyone thinking of it should speak to someone today: a pastor, a friend, a doctor.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Saul died; he and his three sons and all his house died together. And when all the men of Israel who were in the valley saw that the army had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled, and the Philistines came and lived in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All his house died together (v. 6). A reader who knows Samuel will stop here, because Saul’s house did not all die that day. Ish-bosheth reigned two years afterwards, Mephibosheth lived at David's table for decades, and this book has just traced Saul's descendants down to his bowmen. The Chronicler is not contradicting any of that. He is saying that the dynasty died on Gilboa: Saul’s house never ruled all Israel again.

Verse 7 measures the defeat in geography: the men of the valley walked out of their towns and the Philistines moved in. Israel lost the middle of the country in a day.

For readers who had lost far more than a valley, the history begins by showing the loss of a land following a king who would not seek God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — The Head in the Temple of Dagon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines take Saul's head and armour into their temples (vv. 8-10). Then the chapter's one act of loyalty, from the men of Jabesh-gilead (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul's head is nailed up in the house of the god who fell, headless, before the ark (1 Samuel 5:1–5). The Chronicler sets the two stories side by side without comment.
verseByVerse.examples: Kindness done long ago is not wasted: the town Saul once rescued was the only one in Israel to come for his body.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. And they stripped him and took his head and his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to carry the good news to their idols and to the people. And they put his armor in the temple of their gods and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the Philistines do with Saul's body is a religious act.

They send messengers to carry the good news to their idols, and the Greek translators used the word that becomes the New Testament's word for preaching the gospel. The Philistines announce it to their gods as good news; they believe their gods have beaten Israel’s God.

Samuel adds that the body was fastened to the wall of Beth-shan and the armour put in the temple of the Ashtaroth (1 Samuel 31:9–10); each account records a different part of what was done.

The reader is meant to notice the name Dagon. When the captured ark stood in Dagon's house at Ashdod, the god was found face down before it, his head and hands broken on the threshold. Now the head of Israel's king hangs in the same god's temple.

A god who could not stand before the ark is given the head of a king who would not go to the ark for guidance. The trophy is a verdict on the man, not a victory over his God.

The irony runs forward. The apostles' gospel was also news of a king's death, but of a King who died for his people, rose again, and by his cross disarmed the powers that thought they had won (Colossians 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: But when all Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men arose and took away the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons, and brought them to Jabesh. And they buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One act of decency in fourteen verses, from a town nobody expects.

The men of Jabesh-gilead crossed the Jordan to a Philistine-held hill, carried the bodies home, buried the bones under an oak and fasted seven days. Samuel adds that they burned the bodies first and calls the tree a tamarisk (1 Samuel 31:12–13); both words describe a great tree that marked the grave.

Their reason was decades old (Acts 13:21 gives Saul's reign as forty years; the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 13:1 is damaged and gives no reliable figure). Nahash the Ammonite had besieged Jabesh and offered to spare it for the right eye of every man. Saul raised the country, marched all night and broke the siege at dawn (1 Samuel 11). It was the best day of his life.

When everything else about the man had gone wrong, one town remembered the morning he came.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two verses of verdict, and they are why the chapter exists: Saul died for his breach of faith, for not keeping the LORD's command and for consulting a medium instead of the LORD, and the LORD turned the kingdom over to David (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Both the book's key verbs are here: he broke faith, and he did not seek the LORD, which will become the measure of every king after him.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul's failure was not a lack of gifts: he was tall, brave and anointed. What a church should look for in its leaders, and in itself, is whether they seek the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the LORD in that he did not keep the command of the LORD, and also consulted a medium, seeking guidance. He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the verdict, the reason the chapter is in the book.

Broke faith has run through the genealogies from Achan at Jericho, through the eastern tribes, to Judah carried to Babylon. Here it is used of its smallest subject: one man.

Seek is the word the rest of the book is built on. Saul was seeking urgently at the end, at Endor, in the one place forbidden to him. The charge is not that he never asked but that he asked everyone except God.

Watch what the word does from here. Three chapters on, David will say the ark must come back because we did not seek it in the days of Saul. Then he will inquire of God twice before a battle and win twice. Then the ark will go wrong and he will admit we did not seek him according to the rule. Then he will write into a psalm let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice. And at the end of his life he will hand his son a kingdom with one sentence attached: If you seek him, he will be found by you.

Saul died of an arrow and a sword in a battle the Philistines won, and the Chronicler says the LORD put him to death. Both are true, the second is the reason for the first, and this book never sets the two against each other.

Paul preached this transition at Pisidian Antioch: God removed Saul, raised up David, and of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised (Acts 13:21–23). The kingdom turned over to David is the kingdom that arrives at Christ, the King who never once failed to seek his Father, and whose faithfulness covers those who, like Saul, have looked everywhere but to God. The way back is still open: seek the LORD while he may be found (Isaiah 55:6).

Saul “did not seek guidance from the LORD”, though 1 Samuel 28:6 says he inquired and got no answer. His asking was not true seeking: when God was silent he went to a medium. Is it wrong today to use psychics, horoscopes or tarot? Yes: God forbids it (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). To seek the LORD is to come to him in his word and in prayer, waiting on him, helped by the Spirit he gives to those who ask (Luke 11:13).

10.theology:
The chapter states the doctrine of providence the book assumes (v. 14). The arrows and the sword were real causes, and God worked through them; he was not one more cause beside them. The same logic explained the exile (ch. 9) and Assyria (ch. 5).

The two governing verbs are set as opposites. To break faith is to treat what belongs to God as ours to take; to seek is to go to God for what only he can give. Saul was desperate enough at the end to visit a medium in the dark. Desperation is not seeking God. What matters is not how urgently a man asks but whom he asks.
10.examples:
Saul's last decision is about how his body will look to his enemies, the instinct of a man who spent a career managing appearances and once begged Samuel to honour him before the elders after he had been rejected. A life organised around not being humiliated ends on a hill with nobody left to see.

Against that stands Jabesh-gilead. They could not fix the reign or win the battle, but they could walk a long way, bury a man properly and go hungry for a week. Where nothing can be mended, that is often the whole of what love can do, and Scripture records it beside the verdict of God.

11.title: David Crowned and His Mighty Men: The King Who Draws Loyal Hearts
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then all Israel gathered together to David at Hebron and said, "Behold, we are your bone and flesh.<sup>2</sup>In times past, even when Saul was king, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD your God said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over my people Israel.'"<sup>3</sup>So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD. And they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD by Samuel.<sup>4</sup>And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, that is, Jebus, where the Jebusites were, the inhabitants of the land.<sup>5</sup>The inhabitants of Jebus said to David, "You will not come in here." Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David.<sup>6</sup>David said, "Whoever strikes the Jebusites first shall be chief and commander." And Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first, so he became chief.<sup>7</sup>And David lived in the stronghold; therefore it was called the city of David.<sup>8</sup>And he built the city all around from the Millo in complete circuit, and Joab repaired the rest of the city.<sup>9</sup>And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him.<sup>10</sup>Now these are the chiefs of David's mighty men, who gave him strong support in his kingdom, together with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel.<sup>11</sup>This is an account of David's mighty men: Jashobeam, a Hachmonite, was chief of the three. He wielded his spear against 300 whom he killed at one time.<sup>12</sup>And next to him among the three mighty men was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite.<sup>13</sup>He was with David at Pas-dammim when the Philistines were gathered there for battle. There was a plot of ground full of barley, and the men fled from the Philistines.<sup>14</sup>But he took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it and killed the Philistines. And the LORD saved them by a great victory.<sup>15</sup>Three of the thirty chief men went down to the rock to David at the cave of Adullam, when the army of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>16</sup>David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem.<sup>17</sup>And David said longingly, "Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!"<sup>18</sup>Then the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and took it and brought it to David. But David would not drink it. He poured it out to the LORD<sup>19</sup>and said, "Far be it from me before my God that I should do this. Shall I drink the lifeblood of these men? For at the risk of their lives they brought it." Therefore he would not drink it. These things did the three mighty men.<sup>20</sup>Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, was chief of the thirty. And he wielded his spear against 300 men and killed them and won a name beside the three.<sup>21</sup>He was the most renowned of the thirty and became their commander, but he did not attain to the three.<sup>22</sup>And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was a valiant man of Kabzeel, a doer of great deeds. He struck down two heroes of Moab. He also went down and struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen.<sup>23</sup>And he struck down an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits tall. The Egyptian had in his hand a spear like a weaver's beam, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff and snatched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear.<sup>24</sup>These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and won a name beside the three mighty men.<sup>25</sup>He was renowned among the thirty, but he did not attain to the three. And David set him over his bodyguard.<sup>26</sup>The mighty men were Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem,<sup>27</sup>Shammoth of Harod, Helez the Pelonite,<sup>28</sup>Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth,<sup>29</sup>Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite,<sup>30</sup>Maharai of Netophah, Heled the son of Baanah of Netophah,<sup>31</sup>Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the people of Benjamin, Benaiah of Pirathon,<sup>32</sup>Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite,<sup>33</sup>Azmaveth of Baharum, Eliahba the Shaalbonite,<sup>34</sup>Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shagee the Hararite,<sup>35</sup>Ahiam the son of Sachar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur,<sup>36</sup>Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite,<sup>37</sup>Hezro of Carmel, Naarai the son of Ezbai,<sup>38</sup>Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Hagri,<sup>39</sup>Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah,<sup>40</sup>Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,<sup>41</sup>Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai,<sup>42</sup>Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a leader of the Reubenites, and thirty with him,<sup>43</sup>Hanan the son of Maacah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite,<sup>44</sup>Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel the sons of Hotham the Aroerite,<sup>45</sup>Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite,<sup>46</sup>Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite,<sup>47</sup>Eliel, and Obed, and Jaasiel the Mezobaite.
11.overview:
Israel comes to Hebron, makes a covenant with David and anoints him (vv. 1-3); Jerusalem is taken and Joab wins the command by going up first (vv. 4-9); and the rest of the chapter is the roll of the mighty men: the three, the water of Bethlehem, Abishai and Benaiah, and forty-odd more names (vv. 10-47).

The Chronicler passes over seven and a half years of civil war. He is writing how Israel came to have this king, this city and these men, and the answer he keeps giving is in verse 9: the LORD of hosts was with him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Covenant at Hebron, a Stronghold at Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All Israel comes to Hebron, claiming kinship, David's past leadership and the LORD's word that he would shepherd them (vv. 1-2). He makes a covenant with them before the LORD and is anointed (v. 3). Then he takes the stronghold of Zion despite the Jebusites' taunt, and Joab wins the command by striking first (vv. 4-6). The section ends on the sentence that explains the reign: for the LORD of hosts was with him (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The kingship rests on three things: the people choose him, the LORD had already appointed him, and a covenant is made between king and nation before God. Israel’s monarchy never rested on conquest alone or on the people’s choice alone.
verseByVerse.examples: The elders could follow David because he had already served them. God's people still do well to look for leaders who have shepherded before they are given a title (1 Timothy 3:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: Then all Israel gathered together to David at Hebron and said, "Behold, we are your bone and flesh. In times past, even when Saul was king, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD your God said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over my people Israel.'" So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD. And they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD by Samuel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between chapters 10 and 11 lie seven and a half years the Chronicler does not mention: no civil war, no Ish-bosheth, no Abner. Saul dies, and all Israel gathers to David.

They claim kinship and give two reasons: experience, for he had led them even under Saul, and the word of God.

Both reasons stand: they wanted a competent soldier and they knew God had chosen him, and the text does not treat the second as spoiled by the first.

The office they name is not king but shepherd. It is what David was doing when Samuel sent for him, and the word God uses of himself when the kings have failed and he says he will search for his sheep himself (Ezekiel 34:11), promising one shepherd, my servant David (Ezekiel 34:23) long after David was dead. Jesus takes up the promise: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). A king who is called a shepherd is bound to care for his people, and only one Son of David did so perfectly, laying down his life.

Then something easy to skip: the covenant before the LORD. The king binds himself, in God's presence, to the people giving him the throne. Israel's monarchy begins with obligation running both ways.
verseByVerse.note: Chronicles passes over David’s seven years at Hebron and his sin with Bathsheba; it focuses on David as builder of worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, that is, Jebus, where the Jebusites were, the inhabitants of the land. The inhabitants of Jebus said to David, "You will not come in here." Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David. David said, "Whoever strikes the Jebusites first shall be chief and commander." And Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first, so he became chief. And David lived in the stronghold; therefore it was called the city of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem was not Israelite. Centuries after Joshua a Canaanite city sat unconquered on the ridge between Judah and Benjamin, confident enough to shout down from the wall.

It had reason: the spur has valleys on three sides and one approach from the north. The assault takes thirteen words: no siege works, no casualties, no speech.

What is recorded is the incentive and who claimed it. Joab already led David's men at Hebron (2 Samuel 2:13); by one act of nerve he wins command of all Israel's army, and David spent his reign with a general he could neither control nor sack, who would murder Abner in a gateway, Amasa on a road, and Absalom in a tree against a direct order.

Samuel tells the capture differently, with the taunt about the blind and the lame and a water shaft (2 Samuel 5:6–8), and does not name Joab. The two accounts add to each other; they do not conflict.

Then the renaming: a Canaanite fortress with no history in Israel becomes, in one sentence, the city of God’s covenant promises. Every prophecy about Zion for a thousand years is about this hill, and until this verse it belonged to somebody else.

verseByVerse.quote: And he built the city all around from the Millo in complete circuit, and Joab repaired the rest of the city. And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David's first act in the city is building.

The Millo is a terrace or a filled platform on the slope, the engineering that made a steep spur usable. David walls the circuit and Joab repairs what is inside it. The king and his general spend their first months as builders, and the Chronicler, whose whole book is heading towards a building, notices.

Then verse 9, the sentence the reign hangs on: for the LORD of hosts was with him.

The reason given for the greatness is not the man: not his generalship, not the loyalty of the thirty, not the strength of the ridge. Said here at the start of the reign, it governs everything that follows.
verseByVerse.note: The Millo was probably a terraced structure supporting buildings on the hill.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–25 — The Three, and the Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The roll opens with the chiefs who made him king according to the word of the LORD (v. 10): Jashobeam (v. 11) and Eleazar, who stood in a barley field when the army ran, and the LORD saved them (vv. 13-14). Then three men break through to the well at Bethlehem, and David refuses to drink (vv. 15-19). Abishai and Benaiah win names beside the three but do not attain to them (vv. 20-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Courage is real, but it is not what won the battle: Eleazar’s stand is honoured, and the victory is credited to the LORD (v. 14).
verseByVerse.examples: These men are loyal to David before he has given them anything, drawn by the king God had chosen and was with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the chiefs of David's mighty men, who gave him strong support in his kingdom, together with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel. This is an account of David's mighty men: Jashobeam, a Hachmonite, was chief of the three. He wielded his spear against 300 whom he killed at one time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roll opens with what the mighty men were for.

They made him king, a human act, deliberate and costly; all Israel did it with them; and it happened according to the word of the LORD. Human agency and divine word sit in a single verse, and never once is it suggested that the more God did, the less they did.

The roll establishes that the throne was not handed to David by a cheering crowd alone: men bled for it, and their names were written down.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Here Jashobeam kills 300 at one time; in 2 Samuel 23:8 it is eight hundred. Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. This commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error, and takes such differences as copying slips, and none touches what the passage teaches.

verseByVerse.quote: And next to him among the three mighty men was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite. He was with David at Pas-dammim when the Philistines were gathered there for battle. There was a plot of ground full of barley, and the men fled from the Philistines. But he took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it and killed the Philistines. And the LORD saved them by a great victory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eleazar’s story is very short, and it is worth picturing.

A barley field. Not a pass, not a citadel, not a bridge, but somebody's crop. He stood in the middle of a field of grain because it belonged to Israel and the Philistines wanted it, and he stayed there while everyone he knew was running away behind him.

And then the verse that keeps the chapter honest: not Eleazar saved them, but the LORD. A man had just done something extraordinary, and the credit is handed straight past him.

verseByVerse.quote: Three of the thirty chief men went down to the rock to David at the cave of Adullam, when the army of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim. David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem. And David said longingly, "Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!" Then the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and took it and brought it to David. But David would not drink it. He poured it out to the LORD and said, "Far be it from me before my God that I should do this. Shall I drink the lifeblood of these men? For at the risk of their lives they brought it." Therefore he would not drink it. These things did the three mighty men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The finest story in the chapter, and it changes nothing in the war.

David is in the stronghold; the Philistine garrison is in Bethlehem, sitting on the town he grew up in. Three of the thirty come down to him at the cave of Adullam, and he says out loud what he is thinking.

He is homesick. He is not giving an order; he is a man in a cave remembering the taste of water from a particular well.

Three men hear him, break through the camp, draw the water and bring it back.

And he will not drink it. He calls the water their blood, because that is what it cost, and pours it on the ground as an offering to the LORD. His refusal is the point. He wanted it. They fetched it. It was freely given and he had every right to it, and he would not enjoy a comfort bought at the risk of other men’s lives. Some things are too expensive to be enjoyed by the person they were bought for, and the only fit thing to do with them is to give them back to God.

Christians can hardly read this without thinking of another son of that town, who poured out his blood at a cost nobody had asked him to pay and nobody could repay. That gift is not too costly to receive. It was bought precisely so that it could be drunk, and the Son who paid for it puts the cup into his people's hands and tells them to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, was chief of the thirty. And he wielded his spear against 300 men and killed them and won a name beside the three. He was the most renowned of the thirty and became their commander, but he did not attain to the three.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The official chronicle records that one of Israel's bravest men was not quite in the first rank, and nobody softens it.

Abishai spent his life a step behind: behind Joab, his brother, who held the command; behind the three, whom he never joined. He was the man who offered to kill Saul in his sleep and twice to kill Shimei, and was refused every time. And he stayed.

verseByVerse.quote: And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was a valiant man of Kabzeel, a doer of great deeds. He struck down two heroes of Moab. He also went down and struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen. And he struck down an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits tall. The Egyptian had in his hand a spear like a weaver's beam, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff and snatched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear. These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and won a name beside the three mighty men. He was renowned among the thirty, but he did not attain to the three. And David set him over his bodyguard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benaiah gets four verses and three feats, and the third of them is written to recall an older story.

A giant with a spear like a weaver's beam sounds like Goliath. That is the phrase 1 Samuel uses of the shaft of his spear (1 Samuel 17:7), and it will be used once more in this book, of Goliath's brother (20:5). And a man who goes down to him with a staff in his hand recalls David, who took his staff and five stones out of a brook.

Benaiah wrenched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with it, which is what David did with Goliath's sword. The king's man repeats the king's victory, in the king's manner, with the king's kind of weapon, and the writer sets it down without a word of comment.

That is what a good king does to the men around him: they start doing what he does. And still he did not attain to the three, and Benaiah went on to command David's bodyguard and Solomon's army, and never seems to have complained about his rank.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–47 — The Roll of the Mighty Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Forty-odd names with their towns, ending in a run of outsiders, Zelek the Ammonite (v. 39) and Ithmah the Moabite (v. 46), and in verse 41, without comment, Uriah the Hittite.
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler never tells the story of Bathsheba, yet writes Uriah into the roll of honour. A cover-up would have left the name out.
verseByVerse.examples: An Ammonite, a Moabite and a Hittite among David's men: the King of Israel was never meant to rule Israel alone, and his greater Son gathers his people from every nation (Revelation 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: The mighty men were Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem, Shammoth of Harod, Helez the Pelonite, Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth, Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite, Maharai of Netophah, Heled the son of Baanah of Netophah, Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the people of Benjamin, Benaiah of Pirathon, Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roll proper is mostly geography.

Asahel is first, though he had been dead for years, killed by Abner in the retreat from Gibeon after being told twice to turn aside. He is in the honour roll all the same, which is what an honour roll is for.

Anathoth, the priestly town of chapter 6, sends fighting men; and Tekoa, which will send a wise woman to bring Absalom home, and later a shepherd called Amos.

verseByVerse.quote: Azmaveth of Baharum, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shagee the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sachar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur, Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite, Hezro of Carmel, Naarai the son of Ezbai, Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Hagri, Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eight more verses of names, and the towns are the point.

These men are not from one clan or one tribe. They come from the hill country and the coastal edge, from Judah and Benjamin and the far north and beyond the Jordan, and one of them is an Ammonite.

The Chronicler is writing for a community of a few thousand people who had come home from one city in one empire. A list like this says something a sermon could not: the people of God has never been a single village, and the men who put the first king of Jerusalem on his throne walked in from thirty different places.

verseByVerse.quote: Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai, Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a leader of the Reubenites, and thirty with him, Hanan the son of Maacah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite, Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel the sons of Hotham the Aroerite, Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite, Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite, Eliel, and Obed, and Jaasiel the Mezobaite.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, in a list of names, Uriah the Hittite.

No note, no explanation; the name sits between Gareb the Ithrite and Zabad the son of Ahlai.

David’s adultery with Uriah’s wife Bathsheba and his killing of Uriah, with Nathan’s rebuke and the child that died, are absent from this book: the largest deliberate omission in Chronicles. Its readers already had 2 Samuel 11–12, and this book was written to show the returned exiles what God had promised David's house, a promise that stood on God's faithfulness, not David's.

But it is not concealment, because here is the name: a foreigner faithful to a king who was not faithful to him, set among the men who made David king. The silence around his name is louder than comment.

Zelek the Ammonite and Ithmah the Moabite close the roll, and the man who led them was the great-grandson of a Moabite woman who came home to Bethlehem behind her mother-in-law.

11.theology:
Twice in six verses the credit is moved off the men and onto God (vv. 9, 14). Neither statement diminishes what the men did; the Chronicler records their feats in detail. He simply refuses to let the achievement be the explanation.

And the kingship rests on a covenant made before the LORD, not on the conquest of a city. David takes Zion in verse 5, but he is already king in verse 3: the covenant made him king, not the conquest.
11.examples:
David would not drink water that had cost three men their safety. Understanding what others spend on us is rarer than courage, and the hardest gifts to receive are the ones we would never have asked anybody to pay for.

Abishai and Benaiah are recorded as not making the first rank, and both went on serving. Some servants can be told exactly where they stand and go on working, and Scripture puts their names in the chronicle.

12.title: Those Who Came to David: Voluntary Allegiance and the Spirit's Work
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the men who came to David at Ziklag, while he could not move about freely because of Saul the son of Kish. And they were among the mighty men who helped him in war.<sup>2</sup>They were bowmen and could shoot arrows and sling stones with either the right or the left hand; they were Benjaminites, Saul's kinsmen.<sup>3</sup>The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, both sons of Shemaah of Gibeah; also Jeziel and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; Beracah, Jehu of Anathoth,<sup>4</sup>Ishmaiah of Gibeon, a mighty man among the thirty and a leader over the thirty; Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan, Jozabad of Gederah,<sup>5</sup>Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah, Shephatiah the Haruphite;<sup>6</sup>Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korahites;<sup>7</sup>And Joelah and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor.<sup>8</sup>From the Gadites there went over to David at the stronghold in the wilderness mighty and experienced warriors, expert with shield and spear, whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were swift as gazelles upon the mountains:<sup>9</sup>Ezer the chief, Obadiah second, Eliab third,<sup>10</sup>Mishmannah fourth, Jeremiah fifth,<sup>11</sup>Attai sixth, Eliel seventh,<sup>12</sup>Johanan eighth, Elzabad ninth,<sup>13</sup>Jeremiah tenth, Machbannai eleventh.<sup>14</sup>These Gadites were officers of the army; the least was a match for a hundred men and the greatest for a thousand.<sup>15</sup>These are the men who crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it was overflowing all its banks, and put to flight all those in the valleys, to the east and to the west.<sup>16</sup>And some of the men of Benjamin and Judah came to the stronghold to David.<sup>17</sup>David went out to meet them and said to them, "If you have come to me in friendship to help me, my heart will be joined to you; but if to betray me to my adversaries, although there is no wrong in my hands, then may the God of our fathers see and rebuke you."<sup>18</sup>Then the Spirit clothed Amasai, chief of the thirty, and he said, "We are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse! Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers! For your God helps you." Then David received them and made them officers of his troops.<sup>19</sup>Some of the men of Manasseh deserted to David when he came with the Philistines for the battle against Saul. (Yet he did not help them, for the rulers of the Philistines took counsel and sent him away, saying, "At peril to our heads he will desert to his master Saul.")<sup>20</sup>As he went to Ziklag, these men of Manasseh deserted to him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zillethai, chiefs of thousands in Manasseh.<sup>21</sup>They helped David against the band of raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and were commanders in the army.<sup>22</sup>For from day to day men came to David to help him, until there was a great army, like an army of God.<sup>23</sup>These are the numbers of the divisions of the armed troops who came to David in Hebron to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, according to the word of the LORD.<sup>24</sup>The men of Judah bearing shield and spear were 6,800 armed troops.<sup>25</sup>Of the Simeonites, mighty men of valor for war, 7,100.<sup>26</sup>Of the Levites 4,600.<sup>27</sup>The prince Jehoiada, of the house of Aaron, and with him 3,700.<sup>28</sup>Zadok, a young man mighty in valor, and twenty-two commanders from his own fathers' house.<sup>29</sup>Of the Benjaminites, the kinsmen of Saul, 3,000, of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul.<sup>30</sup>Of the Ephraimites 20,800, mighty men of valor, famous men in their fathers' houses.<sup>31</sup>Of the half-tribe of Manasseh 18,000, who were expressly named to come and make David king.<sup>32</sup>Of Issachar, men who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do, 200 chiefs, and all their kinsmen under their command.<sup>33</sup>Of Zebulun 50,000 seasoned troops, equipped for battle with all the weapons of war, to help David with singleness of purpose.<sup>34</sup>Of Naphtali 1,000 commanders with whom were 37,000 men armed with shield and spear.<sup>35</sup>Of the Danites 28,600 men equipped for battle.<sup>36</sup>Of Asher 40,000 seasoned troops ready for battle.<sup>37</sup>Of the Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh from beyond the Jordan, 120,000 men armed with all the weapons of war.<sup>38</sup>All these, men of war, arrayed in battle order, came to Hebron with a whole heart to make David king over all Israel. Likewise, all the rest of Israel were of a single mind to make David king.<sup>39</sup>And they were there with David for three days, eating and drinking, for their brothers had made preparation for them.<sup>40</sup>And also their relatives, from as far as Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, came bringing food on donkeys and on camels and on mules and on oxen, abundant provisions of flour, cakes of figs, clusters of raisins, and wine and oil, oxen and sheep, for there was joy in Israel.
12.overview:
The chapter runs backwards before it runs forwards. It opens years before the coronation at Ziklag, where men were slipping out of Israel to join a fugitive: Benjaminites from Saul's own clan (vv. 1-7), Gadites who crossed a flooded Jordan (vv. 8-15), a mixed party vouched for by the Spirit (vv. 16-18), and deserters from Manasseh days before Ziklag burned (vv. 19-22). Then Hebron, the muster of all twelve tribes to make him king (vv. 23-37), and a three-day feast (vv. 38-40).

It has no parallel in Samuel. It answers a question the Chronicler's readers were living inside: how does the kingdom God promised arrive? One person at a time, over years, while nothing looks like working.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Men Who Came While It Cost Something
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The clock turns back to Ziklag, where David cannot move about freely because of Saul (v. 1), and men walk out of Israel to join him: Benjaminites, Saul's own relatives, skilled with bow and sling (vv. 2-7); then Gadites with faces like lions, ranked first to eleventh (vv. 8-13), the least a match for a hundred, who crossed the Jordan in flood (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Every man in this list backed David when the kingdom God had promised was one hunted man in a foreign town. They went by God’s promise, not by David’s chances.
verseByVerse.examples: The Gadites came when the Jordan is hardest to cross and did not wait for the water to drop. Some decisions cannot wait for an easier day.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the men who came to David at Ziklag, while he could not move about freely because of Saul the son of Kish. And they were among the mighty men who helped him in war. They were bowmen and could shoot arrows and sling stones with either the right or the left hand; they were Benjaminites, Saul's kinsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 11 crowned David at Hebron. Chapter 12 goes back to a Philistine border town where he had a price on his head, and names the men who came to him there.

The wilderness of Ziph, the cave at Adullam, the sixteen months under a Philistine warlord's protection: all of it is compressed into one clause, and the reader supplies the rest.

What the clause shows is the cost. Coming to Ziklag was not joining a winning side; it was leaving the country to attach yourself to a wanted man in enemy territory, with no spoil to share and a good chance of ending on a list of traitors.

Then the detail that ought to stop a reader: these were Benjaminites, Saul's kinsmen.

Ambidextrous slinging is what Benjamin was famous for: Ehud was a left-handed Benjaminite, and the tribe once fielded seven hundred left-handed men who could sling at a hair and not miss. These were Benjamin's best, and they walked away from the head of their own clan to stand behind a man from Judah.

Saul had asked men like these whether the son of Jesse would give them fields and vineyards. He was betting that family loyalty would hold them, and it did not hold all of them. Some of his cousins had worked out what God had said about the throne, and went to the man God had named.
verseByVerse.note: Ziklag was David’s base while he was hiding from Saul among the Philistines.

verseByVerse.quote: The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, both sons of Shemaah of Gibeah; also Jeziel and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; Beracah, Jehu of Anathoth, Ishmaiah of Gibeon, a mighty man among the thirty and a leader over the thirty; Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan, Jozabad of Gederah, Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah, Shephatiah the Haruphite; Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korahites; And Joelah and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five verses of names, and the Chronicler is doing with them what he has done all through this book: putting individuals on record.

Two come from Gibeah, Saul's own town; one from Anathoth, the priestly village Jeremiah will come from; and Ishmaiah of Gibeon is marked out as a leader over the thirty. Roughly two dozen men, and about half of them are pinned to a village. That is the point of a list like this to the people first reading it. These are not legends; they are somebody's great-grandfather from a place you can walk to in a day.

The community the Chronicler wrote for was a few thousand returned exiles rebuilding a provincial town, and their besetting fear was that they were too small to matter. He hands them a list of men from Gibeah and Gibeon and Gederah who changed the history of Israel by getting up and walking to Ziklag, and he does not tell them what to make of it.

verseByVerse.quote: From the Gadites there went over to David at the stronghold in the wilderness mighty and experienced warriors, expert with shield and spear, whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were swift as gazelles upon the mountains: Ezer the chief, Obadiah second, Eliab third, Mishmannah fourth, Jeremiah fifth, Attai sixth, Eliel seventh, Johanan eighth, Elzabad ninth, Jeremiah tenth, Machbannai eleventh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gadites lived east of the Jordan, on the far side of the river from everything the story cares about, and chapter 5 has already told how their story ended: the tribes east of the Jordan broke faith with the God of their fathers and were carried into exile. Here, generations earlier, their fighting men are crossing the water in the opposite direction to find a fugitive in a desert hole.

Then a sentence of description, which no army list needs. Mighty and experienced warriors, expert with shield and spear, whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were swift as gazelles upon the mountains. A lion's face is what an enemy sees; a gazelle's speed is what he cannot catch. Somebody who had fought alongside these men remembered them well enough to say both at once.

Then eleven names with a number attached to each: Ezer the chief, Obadiah second, Eliab third, down to Machbannai eleventh. They were ranked, and the ranking was written down, and the man who came eleventh is in Scripture by name.

It is a small thing and it says something about how God keeps records. There is a public and permanent register of an eleventh-best swordsman from a tribe that would later be deported for unfaithfulness, and he is in it because for one season of his life he risked everything on the LORD's anointed. Nothing done for the true King is forgotten because it came eleventh.

verseByVerse.quote: These Gadites were officers of the army; the least was a match for a hundred men and the greatest for a thousand. These are the men who crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it was overflowing all its banks, and put to flight all those in the valleys, to the east and to the west.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses of assessment, and both of them are measurements.

The first: the least was a match for a hundred men and the greatest for a thousand. Even allowing for the way soldiers talk about soldiers, the sentence is telling us that David's desert band had gone from four hundred debtors and malcontents to a corps of professionals, and that the change happened while nothing outwardly was going his way at all.

The first month is Nisan, spring, when the snow comes off Hermon and the Jordan runs high and wide and fast. It is the season nobody crosses if he can help it. It is also the month and the exact condition of the river when Joshua brought Israel over into the land (Joshua 3:15; 4:19), and the reader who has been given chapters of genealogy running back to Adam will hear the echo. But there is no ark here, and no dry ground, and no priests standing in the riverbed. These men crossed it in flood anyway.

And having crossed it they scattered everyone in the valleys east and west: they came out of the water fighting on both banks.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Men of Benjamin and Judah arrive, and David, sold twice already by his countrymen, meets them at the gate and puts the question of their motives before God (v. 17). Then the Spirit clothed Amasai, and an oath comes out as poetry (v. 18). An aside admits that David had marched out with the Philistines against Saul and was sent home by suspicious pagans (vv. 19-20). The trickle becomes a great army, like an army of God (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: In a passage full of men helping David, the Spirit names the real helper: your God helps you (v. 18). The army is real, and it is not the reason David will reign.
verseByVerse.examples: David could not tell friend from assassin by looking, so he put the question before God and waited: what a man does when discernment runs out and a decision still has to be made.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the men of Benjamin and Judah came to the stronghold to David. David went out to meet them and said to them, "If you have come to me in friendship to help me, my heart will be joined to you; but if to betray me to my adversaries, although there is no wrong in my hands, then may the God of our fathers see and rebuke you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A strange combination: Benjamin is Saul's tribe and Judah David's, and men from both arrive together.

David has grounds for suspicion. Keilah, whose town he had just saved, was ready to hand him over; the Ziphites twice betrayed his hiding places; Doeg's report got eighty-five priests killed. A man can smile at you in the morning and sell you before dark.

So he tells them out loud what he is afraid of, and, unable to see inside them, hands the question to the one who can.

He neither pretends the suspicion is absent nor acts on it. He names it and leaves the judgment with God. Then he waits to see what God will do, which turns out to be the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Spirit clothed Amasai, chief of the thirty, and he said, "We are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse! Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers! For your God helps you." Then David received them and made them officers of his troops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David has asked a question he cannot answer, and the answer comes from God himself.

The verb is the ordinary word for putting on a garment: the Spirit clothed himself with the man and wore him, as with Gideon before the trumpet and Zechariah the priest before the words that got him stoned. A man becomes the clothing God speaks through, and what comes out is not the man's own.

Take the title first. Son of Jesse was an insult: Saul used it at his table when he could not bring himself to say the name, Nabal when he refused him food, and later the rebel Sheba used it to call the northern tribes away from David (2 Samuel 20:1). It meant a small farmer’s boy from a village nobody visits.

Amasai picks up the sneer and swears by it, pledging himself by name to the son of Jesse while that man is a fugitive with nothing to offer. The insult becomes the oath. Something like it happens again when a charge fixed to a cross, king of the Jews, turns out to be the plain truth, and the church has sworn by it ever since.

Then peace three times over, and the last clause, For your God helps you, turns from David to God: Amasai hands over an army and in the same breath says the army is not why he will win.

Nobody asked for this. David asked about motives; the Spirit answered with a confession of faith the man had not known a moment earlier he would make. The suspicion was ended by God speaking through the very men under suspicion. The same Spirit, now given to every believer, still gives the confession of the true King that no one makes on his own (1 Corinthians 12:3), and the LORD has never left his anointed standing at a gate without a witness.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the men of Manasseh deserted to David when he came with the Philistines for the battle against Saul. (Yet he did not help them, for the rulers of the Philistines took counsel and sent him away, saying, "At peril to our heads he will desert to his master Saul.") As he went to Ziklag, these men of Manasseh deserted to him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zillethai, chiefs of thousands in Manasseh. They helped David against the band of raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and were commanders in the army.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a sentence the Chronicler could have left out, and did not.

In the days before Gilboa, David and his men were marching with the Philistine army, in line with the enemies of God’s people. The outlaw years had taken him that far.

Five pagan warlords decided the Hebrew could not be trusted and sent him home. They were protecting their own necks, and without knowing it they kept the future king from having Israelite blood on his hands on the day the throne fell vacant.

David did not get himself out; he was sent out, by men who despised him, for reasons of their own. It is not a comfortable rescue, but it is a common one: a man walks into a mess with his eyes open, and God gets him out through the suspicion of the very people he had leaned on. David's standing rested on God's choice, not his record, and God's mercy reached him in the middle of his worst compromise.

Seven officers of Manasseh came over during that retreat and helped David against the band of raiders, probably the Amalekites who burned Ziklag and carried off every wife and child. They arrived days before the worst day of David's life, and he did not know it when he took them in.

verseByVerse.quote: For from day to day men came to David to help him, until there was a great army, like an army of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Day to day. Not a movement, not a rising, not a moment when the country turned. Two men this week and a dozen the next, walking in from Gibeah and Gilead and the far side of the river, one decision at a time, over years, until somebody counted and found there was an army.

That is how it was built, and the Chronicler has spent twenty-one verses proving it by naming them. Each of them made a private calculation about a hunted man and a promise, and got up.

Then the phrase at the end: like an army of God. Hebrew sometimes uses God's name to mean simply very great, and that may be all it means here. But it is also the word Jacob used when the angels of God met him on the road home and he called the place Mahanaim, God's camp (Genesis 32:1–2). The Chronicler is not saying David's men were angels. He is saying that a force assembled out of nothing, around a man with no crown, no capital and no army pay, was best compared to a host not of this earth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the roll of what came to Hebron to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, according to the word of the LORD (v. 23). Twelve tribes, counted: Judah 6,800 and Simeon 7,100; the Levites 4,600, with Jehoiada of Aaron's house and a young man named Zadok (vv. 26-28); Benjamin only 3,000, of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul (v. 29); Ephraim and half-Manasseh in their thousands; two hundred chiefs of Issachar who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do (v. 32); Zebulun's fifty thousand who came with singleness of purpose (v. 33); and at the end the largest contingent of all, 120,000 from beyond the Jordan (v. 37).
verseByVerse.theology: A vast number of free decisions are all placed under a promise God made years before anyone counted anything (v. 23).
verseByVerse.examples: Issachar's two hundred contributed judgment, not numbers. A community that counts only what it can arm will not notice when it has lost the people who understand what is happening and what to do.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the numbers of the divisions of the armed troops who came to David in Hebron to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, according to the word of the LORD. The men of Judah bearing shield and spear were 6,800 armed troops. Of the Simeonites, mighty men of valor for war, 7,100. Of the Levites 4,600. The prince Jehoiada, of the house of Aaron, and with him 3,700. Zadok, a young man mighty in valor, and twenty-two commanders from his own fathers' house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
According to the word of the LORD (v. 23): that clause governs everything counted after it. This is not a coup or an election result. God had spoken about a shepherd boy years before, and the numbers are now catching up with his word.

Judah's number is small, fewer than Simeon's, because Judah had crowned him seven years earlier and fought for him since. The tribe committed longest has the least to prove at the parade.

Then the Levites, with Jehoiada of Aaron's house. The priests came armed, and the Chronicler, who cares more for Levites than any Old Testament writer, counts them among the troops without apology.

And in verse 28, a young man with twenty-two officers behind him: Zadok. The genealogies have probably listed him (6:8); here the story meets him. He will stand by David against Absalom, anoint Solomon at Gihon, and his line will hold the sanctuary so long that Ezekiel still measures a faithful priesthood by the sons of Zadok (Ezekiel 44:15). He enters unannounced, a youngster with a sword who guessed right about the king.

Are 340,000 men credible? The figures may count military units rather than individuals, or have been enlarged in copying; the point is that all Israel came to make David king.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the Benjaminites, the kinsmen of Saul, 3,000, of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul. Of the Ephraimites 20,800, mighty men of valor, famous men in their fathers' houses. Of the half-tribe of Manasseh 18,000, who were expressly named to come and make David king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin sends 3,000, and then comes a clause no propagandist would have written. Of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul.

Most of Saul's tribe had not come. They were not at Hebron out of conviction; they came late, and the record says so. This is the same book that has just spent seven verses honouring Benjaminites who defected to Ziklag when it was dangerous, and it will not let the exception stand in for the tribe. Some of Benjamin were heroes and most of Benjamin held on to a dead king's household as long as it was standing.

Writing to persuade a discouraged community that God's purposes go forward, the Chronicler could have left the sentence out. Instead he reports a divided tribe arriving with mixed motives, and the coronation happens anyway.

Ephraim sends 20,800, famous men in their fathers' houses, and half-Manasseh 18,000 who were expressly named to come and make David king. Somebody in Manasseh sat down and wrote out a list of who was going. The commitment was not a mood on the day; it was written down in advance, name by name, by men who intended to be held to it.

verseByVerse.quote: Of Issachar, men who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do, 200 chiefs, and all their kinsmen under their command.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beside Zebulun's fifty thousand and the east's hundred and twenty thousand, Issachar is entered with two hundred men, counted because they could tell what time it was.

The description has two halves. Understanding the times is diagnosis: seeing what is happening rather than what the last ten years trained you to expect. Knowing what Israel ought to do is harder, and the verse commends men who could say what the next step was, and whose kin would move when they said it.

And what did they discern? Not a trend or a mood. Verse 23 has said it: the kingdom was turning to David according to the word of the LORD. They had heard what God said and could see it arriving, and reading the moment meant lining their tribe up with a promise while the outcome was still open.

That sets a test. The question is whether our reading of the times is governed by what God has said, and whether it ends in something to do. Diagnosis that never reaches a next step is not Issachar's gift; it is talk with a serious face.

verseByVerse.quote: Of Zebulun 50,000 seasoned troops, equipped for battle with all the weapons of war, to help David with singleness of purpose. Of Naphtali 1,000 commanders with whom were 37,000 men armed with shield and spear. Of the Danites 28,600 men equipped for battle. Of Asher 40,000 seasoned troops ready for battle. Of the Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh from beyond the Jordan, 120,000 men armed with all the weapons of war.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zebulun sends 50,000 seasoned troops, equipped for battle with all the weapons of war, to help David with singleness of purpose. Underneath that last phrase the Hebrew says something plainer: not with a double heart. They came without keeping anything back in case David lost.

That is the second thread running through this chapter, alongside the helping. The word heart keeps appearing: David offering to have his heart joined to theirs, Zebulun undivided, and in a few verses the whole assembly arriving with a whole heart. A double heart is not treachery. It is a man who marches with you and privately keeps a line open to the other side, and it is the ordinary condition of most allegiance most of the time.

Then Naphtali with a thousand commanders and thirty-seven thousand men behind them, the Danites 28,600, Asher 40,000. Dan and Zebulun are worth a second look: those are the two tribes the long genealogy of chapters 2 to 8 never gave a list to. They are missing from the family record and they are both here, in the field, in strength, making David king. Absence from a register is not absence from the people of God.

And the largest contingent in Israel comes from the place with the least reason to send one: of the Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh from beyond the Jordan, 120,000 men armed with all the weapons of war. Those tribes had asked Moses for land outside the promise and got it. They were furthest from Hebron, furthest from the sanctuary, and would be the first taken into exile for breaking faith. And on this day they outnumbered everyone. The reach of the king ran out past the river to the people on the edge of the map, and they came.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38–40 — Three Days at the Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter that began with a fugitive ends with a feast. The men come with a whole heart and Israel is of a single mind (v. 38); they eat for three days (v. 39), supplied from the far north (v. 40), and the verdict on the chapter is there was joy in Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: An army was raised and no battle fought. The kingdom of God's choosing arrives as a table with enough for everybody and three days to sit at it.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter's last word is joy (v. 40). Unity under the right king is meant to be enjoyed, not merely endured.

verseByVerse.quote: All these, men of war, arrayed in battle order, came to Hebron with a whole heart to make David king over all Israel. Likewise, all the rest of Israel were of a single mind to make David king. And they were there with David for three days, eating and drinking, for their brothers had made preparation for them. And also their relatives, from as far as Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, came bringing food on donkeys and on camels and on mules and on oxen, abundant provisions of flour, cakes of figs, clusters of raisins, and wine and oil, oxen and sheep, for there was joy in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Arrayed in battle order, and there is no battle: the armed men march to Hebron and sit down to eat for three days.

The provisioning is described in the detail of somebody who was pleased about it, and it came from as far as Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, the longest road.

Nothing in between was engineered by David. He did not recruit the Benjaminites, could not read the men at the gate, and had marched in a Philistine column. The kingdom assembled around him, day by day, according to a word God had spoken before any of it started.

Set the two ends of this chapter beside each other. It opens with one man who cannot walk about in his own country and a handful of defectors slipping into a Philistine town. It closes with every tribe in Israel around a table with more than they can eat, and the narrator's summary is five words long: there was joy in Israel.

And this is the shape the story keeps: a rejected king with a few followers who came while it cost something; then a countless multitude from every tribe, gathered from the edges of the map, at a table somebody else provided. The last book of the Bible calls it the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 7:9; 19:9), and the King at its head is the Son of David rejected first and crowned after. The three days at Hebron were a small foretaste of it.

12.theology:
The verb help runs through the first twenty-two verses (vv. 1, 17, 18, 21, 22), and at the centre the Spirit says whose help it finally is: peace to your helpers! For your God helps you (v. 18). The men’s help is real, but it is not what explains David’s rise; the book said the same at 11:9 and 11:14.

And the whole muster stands under one clause: according to the word of the LORD (v. 23). Hundreds of thousands of free decisions, a Benjaminite weighing his family, a Gadite looking at the river, are each treated as real decisions and all together as the keeping of a promise. Scripture never treats the two as rivals.
12.examples:
Coming to David at Ziklag cost something, and coming to Christ still can: a family's disapproval, a career, a reputation. These men are on record because they moved before the kingdom was visible, which is what faith does (Hebrews 11:1), and it is the Spirit, who moved Amasai, who still gives that faith.

Most of Benjamin came late, and the record does not shut them out. Christ's kingdom receives late-comers and those who have hedged: in his parable the last-hour labourers were paid the same as the first (Matthew 20:1–16), because the wage is grace, not a reward for our record.

And the chapter ends at a table where everyone had enough: the church too is gathered one person at a time, around a feast it did not provide.

13.title: The Ark and Uzzah: When Good Intentions Are Not Enough
13.text: <sup>1</sup>David consulted with the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, with every leader.<sup>2</sup>And David said to all the assembly of Israel, "If it seems good to you and from the LORD our God, let us send abroad to our brothers who remain in all the lands of Israel, as well as to the priests and Levites in the cities that have pasturelands, that they may be gathered to us.<sup>3</sup>Then let us bring again the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul."<sup>4</sup>All the assembly agreed to do so, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people.<sup>5</sup>So David assembled all Israel from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath, to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim.<sup>6</sup>And David and all Israel went up to Baalah, that is, to Kiriath-jearim that belongs to Judah, to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim.<sup>7</sup>And they carried the ark of God on a new cart, from the house of Abinadab, and Uzzah and Ahio were driving the cart.<sup>8</sup>And David and all Israel were celebrating before God with all their might, with song and lyres and harps and tambourines and cymbals and trumpets.<sup>9</sup>And when they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah put out his hand to take hold of the ark, for the oxen stumbled.<sup>10</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and he struck him down because he put out his hand to the ark, and he died there before God.<sup>11</sup>And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzza to this day.<sup>12</sup>And David was afraid of God that day, and he said, "How can I bring the ark of God home to me?"<sup>13</sup>So David did not take the ark home into the city of David, but took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.<sup>14</sup>And the ark of God remained with the household of Obed-edom in his house three months. And the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that he had.
13.overview:
David's first act as king of a united Israel is to fetch the ark. He consults the commanders and the assembly (vv. 1-4), summons the nation (v. 5), and brings the ark from Kiriath-jearim on a new cart with singing and every instrument Israel owned (vv. 6-8). At Chidon the oxen stumble, Uzzah steadies the ark and is struck dead (vv. 9-10). David is angry, then afraid, and diverts the ark to Obed-edom's house, which is blessed for three months (vv. 11-14).

It is not a story about one man's mistake. It is a nation doing a right thing in a way it had never checked against God’s law, with the men who were supposed to carry the ark walking beside the cart it rode on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — All Israel, and a New Cart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David consults every commander and puts the plan to the assembly with two tests, if it seems good to you and from the LORD our God (v. 2), and a reason: we did not seek it in the days of Saul (v. 3). All Israel goes up to Kiriath-jearim for the ark of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim (vv. 5-6). Then the detail on which the chapter turns: a new cart (v. 7), with music going before it (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 3 is the hinge of the book. Saul did not seek the LORD and died for it (10:13-14); David's first act is to seek him. The word will run to the last charge David gives his son.
verseByVerse.examples: The priests and Levites were summoned (v. 2) and then said nothing about the cart. Knowing what God has said is of little use if no one speaks up when it is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: David consulted with the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, with every leader. And David said to all the assembly of Israel, "If it seems good to you and from the LORD our God, let us send abroad to our brothers who remain in all the lands of Israel, as well as to the priests and Levites in the cities that have pasturelands, that they may be gathered to us. Then let us bring again the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom is new and David calls a council: not about the Philistines, who will attack the moment they hear, nor the treasury or the borders, but about a box sitting for decades in a private house in the hills.

He joins two tests in one sentence without ranking them: the people must want it and God must be in it. A king with 340,000 men at his back is asking permission.

Then the reason, the sentence the Chronicler has waited three chapters to write: we did not seek it in the days of Saul.

The verdict on Saul used the same word: he did not seek guidance from the LORD (10:13-14). Nobody forbade the ark. It sat in Abinadab's house through a whole reign because no one got round to it, and a generation grew up that had never seen the throne of God.

That is what neglect looks like from inside: no day came when Israel voted to leave the ark in the hills; there were simply years of days when nobody went to get it.

verseByVerse.quote: All the assembly agreed to do so, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people. So David assembled all Israel from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath, to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim. And David and all Israel went up to Baalah, that is, to Kiriath-jearim that belongs to Judah, to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The assembly agrees, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people, and David summons the nation from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath: the southern edge of the promise and the far northern pass, the whole territory God had described to Abraham and Moses.

For a small community around one rebuilt town in a foreign empire, those two place names are not nostalgia. They are a map of what God said, laid over what they could see out of the window.

Then the ark is described. It is called by the name of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim.

Not a relic, not a national treasure, but a throne: a gold-covered lid with two winged figures facing each other across it, and the God of heaven seated between them. Everything that follows in this chapter depends on that clause being true, and everything that goes wrong in this chapter goes wrong because the men handling it were treating it as furniture.

verseByVerse.quote: And they carried the ark of God on a new cart, from the house of Abinadab, and Uzzah and Ahio were driving the cart. And David and all Israel were celebrating before God with all their might, with song and lyres and harps and tambourines and cymbals and trumpets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new cart: clean, purpose-built, the best they had, and exactly what the Philistines had used. Their priests and diviners had sent the ark home on a new cart behind two milk cows (1 Samuel 6:7–8). Israel copied the method, and nobody asked whether pagans with no law were the right people to learn transport from.

There was a law, and it is specific. At Sinai the Gershonites and Merarites received wagons, but the sons of Kohath none, because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on their shoulders (Numbers 7:9). And the Kohathites must not touch the holy things, or they would die (Numbers 4:15).

So the wagon was not a slip over some small detail. It was the one method God had expressly withheld, for the one object now sitting on it. And the Levites summoned in verse 2 were somewhere in the procession, walking beside the cart.

Meanwhile the noise is tremendous, and every word of the celebration is sincere. But sincerity is not obedience, and none of it was what God had commanded.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Chidon the oxen stumble, Uzzah steadies the ark, and God strikes him down there before God (vv. 9-10). David's first reaction is anger, and the place is named Perez-uzza ever after (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness here is not a mood of God's but what he is. The law had long warned that even Levites must not touch the holy things or they would die (Numbers 4:15), and the warning was itself a mercy, given so Israel could come near and live.
verseByVerse.examples: A reader who has lost someone suddenly may find this passage frightening. It does not teach that every sudden death is a judgment; Jesus denied exactly that (Luke 13:1–5). It records one moment when God made his holiness visible so that a nation would learn to come to him rightly.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah put out his hand to take hold of the ark, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and he struck him down because he put out his hand to the ark, and he died there before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The track up to a threshing floor is rough. The oxen stumble, the cart lurches, and Uzzah does what anyone would do.

The ark had stood for decades in the house of Abinadab, probably his father. Uzzah had lived for years beside the throne of God, and that is the problem: familiarity had worn the edge off the holiest object on earth, and his hand went out without a thought in it.

He was trying to help, and the text does not soften it. He was not stealing or scoffing; he reached out to stop the ark going down in the dirt in front of the nation.

Two things must be held together. The law said no hand touches this, and Uzzah’s did. And the larger fault David will name himself: we did not seek him according to the rule (15:13). The whole expedition was wrong before the oxen stumbled. Uzzah happened to be walking beside a cart that should never have existed, and the carelessness that killed him was the nation's before it was his.

Was God unjust? The law was plain and old, the Levites were present, and the ark was the throne of the holy God, not an object Israel could handle as it liked. Scripture's surprise is not that a sinner died at the throne of God but that sinners are allowed to live near him at all (Lamentations 3:22).

His reflex assumed that God’s honour depends on our protecting it. The God enthroned above the cherubim had not asked to be caught.

verseByVerse.quote: And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzza to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
