Angry, and Scripture says it before it says anything else about him. The music has stopped, a man is lying dead on the road, the greatest day of the reign has collapsed, and the king is furious with God. The Chronicler had every opportunity to leave that clause out and did not.

He names the place for what happened there, and the name is still on the map when the book is written. Israel kept a marker on the spot where God’s holiness had struck, and told the story to its children.

Now remember the verb broken out, because it comes back almost immediately. In the very next chapter the Philistines come up against David and God gives him the victory, and David says: God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood. He calls that place Baal-perazim, "Lord of breaking through." It is the same word. One chapter apart, the same God bursts out, and the first time it destroys a man on a cart track and the second time it scatters an army in front of the king.

The lesson is not that God is unpredictable. There is one God with one kind of power, and Israel had been treating it as manageable: a God who breaks through an army like floodwater is not a God who can be carried about on a farm cart.
verseByVerse.note: “Perez-uzza” means “the breaking out against Uzzah” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Anger turns to fear and fear into a question (v. 12). The ark is diverted to Obed-edom the Gittite instead of the city of David (v. 13), and for three months the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The ark that killed a man in the road blessed a household for a quarter of a year, and nothing about it changed. The presence of God is neither safe nor hostile; it is holy, and whether it meets a man in blessing or in judgment is not chance.
verseByVerse.examples: Fear that asks how to come to God rightly is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). Fear that simply stays away is not, and David did not stay away.

verseByVerse.quote: And David was afraid of God that day, and he said, "How can I bring the ark of God home to me?" So David did not take the ark home into the city of David, but took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. And the ark of God remained with the household of Obed-edom in his house three months. And the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that he had.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the right question. David does not ask God why he did it. He asks, How can I bring the ark of God home to me? Rather than abandoning the project or repeating it louder, the king stops and asks. True fear of God does not drive a man off; it makes him careful about the way in.

The answer took three months. In chapter 15 David will say first that only the Levites may carry the ark, and second that they went wrong because they did not seek God according to the rule. What had been written for centuries had been available the whole time.

Meanwhile the ark goes to Obed-edom the Gittite, perhaps a Philistine from Gath or a Levite from Gath-rimmon; Chronicles later lists him among the gatekeepers, with sixty-two descendants and the note that God blessed him. Either way, the most dangerous object in the world is parked in his yard because the king is afraid to take it home.

The ark Uzzah's hand touched was crowned by a lid with a name. It was the mercy seat, the place where blood was put once a year, on the Day of Atonement, by the high priest, who would not have survived going in without it. No hand touched that lid and lived. And the letter to the Romans uses the mercy seat's own word when it says that God put forward his Son as a propitiation, a sacrifice that turns away wrath, for all to see (Romans 3:25). What could not be touched has been displayed and offered. The hands that reached for Christ came away clean, and the leper he laid his hand on did not make him unclean but was made whole instead (Mark 1:41). Perez-uzza is a real place with a real grave in it, and the way home was opened by One who went to the holy God on our behalf and bore the wrath himself, so that sinners could live near him and be blessed, as Obed-edom’s household was.

13.theology:
Verse 3 carries the word the book is built around, and by chapter 15 David will have learned that seeking God means coming the way he said (15:13). Sincerity was never in doubt; the whole nation was singing with all its might.

And one verb, break out, runs through both halves of God’s dealing with David, against Uzzah (v. 11) and through the Philistines (14:11). Israel's danger was never that God was weak; it was that they had grown used to him.
13.examples:
The man who handled the ark most casually had lived nearest it longest. Long familiarity with holy things is not reverence for them; more often it wears reverence away.

Uzzah's reflex assumed that God's honour is fragile and depends on our steadying it, an assumption that shows up whenever people bend or hide the truth to keep God from looking bad.

David was angry with God, and Scripture records it without excusing or condemning it, then records what the anger became: fear, a question, three months, and a man who came back having learned what he should have known. Anger at God is not the end of a life with him, and the God who met David's failure with a way back still does, because Christ has already come near on our behalf.

14.title: David's House, Victories, and the Pattern of Seeking God
14.text: <sup>1</sup>And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also masons and carpenters to build a house for him.<sup>2</sup>And David knew that the LORD had established him as king over Israel, and that his kingdom was highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel.<sup>3</sup>And David took more wives in Jerusalem, and David fathered more sons and daughters.<sup>4</sup>These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,<sup>5</sup>Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet,<sup>6</sup>Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,<sup>7</sup>Elishama, Beeliada and Eliphelet.<sup>8</sup>When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went out against them.<sup>9</sup>Now the Philistines had come and made a raid in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>10</sup>And David inquired of God, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up, and I will give them into your hand."<sup>11</sup>And he went up to Baal-perazim, and David struck them down there. And David said, "God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim.<sup>12</sup>And they left their gods there, and David gave command, and they were burned.<sup>13</sup>And the Philistines yet again made a raid in the valley.<sup>14</sup>And when David again inquired of God, God said to him, "You shall not go up after them; go around and come against them opposite the balsam trees.<sup>15</sup>And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then go out to battle, for God has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."<sup>16</sup>And David did as God commanded him, and they struck down the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer.<sup>17</sup>And the fame of David went out into all lands, and the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations.
14.overview:
Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen and David reads the gift correctly (vv. 1-2); more wives are taken and thirteen sons listed, Nathan and Solomon among them (vv. 3-7); and the Philistines, provoked by the coronation, attack twice and are beaten twice (vv. 8-17).

Where the chapter is placed makes the point. In 2 Samuel this material comes before the ark narrative; the Chronicler has moved it into the three months while the ark sits at Obed-edom's. The king who did not seek God according to the rule in chapter 13 inquires twice here, and wins twice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hiram sends cedar and craftsmen (v. 1), and David concludes that the LORD had established him as king, for his people's sake (v. 2). Then more wives in Jerusalem and thirteen sons, among them Nathan and Solomon (vv. 3-7).
verseByVerse.theology: An embassy from a great power can persuade a man he has arrived. David read the cedar instead as evidence that God had put him there, for the nation's sake rather than his own.
verseByVerse.examples: Did God approve of polygamy? No. From the beginning marriage was one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24), Jesus restated it (Matthew 19:4–6), and the law forbade the king to multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17). The Old Testament records polygamy honestly, and nearly every time it records the jealousy and grief that came with it. God bore with it for a time; he never held it up as his design.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also masons and carpenters to build a house for him. And David knew that the LORD had established him as king over Israel, and that his kingdom was highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look first at where this chapter sits, in the three months while the ark stands in another man's yard. David's great project has stopped dead and a man lies buried at Perez-uzza, and in that interval a Phoenician king sends cedar, the family grows, and the Philistines are beaten twice. God did not put the reign on hold while David worked out how to carry a box.

Tyre ran the richest port on the coast and traded the timber every great court wanted. Its king's shipment inland is a diplomatic judgment: the new man in the hills is worth an embassy. (Hiram's reign seems to have begun later in David's, so both books probably place the gift by theme rather than date.)

Both halves of David's reading are unusual. He takes an international compliment as evidence about God, the timber as proof of what the LORD had done. And he sees that he has been raised up not for himself but for the sake of his people Israel. A man surrounded by cedar worked out that the cedar was not the point, and neither was he.

Keep the cedar in view. Three chapters on, David will sit in the finished house and find he cannot enjoy it, because the ark is still under a tent.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took more wives in Jerusalem, and David fathered more sons and daughters. These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Beeliada and Eliphelet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David took more wives in Jerusalem, and the Chronicler adds nothing. He does not defend it and he does not condemn it, and the law he knew perfectly well had said that a king must not multiply wives to himself, lest his heart turn away (Deuteronomy 17:17). This book leaves out the affair with Bathsheba altogether, and then writes this sentence, which shows where the trouble in David's house grew from. Amnon and Absalom and Adonijah had been born to earlier wives at Hebron (3:1-2), and this verse enlarges the same crowded house that every one of them would tear apart.

Then thirteen names, and two of them stand next to each other in verse 4. Nathan. Solomon.

Solomon is fourth on a routine list. The man who will build the temple this whole book is heading towards is entered here like any other child born in the capital that year. And beside him is a brother nobody remembers, whose line Luke traces when he comes to give the ancestry of Jesus: Matthew's genealogy comes down through Solomon and Luke's through Nathan, and both of them arrive at the same manger. Two names in one verse of a list, and the whole of the promise runs through the pair of them.

The last name but one is Beeliada, built on the word baal, and in 2 Samuel the same son is called Eliada, built on El, God. Before Baal-worship poisoned the word, baal simply meant lord or master, and Israelites used it of the LORD without a qualm; one of the men who came to Ziklag two chapters back was called Bealiah (12:5), a name joining baal to the divine name. A day came when the word could not be used at all, and God himself said through Hosea that his people would stop calling him my baal and call him my husband instead (Hosea 2:16).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The coronation provokes the war (vv. 8-9). David asks two questions and receives both answers (v. 10), wins, names the place for the way God won (v. 11), and burns the gods the Philistines left on the field (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Chapter 10 ended with Saul's armour in Dagon's house. Here the idols are left lying on a battlefield, and Israel's king does with them what the law said.
verseByVerse.examples: David asked, Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand? He would not assume either from the fact that he had just been crowned.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went out against them. Now the Philistines had come and made a raid in the Valley of Rephaim. And David inquired of God, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up, and I will give them into your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Philistines had left David alone for years: he had been their vassal at Ziklag, and a divided Israel suited them.

They come the moment he is crowned, hunting a person. What they tolerated while Israel was in pieces is intolerable now that a shepherd has the whole country behind him: a united people under God's king is the one arrangement God's enemies cannot live beside.

They raid the Valley of Rephaim, almost at Jerusalem's gates. David, who had beaten them all his life and could have moved on instinct, stops and asks.

He will not presume that a crown is a licence to act, or that a righteous cause guarantees a result. The last king went to Endor because heaven had stopped answering; this one puts a plain question to God and gets a plain answer.

David inquired of God through the priest with the ephod, the priestly garment used in asking God’s will (1 Samuel 23:9–12). Christians seek guidance through God’s completed word, prayer and wise counsel, led by the Spirit given to God's children (Romans 8:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And he went up to Baal-perazim, and David struck them down there. And David said, "God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim. And they left their gods there, and David gave command, and they were burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The picture is the bank of a dry stream bed giving way in a spring storm: water building behind an obstruction until the obstruction is simply gone. David does not say he outfought them. God burst through, by my hand, which is the whole doctrine of this book in three words: the flood was God’s and the sword was David’s.

Breaking out is the word used a chapter ago of Uzzah. David had been angry at a God who breaks out; now, in a field of dead Philistines, he makes the same word a name to bless God by. Nothing about God had altered between the two hillsides. It was David who had changed.

Then the idols, lying where their people dropped them running, and the king does what the law said: burn the carved images. He got the ark wrong; he does not get this wrong. A man just taught what obedience costs is careful with the next commandment he meets.

Second Samuel says David carried the idols away (2 Samuel 5:21); here he had them burned. They took them, and then burned them, as the law required (Deuteronomy 7:5).
verseByVerse.note: “Baal-perazim” means “Lord of breaking through” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Wait for the Sound in the Trees
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines return, David asks again, and this time the orders are different: go around, and attack at the sound in the balsam trees (vv. 13-15). He obeys, and the LORD brings the fear of him upon all nations (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Yesterday's answer is not today's orders. God said go up once and says do not go up now, about the same enemy in the same field, and the only way to know was to ask again.
verseByVerse.examples: Much of the life of faith is like this: not inventing victories but following where God has already gone, and moving when he makes the way plain.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Philistines yet again made a raid in the valley. And when David again inquired of God, God said to him, "You shall not go up after them; go around and come against them opposite the balsam trees. And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then go out to battle, for God has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They come back. Same enemy, same valley, and David has a proven method.

And when David again inquired of God: these are the most impressive words in the chapter. He had a recent answer from God for this exact situation, and a battlefield named after the result. Repeating it would not have felt like presumption; it would have felt like faith. He asked anyway.

And the orders had changed. You shall not go up after them; go around and come against them opposite the balsam trees. Not up the valley this time but round behind, and then wait.

The signal is a rustle overhead that sounds like men on the move, a sound no commander can arrange and no scout can fake, and which means that the God who broke out like a flood is already in the trees ahead of the infantry. By the time David's men step out of cover the fighting has begun without them. His whole task is to move when he hears it and finish what somebody else has started.

Two chapters ago the men gathering to a fugitive were described as an army like the army of God. Here the army of God is in the treetops going out ahead of them, and the only thing required of Israel is to keep step with a march they can hear and cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: And David did as God commanded him, and they struck down the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer. And the fame of David went out into all lands, and the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And David did as God commanded him: seven words that could not have been written of chapter 13. Fifteen miles of pursuit drove the Philistines off Israel's ridge onto the coastal plain. (2 Samuel 5:25 has Geba, a nearby town easily confused with Gibeon.)

Then the last verse does what the first two did: his name travelled, and God carried the fear. The chapter opens with the LORD establishing him and closes with the LORD frightening the nations, and the cedar, the sons and the victories sit between the two. Neither David's asking nor his obeying made the Philistines run. God went out in front, in the treetops, where nobody could see him and everybody could hear him coming.

14.theology:
Twice David asks before he moves, and the second time he was told something different (vv. 10, 14). God's word to us yesterday is not a standing order for tomorrow.

The chapter begins and ends with God’s action (vv. 2, 17). In between David fights and says God broke through by my hand (v. 11), the same refusal to separate God's work from the man's that ran through chapter 11.
14.examples:
Everyone draws a conclusion from his own success; the test is what he concludes (v. 2). David concluded that God had put him where he was for others' benefit.

Scripture often reports a sin without comment and lets the reader watch it grow, as with the wives of verse 3.

And David went out only when God had gone out ahead of him. The Son of David has gone ahead of his people into the battle that matters most, and won it: But take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33).

15.title: The Ark Comes Right: Worship on God's Terms
15.text: <sup>1</sup>David built houses for himself in the city of David. And he prepared a place for the ark of God and pitched a tent for it.<sup>2</sup>Then David said that no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD had chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever.<sup>3</sup>And David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the LORD to its place, which he had prepared for it.<sup>4</sup>And David gathered together the sons of Aaron and the Levites:<sup>5</sup>of the sons of Kohath, Uriel the chief, with 120 of his brothers;<sup>6</sup>of the sons of Merari, Asaiah the chief, with 220 of his brothers;<sup>7</sup>of the sons of Gershom, Joel the chief, with 130 of his brothers;<sup>8</sup>of the sons of Elizaphan, Shemaiah the chief, with 200 of his brothers;<sup>9</sup>of the sons of Hebron, Eliel the chief, with 80 of his brothers;<sup>10</sup>of the sons of Uzziel, Amminadab the chief, with 112 of his brothers.<sup>11</sup>Then David summoned the priests Zadok and Abiathar, and the Levites Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab,<sup>12</sup>and said to them, "You are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites. Consecrate yourselves, you and your brothers, so that you may bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, to the place that I have prepared for it.<sup>13</sup>Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule."<sup>14</sup>So the priests and the Levites consecrated themselves to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>15</sup>And the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD.<sup>16</sup>David also commanded the chiefs of the Levites to appoint their brothers as the singers who should play loudly on musical instruments, on harps and lyres and cymbals, to raise sounds of joy.<sup>17</sup>So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brothers Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari, their brothers, Ethan the son of Kushaiah;<sup>18</sup>and with them their brothers of the second order, Zechariah, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, and Mikneiah, and the gatekeepers Obed-edom and Jeiel.<sup>19</sup>The singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were to sound bronze cymbals;<sup>20</sup>Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah were to play harps according to Alamoth;<sup>21</sup>but Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah were to lead with lyres according to the Sheminith.<sup>22</sup>Chenaniah, leader of the Levites in music, should direct the music, for he understood it.<sup>23</sup>Berechiah and Elkanah were to be gatekeepers for the ark.<sup>24</sup>Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, should blow the trumpets before the ark of God. Obed-edom and Jehiah were to be gatekeepers for the ark.<sup>25</sup>So David and the elders of Israel and the commanders of thousands went to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the house of Obed-edom with rejoicing.<sup>26</sup>And because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.<sup>27</sup>David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, as also were all the Levites who were carrying the ark, and the singers and Chenaniah the leader of the music of the singers. And David wore a linen ephod.<sup>28</sup>So all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting, to the sound of the horn, trumpets, and cymbals, and made loud music on harps and lyres.<sup>29</sup>And as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came to the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart.
15.overview:
David prepares a tent in Jerusalem and states the rule he has learned: only Levites may carry the ark (vv. 1-3). Six Levitical houses are mustered (vv. 4-10); priests and chiefs consecrate themselves, and David confesses that the first attempt failed because we did not seek him according to the rule (vv. 11-15). Musicians and gatekeepers are appointed (vv. 16-24). The ark goes up with shouting and sacrifice, the king in a Levite's linen (vv. 25-28), and Michal watches from a window and despises him (v. 29).

The correction is not from loud worship to quiet. There is more music here than in chapter 13. What changed is that somebody found out how God had said to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — This Time, According to the Rule
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David pitches a tent for the ark (v. 1) and states what he has learned: only the Levites may carry it, for the LORD had chosen them (v. 2). Six Levitical houses are mustered, 862 men (vv. 4-10). Zadok, Abiathar and the chiefs are told to consecrate themselves, and David says out loud what went wrong (vv. 11-13). They consecrate themselves, and the ark goes up on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 turns the book's key word back on the king. David set out to seek God and found that wanting to was not enough: seeking him includes coming the way he said.
verseByVerse.examples: When God's people have done something wrongly in public, the way back is the one David took: find out from Scripture what should have been done, say so plainly, and do it right in front of the same people, trusting the God who forgives the confessed sin (1 John 1:9) and lets his people begin again.

verseByVerse.quote: David built houses for himself in the city of David. And he prepared a place for the ark of God and pitched a tent for it. Then David said that no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD had chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever. And David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the LORD to its place, which he had prepared for it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three months on, the ark is in another man's yard, and the first thing verse 1 reports is that David built houses for himself.

Then he prepared a place for the ark. The Chronicler leaves the two clauses in that order. He is not scoring a point; he is telling the truth about how things get done.

From this verse until Solomon's temple Israel has two sanctuaries: the tabernacle with its bronze altar at Gibeon, still standing at the end of the book, and the ark in David's tent. It is Chronicles that tells us where the old one stood; Kings mentions Solomon's sacrifices at Gibeon without saying why he went there (1 Kings 3:4; 2 Chronicles 1:3).

Somewhere in the three months he found out how the ark was to be carried. The instruction had been in writing for centuries, available to anyone who asked a priest. A man who could raise 340,000 soldiers needed a funeral to make him open the book, and it is often a disaster that sends us back to Scripture.

Then, for the second time, David assembled all Israel. A man who has led a nation into a public disaster must decide whether he will ever ask them to assemble again, and David summons the same crowd to the same road to watch him do it properly.

The reason for the rule is not that Levites are safer or stronger but that the LORD had chosen them. The regulation was never crowd control. God had said who.

verseByVerse.quote: And David gathered together the sons of Aaron and the Levites: of the sons of Kohath, Uriel the chief, with 120 of his brothers; of the sons of Merari, Asaiah the chief, with 220 of his brothers; of the sons of Gershom, Joel the chief, with 130 of his brothers; of the sons of Elizaphan, Shemaiah the chief, with 200 of his brothers; of the sons of Hebron, Eliel the chief, with 80 of his brothers; of the sons of Uzziel, Amminadab the chief, with 112 of his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six houses of Levi, counted out. Kohath 120 with Uriel at their head, Merari 220 under Asaiah, Gershom 130 under Joel, and then three clans from within Kohath: Elizaphan 200, Hebron 80, Uzziel 112.

Eight hundred and sixty-two men, named by family, with their chiefs. And verse 4 opens with a distinction the first attempt had ignored: the sons of Aaron and the Levites. Priests and Levites are two orders with two kinds of work, and the first attempt had used neither.

Then look at which families are called. Kohath, Merari and Gershom are Levi's three sons, and all three are here, but the list does not stop there. Elizaphan and Hebron and Uzziel are Kohathite houses too, so four of the six contingents come from one branch of the family, and it is the branch the law had charged with the holy things themselves. When the wagons were handed out at Sinai, Gershon received two and Merari four and Kohath none at all, because what Kohath carried went on the shoulder (Numbers 7:6–9).

So this is not a general call for volunteers with strong backs. David has gone to the exact clan the regulation named, and then summoned the rest of the tribe to walk with them.

Set that against chapter 13, where nobody had been appointed and the ark went up the road in the care of whoever happened to be walking beside it. The difference is not zeal; there was no shortage of zeal at Chidon. This time somebody worked out who God had said should do the job, found them, and wrote down their names, and the Chronicler records the numbers because this careful counting is what repentance looked like.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David summoned the priests Zadok and Abiathar, and the Levites Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab, and said to them, "You are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites. Consecrate yourselves, you and your brothers, so that you may bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, to the place that I have prepared for it. Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David sends for the two high priests and the six Levite chiefs. Zadok is here, the young man with a sword from chapter 12, now at the head of the priesthood, and beside him Abiathar, the one man who got out of Nob alive when Saul had eighty-five priests killed in a day. Two survivors of two very different disasters, summoned to handle the ark.

And then verse 13, which is the sentence this whole part of the book has been moving towards.

Take it in pieces, because every clause is doing work. You did not carry it: the Levites are told, to their faces, that the failure was theirs too; the men who knew the law had stood by and watched the cart go past. The LORD our God broke out against us: the same verb as Perez-uzza and Baal-perazim, and this time David says it was against us, not against Uzzah alone. And then the confession itself: we did not seek him according to the rule.

That is the word this book keeps returning to (10:14; 13:3). Seeking God is not only a matter of wanting him badly enough; it includes finding out how he has said to come and then coming that way, and the difference had cost a life.

What he does not say is as striking. Not that Uzzah was careless, or the oxen stumbled, or God was severe, though three months earlier he had been angry enough to think it. He says we, before the men who did the carrying and a nation that had watched it happen, and then gets on with the arrangements.

verseByVerse.quote: So the priests and the Levites consecrated themselves to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel. And the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consecration meant washing, laundering, abstaining, and setting a distance from ordinary life for a set time: slow, unglamorous, invisible in a procession. The men who would touch the poles took time making themselves fit, and the crowd would never know.

Then verse 15, and the Chronicler writes it with unusual care. And the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD.

The rings on each side of the ark had held those poles since it was made, and the poles were never to be removed (Exodus 25:14–15). Everything needed to carry it correctly had been attached to it all along, including on the day it rode a cart.

The authority is stated twice: as Moses commanded, according to the word of the LORD. For readers who might think an old book of regulations a lower thing than a living encounter with God, to obey what Moses wrote is to obey the LORD.

Not wheels or oxen: the throne of God moved through Israel on the backs of men made ready for it. Centuries later the God enthroned above those cherubim came among his people in flesh, the Word who dwelt among us (John 1:14), and the One no hand could touch at Perez-uzza was carried in his mother's arms.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the ark moves, the music is organised. David tells the chiefs of the Levites to appoint singers with harps and lyres and cymbals to raise sounds of joy (v. 16). Three names head the list, Heman, Asaph and Ethan on bronze cymbals (vv. 17-19), with a second order behind them on harps and lyres tuned two different ways (vv. 20-21). Chenaniah directs, for he understood it (v. 22); gatekeepers are set for the ark itself; and seven priests are to blow the trumpets in front of it (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Nine verses of appointments stand between the confession and the procession. Worship careful about God's word turns out to have more music in it, not less.
verseByVerse.examples: Not everyone is a Heman or an Asaph. Most of those named here played in the second rank or kept a door, and their names are in Scripture too.

verseByVerse.quote: David also commanded the chiefs of the Levites to appoint their brothers as the singers who should play loudly on musical instruments, on harps and lyres and cymbals, to raise sounds of joy. So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brothers Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari, their brothers, Ethan the son of Kushaiah; and with them their brothers of the second order, Zechariah, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, and Mikneiah, and the gatekeepers Obed-edom and Jeiel. The singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were to sound bronze cymbals;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the ark moves, David appoints the choir.

One reading of chapter 13 concludes the lesson was to be more solemn, and this verse forbids it: the aim is to raise sounds of joy, and getting the rule right is what made the shouting safe.

Then three names on the cymbals: Heman, Asaph and Ethan.

Asaph's name stands over a dozen psalms still sung, including the one that admits a man nearly lost his footing over how well the wicked were doing. Two more psalms name a Heman and an Ethan: the darkest prayer in the book, ending on the word darkness (Psalm 88), and the meditation on God’s covenant with David that asks how long the promise will lie in ruins (Psalm 89).

Chapter 6 traced Heman to Kohath and Asaph to Gershom, and Ethan is of the sons of Merari: one chief musician from each of Levi's sons, side by side. No branch was left out of the noise.

Behind them eleven second-rank players, written into Scripture by name. Three men are remembered for the cymbals; these eleven were the sound.

Nobody in that street knew the men on the cymbals were being handed a job that would outlast the city, and that Israel would pray their words in a foreign country centuries later.

Is this a model for church worship? David organised music by God’s command (2 Chronicles 29:25), for the temple. The New Testament calls the church to sing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Colossians 3:16) but sets no pattern of choirs or instruments. Some Reformed churches sing unaccompanied for that reason; others use instruments as aids. Both are faithful if the words come first and all is done in order (1 Corinthians 14:40).

verseByVerse.quote: Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah were to play harps according to Alamoth; but Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah were to lead with lyres according to the Sheminith. Chenaniah, leader of the Levites in music, should direct the music, for he understood it. Berechiah and Elkanah were to be gatekeepers for the ark. Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, should blow the trumpets before the ark of God. Obed-edom and Jehiah were to be gatekeepers for the ark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alamoth and Sheminith are most likely a higher register and a lower, two settings kept distinct so the sound had structure, not volume alone. Both words stand in psalm titles: somebody kept the performance notes.

And a director is appointed, for he understood it.

(The Hebrew word behind music can also mean carrying, so some versions make Chenaniah director of the carrying; either way the reason is the same.) He got the post because he knew what he was doing, and nothing is added about his piety. That is no slight on piety; leading musicians is a competence, and a consecrated man who cannot hear a wrong note is not the man for it.

Berechiah and Elkanah are stationed at the ark itself. Somebody had to stand between the crowd and the thing that had killed a man, and the post was given names and an order rather than left to whoever was nearest, as at the threshing floor.

Seven priests go in front with trumpets, the one instrument God specified himself: two of hammered silver, to call the congregation, move the camp, go out to war, and sound on the day of your gladness over the burnt offerings (Numbers 10:1–10). Every one of those occasions is happening at once on this road.

So the column has silver trumpets at its head, Levites with poles behind, cymbals and strings, doorkeepers beside the ark, a director who understood music, and a king dressed like a porter. Not one of those posts existed in chapter 13.

And Obed-edom, named three times here (vv. 18, 21, 24) and probably the same man, is the one whose house the ark is leaving. He could have watched it go. Instead he took a post at the door and walked beside it to Jerusalem, and his descendants are still on the temple roster later, sixty-two of them, with a note that God blessed him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David and the elders and the commanders go down to fetch the ark from Obed-edom's house with rejoicing (v. 25). Because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark, seven bulls and seven rams are sacrificed (v. 26). The king is dressed in fine linen, the same as every Levite carrying the ark, with a linen ephod (v. 27), and all Israel brings it up with shouting and horns and cymbals (v. 28). And in the last verse Michal the daughter of Saul watches from a window and despises him (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The sacrifice in verse 26 is thanks for being kept alive: nobody had forgotten the threshing floor.
verseByVerse.examples: It is possible to stand at a window while God comes near and feel only contempt for those rejoicing (v. 29); the danger is not only for Saul's daughter.

verseByVerse.quote: So David and the elders of Israel and the commanders of thousands went to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the house of Obed-edom with rejoicing. And because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Same road as last time. Same ark. Same king, and a good many of the same people, walking past a place with a grave in it and a name that meant the breaking out against Uzzah.

And then a clause that only makes sense if you remember why they were frightened: because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.

God helped the carriers. That is the reason given for the sacrifice, and it means the men under the poles got to the end of the journey alive and knew perfectly well that this was not a foregone conclusion. Fourteen animals were killed in thanksgiving for a walk completed. Doing the right thing in the right way had not made these men casual about being near God; it had simply made it possible to be near him.

Helping is the word this part of the book keeps using. Men came to David to help him, and the Spirit told him that his God helped him, and now God helps the men carrying the throne of God up a hill. Every one of them had two hands on a pole and every one of them was being held.

verseByVerse.quote: David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, as also were all the Levites who were carrying the ark, and the singers and Chenaniah the leader of the music of the singers. And David wore a linen ephod. So all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting, to the sound of the horn, trumpets, and cymbals, and made loud music on harps and lyres.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The clothing list shows that the king is not set apart. The king is in the same fine linen as the porters and the choir. He has come out in the uniform of the men doing the lifting, and over it he has put an ephod, which is not royal dress at all. It is what a priest wore, and what the boy Samuel wore in the sanctuary at Shiloh.

He is not seizing the priesthood; a later king of Judah tried that with a censer in his hand and came out of the temple a leper (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). He is doing something else, and it is deliberate. On the day the throne of God enters his capital, David takes off the clothes that mark him out from everyone else and dresses like a servant of the sanctuary.

There is a night in an upper room when the Lord of glory got up from supper, laid aside his outer garments, tied a towel round himself and washed the feet of the men who were about to abandon him (John 13:3–5). David in linen at the head of a procession is a small picture of a very great one: the Son who laid aside not a robe but the privileges of glory, and humbled himself to death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8).

verseByVerse.quote: And as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came to the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends at a window.

She is called the daughter of Saul. She had been David's wife since he brought Saul two hundred Philistine foreskins for her, and she had let him down through a window once before to save his life. The Chronicler gives none of that. He gives her father's name, and the reader who has come through chapter 10 knows exactly what that means: the house that did not seek the ark in the days of Saul is watching the ark arrive.

2 Samuel tells the rest: the row in the doorway, her sarcasm, his answer that he would be more contemptible than this, and the note that she had no child to the day of her death. The Chronicler cuts it all. He stops at six words: she despised him in her heart. Nothing was said. Nobody in the street knew. The contempt stayed inside and it was complete already.

Look at the two vantage points the verse gives. Down in the road there is a king in a linen tunic with no crown on, shouting, out of breath, in the middle of a crowd, going up the hill with the poles ahead of him. Up in the house there is a window, and a person standing at it, and everything she was raised to value telling her that what she is looking at is beneath the dignity of a throne.

She was not wrong about the dignity. That was the whole point of the linen. What she could not see from a window was that the man dancing in the street had understood something her father never did: that when God comes to live among his people there is no dignity worth keeping that would stop a man from going out to meet him.

15.theology:
Verse 13 completes a lesson begun at 10:14: wanting God is not the same as coming the way he has said. The remedy was not less enthusiasm; it was the book of Moses, read, and 862 men called by name.

Verse 15 joins two authorities as one: as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD. And in verse 26 the God whose rule they kept is the one who helped the Levites who were carrying the ark. Obedience did not put them beyond needing help; it put them where help was given. The same holds for Christ's people, who obey not to earn God's nearness but because in Christ he has already come near, and whose obedience is upheld by his Spirit.
15.examples:
David confessed in the first person plural and named the exact fault. Then he organised the thing properly, which is repentance that goes beyond words.

Chenaniah led the music because he understood music. Competence is a genuine qualification, not something unspiritual, and the chapter most concerned with doing things God's way says so.

Obed-edom saw the ark taken from his house and joined the procession as a doorkeeper. A blessing that moves on can be followed rather than mourned.

16.title: The Psalm of Praise: The Ark at Rest and the Song That Fills the Earth
16.text: <sup>1</sup>And they brought in the ark of God and set it inside the tent that David had pitched for it, and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before God.<sup>2</sup>And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD<sup>3</sup>and distributed to all Israel, both men and women, to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins.<sup>4</sup>Then he appointed some of the Levites as ministers before the ark of the LORD, to invoke, to thank, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Asaph was the chief, and second to him were Zechariah, Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-edom, and Jeiel, who were to play harps and lyres; Asaph was to sound the cymbals,<sup>6</sup>and Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests were to blow trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant of God.<sup>7</sup>Then on that day David first appointed that thanksgiving be sung to the LORD by Asaph and his brothers.<sup>8</sup>Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples!<sup>9</sup>Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works!<sup>10</sup>Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice!<sup>11</sup>Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually!<sup>12</sup>Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles and the judgments he uttered,<sup>13</sup>O offspring of Israel his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!<sup>14</sup>He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth.<sup>15</sup>Remember his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations,<sup>16</sup>the covenant that he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac,<sup>17</sup>which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute, to Israel as an everlasting covenant,<sup>18</sup>saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan, as your portion for an inheritance."<sup>19</sup>When you were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it,<sup>20</sup>wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people,<sup>21</sup>he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account,<sup>22</sup>saying, "Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!"<sup>23</sup>Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Tell of his salvation from day to day.<sup>24</sup>Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!<sup>25</sup>For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised, and he is to be feared above all gods.<sup>26</sup>For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens.<sup>27</sup>Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and joy are in his place.<sup>28</sup>Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength!<sup>29</sup>Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering and come before him! Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness;<sup>30</sup>tremble before him, all the earth; yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved.<sup>31</sup>Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice, and let them say among the nations, "The LORD reigns!"<sup>32</sup>Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; let the field exult, and everything in it!<sup>33</sup>Then shall the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth.<sup>34</sup>Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!<sup>35</sup>Say also: "Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather and deliver us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise.<sup>36</sup>Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting!" Then all the people said, "Amen!" and praised the LORD.<sup>37</sup>So David left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the covenant of the LORD to minister regularly before the ark as each day required,<sup>38</sup>and also Obed-edom and his sixty-eight brothers, while Obed-edom, the son of Jeduthun, and Hosah were to be gatekeepers.<sup>39</sup>And he left Zadok the priest and his brothers the priests before the tabernacle of the LORD in the high place that was at Gibeon<sup>40</sup>to offer burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of burnt offering regularly morning and evening, to do all that is written in the Law of the LORD that he commanded Israel.<sup>41</sup>With them were Heman and Jeduthun and the rest of those chosen and expressly named to give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever.<sup>42</sup>Heman and Jeduthun had trumpets and cymbals for the music and instruments for sacred song. The sons of Jeduthun were appointed to the gate.<sup>43</sup>Then all the people departed each to his house, and David went home to bless his household.
16.overview:
The ark is set in the tent, offerings are made, and David gives bread, meat and a raisin cake to every person present, men and women alike (vv. 1-3). A permanent order of Levitical musicians is created, and thanksgiving is first appointed to be sung (vv. 4-7). The psalm follows in three movements: remember the covenant with Abraham (vv. 8-22), sing to the LORD all the earth (vv. 23-33), and give thanks, for his steadfast love endures forever (vv. 34-36). Then the standing arrangements, the ark in Jerusalem and the altar at Gibeon (vv. 37-42), and everyone goes home (v. 43).

The psalm draws on Psalms 105, 96 and 106, and moves from memory to mission to hope.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Ark at Rest, and a Loaf for Everybody
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ark is set in the tent with burnt offerings and peace offerings (v. 1). David blesses the people and gives food to all Israel, both men and women (vv. 2-3). Levites are stationed before the ark to invoke, to thank, and to praise the LORD, Asaph at their head (vv. 4-6), and verse 7 dates the founding of the thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.theology: Worship at the ark ended not in awe alone but in a meal shared from the peace offerings (v. 3), and nobody was left out.
verseByVerse.examples: Thanksgiving was given a place and people to carry it on (v. 4). A church does well to make room for thanks on purpose rather than leave it to mood.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought in the ark of God and set it inside the tent that David had pitched for it, and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before God. And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD and distributed to all Israel, both men and women, to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set it down. After Shiloh, the Philistine capture, decades in a private house on a hill, a death on a threshing floor and three months in a Gittite's yard, the throne of God is set down in a tent in the capital, and the men who carried it straighten up.

The two offerings differ. A burnt offering went up entirely in smoke; a peace offering was shared, part burned, part to the priest, and the rest eaten by the worshipper and his family before God. One says everything here is yours; the other says come and eat with me.

Then David blesses the people in the LORD's name, as Aaron's sons were commissioned to do, and does something that follows straight from the peace offering.

To each, and the text goes out of its way to say men and women. Not just the elders or the Levites who had done the work: a woman at the back of the assembly went home with bread, meat and a raisin cake from the king, off the altar of God.

That is the day at ground level: a hand held out with food in it, to everyone, without a list. The God who came to live among his people set a table when he came, and Scripture's last picture of the finished work is a supper with a seat for every nation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he appointed some of the Levites as ministers before the ark of the LORD, to invoke, to thank, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel. Asaph was the chief, and second to him were Zechariah, Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-edom, and Jeiel, who were to play harps and lyres; Asaph was to sound the cymbals, and Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests were to blow trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verbs, and they are the job description. To invoke is to bring God's acts to remembrance out loud. To thank is to name what he has done as a gift. To praise is to say what he is like. That is the whole of a worship service in three words, and from this day it is somebody's occupation.

Nothing in the law of Moses had said anything about this. The regulations were about blood and bread and incense and the fabric of a tent; there is no order of singers in the book of Leviticus. David reads what has been commanded, obeys it exactly, and then adds a permanent choir, and the Chronicler is entirely happy about it. Getting the rule right at the threshing floor did not turn David into a man who would only ever do what was on the list.

Asaph is the chief. Behind him nine players on harps and lyres, including Obed-edom again, and Asaph himself on the cymbals. And two priests, Benaiah and Jahaziel, to blow trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant of God.

Regularly. The trumpets that had sounded in front of the procession are not put away when the excitement is over. Someone will blow them tomorrow, and the day after, and on the wet ordinary morning when there is no crowd. The most striking word in the paragraph is the dullest one in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then on that day David first appointed that thanksgiving be sung to the LORD by Asaph and his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A date: the thing the readers did every day in the temple began the day the ark came home.

The psalm is recognisable: the opening of Psalm 105, almost all of Psalm 96, and the first and last verses of Psalm 106. Whether it was assembled from three songs or three songs grew from it cannot be settled, and need not be.

Its shape is deliberate: backwards, outwards, forwards. Remember what God swore to your fathers; tell the nations who is on the throne; gather us home. Israel's worship began the day it was given a memory, a mission and a hope, in that order.

Its last lines, gather and deliver us from among the nations, fit any time Israel was scattered, and the returned exiles would have heard them gladly.
verseByVerse.note: David’s psalm (vv. 8–36) is woven from parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–22 — Remember: the Covenant with Abraham
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first movement is memory: give thanks and make his deeds known among the peoples (vv. 8-9), and seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually (vv. 10-11). Remember the covenant made with Abraham, sworn to Isaac, confirmed to Jacob, with the land as its content (vv. 15-18), made when the patriarchs were few in number and God rebuked kings on their account (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 10 and 11 carry the word the book turns on: the congregation is told to seek God's face, and to keep seeking after they have found it.
verseByVerse.examples: To seek his presence continually (v. 11) is the believer's ordinary daily work, not a stage to be outgrown: turning to God in his word and in prayer, today and again tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples! Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works! Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice! Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually! Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles and the judgments he uttered, O offspring of Israel his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The opening commands already have the nations in view. On the day a tent was pitched on a Judean ridge, the congregation is told that what has happened to them is news for everybody else.

Verse 9 joins two commands to sing with a harder one: tell. Telling is not performance or liturgy; it is talking about what God has done, out loud, to someone, the way one person tells another a piece of news.

Then verses 10 and 11, and three times, seek. The word has carried the book since the verdict on Saul, and what is sought changes each time. In chapter 13 David sought it, the neglected ark; in chapter 15 he had learned to seek him according to the rule. Here it is neither the ark nor the rule but God himself: seek his presence continually, literally his face.

That is where the sequence was travelling. A man can get an object into a tent and keep a rule exactly, and neither is wanting the face of God. David was taken through both to arrive at the third.

And continually rules out the obvious mistake. The ark has just been found and sits a few steps away, and the command is to go on seeking, every day. Having God does not mean the seeking stops; and the Spirit God sends into his children's hearts is the one who keeps them seeking (Galatians 4:6).

Verse 12 turns verse 9 inward: the same wondrous works are to be told to outsiders and remembered by insiders, and a congregation that stops remembering will soon have nothing to tell.

A word enters that will not leave the psalm: judgments. First they are the judgments he uttered (v. 12), then they are in all the earth (v. 14), and at the end the trees sing because he comes to judge the earth: what he has said, what he is doing everywhere, what he is coming to do, all grounds for singing.

The congregation is addressed by name in verse 13, not as achievers but as his chosen ones, children of Jacob, a man who spent his life being carried by God rather than impressing him. The command to seek rests on that choice.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth. Remember his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations, the covenant that he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac, which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute, to Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan, as your portion for an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our God, and in all the earth (v. 14): the God of one people rules the whole world, and the rest of the psalm holds both together.

Verse 15 differs from Psalm 105:8, where he remembers his covenant forever. Here Israel is told to remember it: what God never forgets, Israel must keep in mind.

Both are true, and the second depends on the first. The covenant is safe whether or not anyone in Jerusalem thinks of it before breakfast. But people who forget it live like people with no covenant, and Israel had just come through a generation of exactly that: nobody cancelled the ark; they simply stopped thinking about it.

What is remembered is a chain of three: made with Abraham, sworn to Isaac, confirmed to Jacob. The promise outlived all three by a thousand years before this psalm was sung, and by three thousand since.

The congregation singing of the land of Canaan is standing on it. The first readers of this book sang the same words living on a fraction of it under a Persian governor, a harder and better thing to do.

Does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people and modern Israel? Dispensationalists (Christians who read God’s promises to Israel as awaiting a separate, literal fulfilment) hold that it does: God’s promise to Abraham’s physical descendants remains literal, with its borders, and awaits fulfilment. But Joshua says that Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed (Joshua 21:45), and the New Testament widens the promise: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs looked for a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Hebrews 11:16). The land is fulfilled in Christ and the new creation his people will inherit (Matthew 5:5). Faithful Christians differ here, and many on both sides expect a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:25–26); all can share the singers’ confidence that God keeps every word he swears.

verseByVerse.quote: When you were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it, wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people, he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account, saying, "Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second difference is one word.

Where the Psalter says they were few in number, here it says you: the line is addressed to the singers.

Consider who sang it when this book was compiled: a few thousand returned exiles in a half-rebuilt town, of no political consequence, moved between empires twice in living memory. Few in number and of little account was not a flourish to them. It was the census.

The point is not that God pities small people. The covenant the psalm rests on was made with three men who had no land, army or standing, at the mercy of whoever hosted them. Smallness was the condition God chose to work in, and always has been.

God went into Pharaoh's palace and Abimelech's dreams over Sarah, and both times a king with an army was told to keep his hands off a wandering herdsman. And the titles: my anointed ones, the word that will one day be Messiah, for a man who owned a burial cave and a well he had to argue for.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second movement turns outward: Sing to the LORD, all the earth (vv. 23-24), for the gods of the peoples are nothings and the LORD made the heavens (vv. 25-26). The families of the peoples are summoned to bring an offering and come before him (vv. 28-29), creation is called in (vv. 30-32), and the trees sing for he comes to judge the earth (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD reigns (v. 31) is sung over a tent on a small ridge in a minor kingdom. It is a statement about who holds the throne, by people who could see little evidence of it out of the window.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has suffered a wrong that was never put right may find verse 33 the most hopeful line in the psalm: the Judge is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Tell of his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples! For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised, and he is to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens. Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and joy are in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song turns outward here and never really turns back.

Every phrase in verses 23 and 24 takes in the whole world. The ark has just been installed in one tent in one city belonging to one tribe of one small nation, and the liturgy written for the occasion spends its central movement addressing the peoples who were not invited.

The word behind worthless idols is a mocking one: nothings, non-entities, a word that sounds in Hebrew like the word for gods and means the opposite. And the contrast is not that Israel's God is stronger. It is that theirs were made and ours makes. Every god in every temple on that coast had a workshop it came out of and a craftsman who could tell you what it cost. The LORD made the heavens, and the two cannot be compared at all.

One clause describes what it is like where he is: Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and joy are in his place. Strength and joy, together, as the atmosphere of the sanctuary. Not strength and terror. Not joy and sentiment. The place where God is, is the place where power and gladness are found together.

verseByVerse.quote: Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength! Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering and come before him! Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth; yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the nations are addressed directly, and told to do what Israel is doing.

Ascribe means hand over what belongs to him. It is not a request for compliments; it is the return of property. The glory is his already and the peoples have been assigning it elsewhere, and the psalm calls them in to give it back.

They are told to hand over glory and strength. Strength has been running quietly through this psalm. The congregation was told to seek the LORD and his strength; the sanctuary was described as the place where strength and joy are; and now the nations are told to ascribe strength to him. Israel seeks it, God has it, and everyone else is called to admit whose it is, and at no point in the three verses is anybody encouraged to think that he has any of his own.

Then the invitation, which is the surprising part. Bring an offering and come before him!

Foreigners are being told to come into the courts of Israel's God with a gift in their hands. Not to admire from a distance, not to send tribute by messenger, but to come. On the day the ark entered Jerusalem the song appointed for it was already looking at Ammonites and Phoenicians and Egyptians and telling them there was room.

And the terms are set out in the same breath: Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth. Come, and tremble. The door is wide open and what is on the other side of it is holy, and both have to be said together.

And a clause that steadies everything: yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved. Sung by a nation that had been overrun by Philistines in living memory, and sung again, later, by people who had watched their city burn.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice, and let them say among the nations, "The LORD reigns!" Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; let the field exult, and everything in it! Then shall the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD reigns: two words in Hebrew, the summary of the psalm and of the book. He reigns, present tense, over nations who have not yet heard of him.

A tribal confederation with a new king, a tent for a temple, and enemies on every side, on a ridge any serious empire could take: the evidence for what they sang was almost nil, and it was true.

Then creation joins in: sea, field and forest, the parts of the world with no interest in Israelite politics, are called to make a noise.

And the reason is the one nobody expects: for he comes to judge the earth.

Judgment is the good news in that sentence. We hear it as a threat, and rightly. But for a forest, a river, or anything that has suffered under human misrule, a judge's arrival means someone with authority is coming to put things right, and everything groaning applauds.

The New Testament names him. God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man he has appointed, and has given assurance of it by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31), and creation waits with eager longing to be set free (Romans 8:19–21). The judge the trees sing about bears the marks of the nails, which is why his coming can be sung about at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–36 — His Steadfast Love Endures Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm ends with the line Israel would sing for the rest of its history (v. 34), then a petition that does not belong to this day: gather and deliver us from among the nations (v. 35). It closes in doxology, and the people answer Amen (v. 36).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 35 is a prayer for exiles in the mouth of a congregation that was not in exile.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 34 is a sentence to take into any day, including the worst: whatever else has stopped, his steadfast love has not.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever! Say also: "Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather and deliver us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise. Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting!" Then all the people said, "Amen!" and praised the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This line is sung again and again in Israel’s later history. It is sung when Solomon's temple is dedicated and the glory fills the house so that the priests cannot stand up. It is sung when fire falls on the altar. Jehoshaphat puts a choir in front of his army and sends them out to face three nations singing it. Two exiled generations later, when the foundation of a much smaller temple is laid and the old men who remembered the first one are weeping, that is what the builders sing. An entire psalm was eventually written with it as every second line, twenty-six times over.

The key word is steadfast love: covenant loyalty, the settled determination of God to keep faith with people who do not keep faith with him. And the claim made about it is duration. Not that it is warm or generous but that it does not stop, and the people who would eventually need that sentence most were the ones for whom everything else had stopped.

Then the last petition: gather us from among the nations, sung on the most gathered day in Israel's history to date. The prayer does not fit the occasion at all.

It fits the readers. The people holding this book had come back from Babylon, and most of their relatives had not come back, and the word gather was the word their whole generation lived on. The Chronicler has put their prayer into the first song ever sung before the ark, so that when they said it they were not adding a modern complaint to an ancient liturgy. They were singing what David appointed to be sung, and it was already about them.

Then the last line, and the crowd takes it. The choir stops and the nation answers with one word, and the word, Amen, means: let it be so; this prayer is ours too.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asaph and his brothers minister daily before the ark in Jerusalem, with Obed-edom and the gatekeepers (vv. 37-38). Zadok and the priests stay at the tabernacle at Gibeon for the morning and evening burnt offerings, with Heman and Jeduthun (vv. 39-42). Everyone goes home, and David goes to bless his household (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's worship is in two places, both obedient and neither whole, and everything David does for the rest of the book aims at one house.
verseByVerse.examples: The household that once sheltered the ark became one of the clans that served it (v. 38). Small faithfulness can grow into a family's calling.

verseByVerse.quote: So David left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the covenant of the LORD to minister regularly before the ark as each day required, and also Obed-edom and his sixty-eight brothers, while Obed-edom, the son of Jeduthun, and Hosah were to be gatekeepers. And he left Zadok the priest and his brothers the priests before the tabernacle of the LORD in the high place that was at Gibeon to offer burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of burnt offering regularly morning and evening, to do all that is written in the Law of the LORD that he commanded Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the standing arrangements, and they are stranger than they look.

Count Obed-edom's people while passing. He arrived in this story as a man who took in an object nobody else would touch, and he is here with sixty-eight brothers, on the permanent staff of the ark, and by the time the temple rosters are drawn up his family holds the gates with sixty-two more. The household that sheltered the ark for three months has become one of the clans that serve it.

The tabernacle. The tent Moses made at Sinai, with the bronze altar in front of it, is still standing, six miles away on another hill, and it has the altar. So the priests stay there to offer the burnt offering regularly morning and evening, to do all that is written in the Law of the LORD that he commanded Israel.

Read the two halves together and the problem is plain. In Jerusalem there is the ark, which is the throne and the presence, and there is no altar of burnt offering, so the daily sacrifice cannot be kept there. At Gibeon there is the altar and the daily sacrifice and the full order of the law, and the ark is not there, so the mercy seat is bare and the Most Holy Place is empty. Israel's worship has been cut in two, and each half is doing exactly what it has been told, and neither half is whole.

David does not resolve it, because he cannot. He keeps both, obediently, and hands the problem on to his son. Everything he does in the rest of this book (the site bought on a threshing floor, the plans, the gold, the courses of priests, the charge to his son) is aimed at the day the throne and the altar stand under one roof.

They did, for a while, and then that house came down too. The presence of God and the place where blood is shed were finally brought together in one location on a hill outside Jerusalem, in a man who was himself the altar and the offering and the mercy seat and the throne, and there has been no need for a second address since.

verseByVerse.quote: With them were Heman and Jeduthun and the rest of those chosen and expressly named to give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever. Heman and Jeduthun had trumpets and cymbals for the music and instruments for sacred song. The sons of Jeduthun were appointed to the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chosen and expressly named. Somebody wrote a list, and the list was of men whose duty was gratitude. It is a curious thing to be appointed to by name: not to guard a gate or kill a bull, but to say thank you, on the record, in a rota, at a sanctuary six miles from where the crowd was.

And the refrain is quoted again, seven verses after it was sung, as though the Chronicler cannot let it go: for his steadfast love endures forever. It has become the standing text at both sanctuaries. The ark has it in Jerusalem and the altar has it at Gibeon, and whichever hill an Israelite climbed he heard the same sentence about God.

Jeduthun is a name worth carrying away. Three psalms still standing in the Psalter are headed to him or set to his manner, and one of them is the prayer of a man who kept his mouth shut so hard that his heart grew hot within him, and who ended by asking God to look away so that he might smile again before he died (Psalm 39). That prayer carries the name of a man appointed to give thanks. Thanksgiving as an office does not require a man who has never been in the dark.

Then the instruments and the doors: trumpets and cymbals for the music, and the sons of Jeduthun appointed to the gate. The men who play and the men who stand at the entrance are listed in one breath, at equal length, with the same care.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people departed each to his house, and David went home to bless his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd disperses. The greatest day of worship in the nation's history to that point ends the way every service ends, with people walking home to their own front doors, to supper, and to whatever was waiting for them there.

And the king goes to do at his own table what he has just done at the ark. He blessed the people in the name of the LORD in verse 2; now he goes home to bless his household. The same man, the same blessing, a smaller room. Whatever was true in front of a nation had to be true in a house with his children in it, and the last thing recorded of the day is that he went to make it so.

The other account follows him through the door to Michal's scorn (2 Samuel 6:20–23). The Chronicler leaves him on the threshold.

It is a right place to stop: a man going in to pray for the people who live with him. That is where the ark was always heading, not into a building, but into the ordinary rooms of a people God had decided to live among. The God who came into a tent on a ridge has since come nearer than that: by his Spirit he lives in his people, and does not go home at the end of the day, because he is already there.

16.theology:
Verses 10 and 11 are the centre of the book's argument, and what is sought has changed: from Saul who did not seek (10:14), to the ark (13:3), to God according to the rule (15:13), to his presence, sought continually. Having God is not the end of seeking God.

And the psalm faces the singers: remember where the Psalter has he remembers (v. 15), you where it has they (v. 19), and a prayer to be gathered on a day nobody was scattered (v. 35). The first song sung before the ark fits people not born for centuries.
16.examples:
Every person in the crowd went home with bread and meat, with no list and no ranking: the chapter's theology with a loaf in it.

The trumpets sounded regularly, the singers as each day required. The hard part was not the procession but the ordinary days after it. Christians who find their own praise fitful can take heart: the Son sings his Father's praise in the midst of the congregation (Hebrews 2:12), and our thanks are offered through him.

The blessing that costs most is usually the one given at your own table, to the people who know exactly what you are like (v. 43).

17.title: The Davidic Covenant: God's Promise That Changes Everything
