17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when David lived in his house, David said to Nathan the prophet, "Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent."<sup>2</sup>And Nathan said to David, "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you."<sup>3</sup>But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan,<sup>4</sup>"Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: It is not you who will build me a house to dwell in.<sup>5</sup>For I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up Israel to this day, but I have gone from tent to tent and from dwelling to dwelling.<sup>6</sup>In all places where I have moved with all Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'<sup>7</sup>Now, therefore, thus shall you say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people Israel,<sup>8</sup>and I have been with you wherever you have gone and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a name, like the name of the great ones of the earth.<sup>9</sup>And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall waste them no more, as formerly,<sup>10</sup>from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will subdue all your enemies. Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house.<sup>11</sup>When your days are fulfilled to walk with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom.<sup>12</sup>He shall build a house for me, and I will establish his throne forever.<sup>13</sup>I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. I will not take my steadfast love from him, as I took it from him who was before you,<sup>14</sup>but I will confirm him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be established forever.'"<sup>15</sup>In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.<sup>16</sup>Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?<sup>17</sup>And this was a small thing in your eyes, O God. You have also spoken of your servant's house for a great while to come, and have shown me future generations, O LORD God!<sup>18</sup>And what more can David say to you for honoring your servant? For you know your servant.<sup>19</sup>For your servant's sake, O LORD, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness, in making known all these great things.<sup>20</sup>There is none like you, O LORD, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.<sup>21</sup>And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making for yourself a name for great and awesome things, in driving out nations before your people whom you redeemed from Egypt?<sup>22</sup>And you made your people Israel to be your people forever, and you, O LORD, became their God.<sup>23</sup>And now, O LORD, let the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house be established forever, and do as you have spoken,<sup>24</sup>and your name will be established and magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, is Israel's God,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you.<sup>25</sup>For you, my God, have revealed to your servant that you will build a house for him. Therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you.<sup>26</sup>And now, O LORD, you are God, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.<sup>27</sup>Now you have been pleased to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you, for it is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever."
17.overview:
David means to build the ark a house, and Nathan approves (vv. 1-2). That night God overrules the prophet: he has never asked any leader of Israel for a house (vv. 3-6). Instead he turns the word round: the LORD will build you a house, a dynasty from which his steadfast love will not be withdrawn as it was from Saul (vv. 7-15). David then sits before the LORD and prays (vv. 16-27).

The chapter turns on one word with two meanings: David offered God a building, and God gave David a family. In this book the throne is also called God's own (v. 14), which is why it could outlive every man who ever sat on it. The New Testament hears the promise of a son and a throne forever fulfilled in Jesus (Luke 1:32–33; Hebrews 1:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A House of Cedar and a Tent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David, settled in his cedar house, wants to build the ark a house (v. 1). Nathan approves (v. 2), and that same night God overrules the prophet (vv. 3-4), not because the plan is unworthy but because God has never asked for one: in four hundred years of moving from tent to tent he never said to a single judge, Why have you not built me a house of cedar? (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: God's silence about his own accommodation is the striking thing here. The initiative in this chapter was never going to be a man's, because God had no unmet need for a man to meet.
verseByVerse.examples: Nathan gave sincere, godly-sounding advice on his own authority and was wrong. God corrected him the same night, before the king had laid a stone, and the prophet was humble enough to go back in the morning and say so.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when David lived in his house, David said to Nathan the prophet, "Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent." And Nathan said to David, "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the first time in his life David is living somewhere that does not have to be taken down and carried. He has been in caves, in a Philistine border town, in a wilderness stronghold and in Hebron. Now he has a roof of Lebanon cedar.

Nothing has gone wrong. The ark is where he put it, in a tent he pitched for it, with a choir singing round it every day. It is not neglect that bothers him but the comparison: he is the first man in Israel whose accommodation is better than God's, and comfort, which finally gave him time to sit still and look around, is what made him notice.

It is not a bad instinct. A man in a cave does not compare his roof with anyone's.

Nathan's answer sounds unimpeachable. The heart is devout, the project generous, and God is with David; the Chronicler has said so himself. But the prophet has not been told anything. He has admired the impulse and issued a verdict in the name of a God who has not spoken, and advice is not right merely because it is warm and devout.

verseByVerse.quote: But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan, "Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: It is not you who will build me a house to dwell in. For I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up Israel to this day, but I have gone from tent to tent and from dwelling to dwelling. In all places where I have moved with all Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'
verseByVerse.commentary:
That same night, before anyone had picked up a tool, God overturned the advice of his own prophet, and the speed of it is a mercy to both men.

In 2 Samuel 7:5 God puts it as a question. Here it is a flat statement, It is not you who will build me a house to dwell in: God can say a plain no to a good man's best idea. And the reason is not what anyone would guess: not that David is unworthy, nor that the timing is wrong, but that God has gone from tent to tent.

Four hundred years of that. Every time the tabernacle was taken down and carried on poles and set up in a new place (Gilgal, Shiloh, Nob, Gibeon), the God of heaven went with his people and lived where they lived. He has been, by his own description, a God without a fixed address, because his people did not have one either.

Through the whole disorderly stretch of the judges God never complained about his accommodation to anybody. The God who owns the cedars of Lebanon has no housing need for a king to meet, and that is why the offer, however sincere, had the relationship the wrong way round.

Why could David not build the temple? Because he had shed much blood in war (22:8; 28:3): the temple was to be built in a time of rest, by Solomon, whose name means peace. The two reasons stand together: God had never asked for a house, and when one was built, he chose a man of peace to build it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — I Will Build You a House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rehearses David's life in verbs that are all his own: he took him from the pasture, was with him, cut off his enemies, and will make him a name (vv. 7-8). He promises the people a place (vv. 9-10a). Then the hinge: the LORD will build you a house (v. 10b). A son will build the building; God will build the dynasty, as father to son, with steadfast love not withdrawn as from Saul (vv. 11-14). Nathan reports it all (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The word for house means a building and a family, and the chapter turns on the second meaning. David offered God a roof; God answered with a dynasty.
verseByVerse.examples: The promise had to be delivered by the man whose advice it contradicted, and he delivered all of it (v. 15).

verseByVerse.quote: Now, therefore, thus shall you say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people Israel, and I have been with you wherever you have gone and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a name, like the name of the great ones of the earth. And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall waste them no more, as formerly, from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will subdue all your enemies. Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having refused the gift, God begins to give, and he starts with a biography in which every verb belongs to him: took, been with, cut off. The man in a cedar house with a standing army is reminded that he was last seen walking behind sheep and that nothing in between was self-made. And the word for his office is not king but prince, one appointed under someone.

A name is what men have always tried to take for themselves. At Shinar they said, let us make a name for ourselves, and God scattered them; then he told one childless nomad, I will make your name great. It is the same offer here. David set out to build God a house; God hands David a name instead.

Before the dynasty, God speaks about the people: he will plant them and end the wasting by violent men that had gone on since the judges. The covenant with the king is set inside a promise to the nation; David is exalted for the sake of his people.

Does the promise of a place where Israel will be planted (v. 9) mean the land still belongs to the Jewish people and modern Israel? Dispensationalists hold that it does, with its borders, still awaiting fulfilment. This commentary reads the New Testament as widening it: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), the patriarchs looked for a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Hebrews 11:16), and the place is fulfilled in Christ and the new creation his people will inherit (Matthew 5:5). Faithful Christians differ, and the comfort of verse 9 belongs to all of them: God himself plants his people where no violent man can uproot them.

verseByVerse.quote: When your days are fulfilled to walk with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for me, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. I will not take my steadfast love from him, as I took it from him who was before you, but I will confirm him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be established forever.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David offered stone and cedar; God says the LORD will build you a house, meaning sons and a throne and a line that does not stop. The king was given a dynasty he had no way of asking for, because it had not entered his head.

And David will be dead before any of it happens. The promise is made to a man who will not see it, about a boy who is at this point a name on a list in chapter 14.

So David's project is not cancelled, only reassigned, and the rest of this book shows what he did with that answer: he spent the remainder of his life buying the site, gathering the gold, drawing the plans and organising the priests for a building he would never enter.

Saul is in the sentence without being named. The last house God set up in Israel lasted one generation and ended on Gilboa. This one will not go that way, and the reason given is not how well the son performs but a relationship: father and son.

The account in Samuel adds that when the son commits iniquity, God will discipline him with the rod of men. The Chronicler does not deny it; his second volume records exactly that discipline falling on Solomon's line. But he writes for people whose kings are gone and whose city has been burned, and he gives the half of the promise they needed: the steadfast love will not be withdrawn.

And the last verse of the promise holds the difference this book cares about most. Samuel says: your house and your kingdom. Chronicles says: my house and ... my kingdom. David's son is confirmed inside something that was never David's to hand on; later this book calls the throne in Jerusalem the throne of the LORD, and this verse is the ground for it. Israel’s kings held the throne as tenants in God’s own kingdom, which is why that kingdom could survive the loss of every king who ever held it.

The son finally in view is not Solomon, whose throne lasted four hundred years and then fell. It is the one whose kingdom the word forever was always waiting for.

Is the son Solomon or Christ? Both. Solomon built the temple (v. 12), but no son of David’s line reigned for ever except Christ; Hebrews applies verse 13 to him (Hebrews 1:5). Is Christ reigning on David’s throne now? Peter says God fulfilled this oath by raising Christ to his right hand (Acts 2:30–36). Dispensationalists look for a future earthly throne in Jerusalem, reading the throne and the place literally; this commentary holds, with Peter’s sermon, that the throne is Christ’s now and his kingdom has no end, and gladly owns those who differ as brothers waiting for the same King.

verseByVerse.quote: In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these words, all this vision: the verse says twice that nothing was left out, and what could most easily have been left out is the beginning, where God says a plain no to the plan Nathan had blessed the day before.

So the prophet walked back into the throne room and told the king that yesterday's counsel had been overruled. He does not seem to have softened it, and he does not seem to have made excuses. The record simply notes that he delivered the whole thing, and then leaves him out of the rest of the chapter.

He will come back, in 2 Samuel 12, with a word about a lamb and a rich man and a sin nobody else dared name, and he will not soften that either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David goes in and sat before the LORD, and what comes out is a question: Who am I, O LORD God? (v. 16). God has shown him the future (v. 17), and David runs out of words (v. 18); it was done according to your own heart (v. 19). Then two incomparables: there is none like God (v. 20), and no people like Israel, whom God went in person to redeem (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer moves from David's house to God himself: before he asks for anything, he confesses who God is and what God has done for Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: Faced with a gift he cannot account for, David does not bargain or protest. He sits, asks why, and then praises, and the order is worth copying.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far? And this was a small thing in your eyes, O God. You have also spoken of your servant's house for a great while to come, and have shown me future generations, O LORD God! And what more can David say to you for honoring your servant? For you know your servant. For your servant's sake, O LORD, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness, in making known all these great things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sat. He did not kneel or stand, and the writer thought the posture worth recording. A man does not stand to attention at his father's table.

What comes out first is a question about identity. Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far? He has just been handed an everlasting dynasty and his opening line is that he cannot see why. There is no false modesty in it and no bargaining. He is genuinely at a loss.

The second half of verse 17 is one of the hardest lines in Chronicles to translate, which is why older versions differ (the KJV has hast regarded me according to the estate of a man of high degree); the sense is not in doubt. He has been given a view down the centuries, and it stops him.

He has run out of words and says so, a strange admission for the man whose name stands over nearly half the psalms. And he gives the reason he can stop: you know your servant. There is no need to explain himself to someone who already knows what he is.

Verse 19 gives the cause of the whole thing, and it is not David: according to your own heart. Not his record, not the kingdom’s need, not a reward for bringing up the ark. A covenant founded on what God is like cannot be undone by anything the other party turns out to be.

verseByVerse.quote: There is none like you, O LORD, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making for yourself a name for great and awesome things, in driving out nations before your people whom you redeemed from Egypt? And you made your people Israel to be your people forever, and you, O LORD, became their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer now lifts away from David's house altogether and says two things that cannot be said about anybody else.

First: none like him and none besides him, according to all that we have heard with our ears. The ground is testimony handed down; David believes it because Israel remembered it.

Then: no people like Israel, and the second claim rests entirely on the first. Israel is not incomparable because of anything in Israel; it is incomparable because of who came to fetch it. The nation was a company of slaves in a brickyard, and the distinguishing fact about them is that God himself went down to fetch them.

Note the verb: God went to redeem. He did not send. And the purpose given is not the slaves' comfort but God’s reputation: making for yourself a name for great and awesome things. God rescued a nation and got a name by it, and then turned round and made a name for David. All through the chapter God gives away what he could have kept.

Verse 22 settles it: both halves were his doing. He made them his, and he became theirs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–27 — Do As You Have Spoken
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer turns into petition, and the petition is that God will keep his own promise: let the word that you have spoken ... be established forever, and do as you have spoken (v. 23), so that God’s name is magnified and men say The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, is Israel's God (v. 24). Then David explains his own boldness: because God revealed the promise, therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you (v. 25). It ends where it must: you are God, and you have promised this good thing (v. 26), and it is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The goal David names is not the security of his family but the magnifying of God's name: his house is the means and God's reputation is the end.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 25 gives the reason a man dares to pray at all, and it is not his mood or his record. God had spoken first. Courage in prayer is a response to a promise, and David says so in as many words.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O LORD, let the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house be established forever, and do as you have spoken, and your name will be established and magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, is Israel's God,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you. For you, my God, have revealed to your servant that you will build a house for him. Therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do as you have spoken. He asks God for precisely what God has just offered, and adds nothing of his own. Every petition in this prayer was first a promise, which is what praying largely is: handing God's word back to him as a request.

Therefore. The boldness has a cause outside him. 2 Samuel says, literally, that he found his heart to pray, and what gave him heart was not a surge of feeling or a run of obedient days but a promise, spoken first, by God. Take the promise away and there is nothing to be confident about; leave it there and a shepherd can sit before the ark and ask the Almighty to keep his word.

That is still the only door in. Hebrews tells frightened people to come to the throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:16), and the confidence is never in the one approaching. It is in the one who went before, whose perfect obedience stands where ours fails, and in what God has said he will do.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O LORD, you are God, and you have promised this good thing to your servant. Now you have been pleased to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you, for it is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer ends in two short sentences that do not ask for anything more.

He rests on two facts. You are God, so you are able. You have promised, so you are willing. Everything a man needs to be sure of is contained in that pair, and David has stopped trying to add to it.

It is blessed. Not it will be blessed if the sons behave. What God has blessed stays blessed, because the blessing never depended on the worth of the one blessed.

Eight times in this chapter the word forever appears, and David uses the last two of them. He is sitting in a tent city, in a young kingdom, with a son not yet grown and a throne no descendant of his has ever inherited, and he says forever twice in one breath.

He was right, though not in the way he could have measured. His line held Jerusalem for four centuries and then lost it, and the last of his sons to wear the crown was blinded and taken to Babylon in chains. Nearly six hundred years after that, an angel stood in a village in Galilee and told a girl that her son would be given the throne of his father David and would reign over the house of Jacob with no end to his kingdom. The house is still standing. It is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever.

17.theology:
The covenant rests on God's character and nothing else: according to your own heart (v. 19), not for services rendered and not to meet a need of God's own (vv. 5-6).

Chronicles gives the promise without the discipline clause that stands in 2 Samuel 7:14 and calls the throne God's own (v. 14). Both changes point the same way, at readers who had no king left: the kingdom was never David's property, so its loss was not the loss of the promise. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son is applied in the New Testament not to Solomon but to Christ, and the word forever, used eight times here, finally means what it says.
17.examples:
Being sincerely encouraging is not the same as having heard from God. Nathan's approval was warm and mistaken, and his readiness to reverse it is as much an example as the mistake.

David wanted to build and was told his son would. He spent the rest of his life buying the site, stockpiling the materials, drawing the plans and organising the priesthood for a building he would never walk into. A refused ambition can be worked at for the rest of a life by somebody who has accepted the refusal.

18.title: David's Victories: The King Who Subdues the Nations
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and he took Gath and its villages out of the hand of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>And he defeated Moab, and the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.<sup>3</sup>David also defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah-Hamath, as he went to set up his monument at the river Euphrates.<sup>4</sup>And David took from him 1,000 chariots, 7,000 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but left enough for 100 chariots.<sup>5</sup>And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians.<sup>6</sup>Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.<sup>7</sup>And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem.<sup>8</sup>And from Tibhath and from Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took a large amount of bronze. With it Solomon made the bronze sea and the pillars and the vessels of bronze.<sup>9</sup>When Tou king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah,<sup>10</sup>he sent his son Hadoram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him; for Hadadezer had often been at war with Tou. And he sent all sorts of articles of gold, of silver, and of bronze.<sup>11</sup>These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he had carried off from all the nations, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek.<sup>12</sup>And Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, killed 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.<sup>13</sup>Then he put garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.<sup>14</sup>So David reigned over all Israel, and he administered justice and equity to all his people.<sup>15</sup>And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;<sup>16</sup>and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests; and Shavsha was secretary;<sup>17</sup>and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David's sons were the chief officials in the service of the king.
18.overview:
The wars are told at speed: Philistia, Moab, Hadadezer of Zobah at the Euphrates, and Damascus (vv. 1-6). The gold comes to Jerusalem, the bronze is set aside for a temple that does not exist yet, and the plunder of five nations is dedicated to the LORD (vv. 7-13). Then the verse the chapter exists for: David administered justice and equity to all his people (v. 14), and his officials (vv. 15-17).

Twice, in identical words, the campaigns are bracketed by the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went. The verb is the word for saving.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Victories, and Bronze for a Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Philistia, Moab, Zobah and Damascus fall in turn (vv. 1-5), and David cripples the captured chariotry (v. 4). Then the refrain (v. 6). The gold shields go to Jerusalem, and the bronze goes somewhere the parallel account never mentions: into Solomon's bronze sea and pillars (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: David won every war he fought, and the record calls it rescue rather than conquest: the LORD saved him wherever he went (vv. 6, 13).
verseByVerse.examples: Victory did not teach David to trust in horses. He disabled the captured chariot teams rather than build a chariot army of his own (v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and he took Gath and its villages out of the hand of the Philistines. And he defeated Moab, and the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first entry carries years of history in one place name: Gath.

Gath was Goliath's town. It was also where a young fugitive had once run for asylum with the giant's own sword strapped to his back, realised the servants of Achish had recognised him, and got out alive only by scrabbling at the gateposts and letting spittle run into his beard until they threw him out as a madman. He went back later and lived sixteen months in Philistine country as a vassal of Gath, with nowhere else to go.

Now he owns it. The Chronicler writes the name of the town and moves on.

Then Moab. David's great-grandmother had walked out of Moab behind Naomi, and when Saul was hunting him David had asked the king of Moab to shelter his parents. Now the Moabites bring tribute. The account in Samuel adds a detail about prisoners measured with a line, and the Chronicler leaves it out.

verseByVerse.quote: David also defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah-Hamath, as he went to set up his monument at the river Euphrates. And David took from him 1,000 chariots, 7,000 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but left enough for 100 chariots. And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians. Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hadadezer of Zobah is the largest enemy in the chapter — an Aramean king whose reach ran north-east towards the Euphrates, and who was setting up a monument on that river when David caught him. The Hebrew leaves it slightly open whose monument it was, and most readers take it as Hadadezer's. Either way the fighting has reached the river God named to Abraham when he first described the land.

The spoil is counted: a thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, twenty thousand foot. Then a detail that would look like vandalism to any other king in the region: David cripples nine tenths of the most valuable military asset in the ancient Near East on the spot. Modern readers flinch for the animals; in that world it was the usual way to put captured war horses beyond use.

The law of the king had said he must not multiply horses to himself, and Joshua had done precisely this at the waters of Merom because God told him to. David is refusing to build the kind of army that makes a nation trust its own hardware. His son will keep fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, and the difference between father and son is already visible here.

And verse 6 names what the whole run of victories was: not a campaign season but a rescue, repeated.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations; and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Here Chronicles has a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen where the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 8:4 has seventeen hundred horsemen, and the Greek translation of Samuel agrees with Chronicles, which points to a copying slip. Neither touches what the passage teaches. Those who hold, as this commentary does, that Scripture as God first gave it is true in all it affirms see such differences as slips in copying or differences in counting, not contradictions.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. And from Tibhath and from Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took a large amount of bronze. With it Solomon made the bronze sea and the pillars and the vessels of bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses about metal, and the second one is why this chapter is in the book at all.

First the gold: ceremonial shields, made to be seen rather than used, the sort of thing a king's guard carried to display what he could afford.

Then the bronze, and a sentence the parallel account does not have.

The bronze sea was the great basin on twelve oxen where the priests washed before they went in to God; the pillars were Jachin and Boaz at the entrance. The metal came out of a Syrian war fought a generation before the building existed, carried home by a king who was told he would never build the house.

That is the point of the sentence. David could not lay a stone, so he spent his wars stockpiling the material and left it for his son to melt down into the furniture of God's house.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tou of Hamath sends his son with gifts (vv. 9-10), and every bit of it is dedicated to the LORD with the plunder of five nations (v. 11). Abishai beats Edom in the Valley of Salt, garrisons are set, and the refrain closes the section (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: A generation later Solomon will build a temple out of a treasury his father never spent, and verse 11 is where it started.
verseByVerse.examples: Even a neighbour's self-interested gifts went into the pile set apart for God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Tou king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, he sent his son Hadoram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him; for Hadadezer had often been at war with Tou. And he sent all sorts of articles of gold, of silver, and of bronze. These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he had carried off from all the nations, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tou of Hamath has been at war with Hadadezer for years and someone else has just beaten him, so he sends his son Hadoram with congratulations and gifts.

It is self-interested diplomacy: a northern king would rather be the new power's friend than find out. The Chronicler makes no comment on the motive.

Five nations named, and everything taken from every one of them handed over: not tithed, not shared among the commanders, not put in a royal treasury, but dedicated, set apart from any other use.

A man who has been told his life's ambition belongs to someone else could have spent the rest of it comfortably. Instead he ran a lifelong campaign of acquisition on behalf of a building he would never see, and by chapter 29 the pile is so large that the numbers stop sounding real.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, killed 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt. Then he put garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abishai is the man chapter 11 recorded as the most renowned of the thirty, who did not attain to the three. He is still fighting, still winning, still second, and his record holds both that sentence and eighteen thousand Edomites.

Samuel credits this battle to David (2 Samuel 8:13), the title of Psalm 60 to Joab, and this verse to Abishai, who led the action in the field. A king is credited with his generals’ victories; the three answer different questions about the same day. The psalm’s title gives 12,000 dead rather than 18,000, perhaps counting one part of the battle.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the sentence the wars existed for: justice and equity to all his people (v. 14). A list of officials follows, ending with David's sons as the chief officials in the service of the king (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Justice and equity is the pair the prophets use ever afterwards to test a king, and the phrase to all his people is doing as much work as the nouns.
verseByVerse.examples: The king's sons come last in the list, with a civil title (v. 17). In this book even princes do not take a priest's place.

verseByVerse.quote: So David reigned over all Israel, and he administered justice and equity to all his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After thirteen verses of armies and tribute, this is not a change of subject but the point of everything before it. Without it the chapter would only be the record of a successful warlord.

Justice is the verdict being right; the second word, often translated righteousness, is the whole arrangement being right, so that verdicts do not have to keep rescuing people from a system built to crush them. Jeremiah would ask a descendant of David whether kingship consisted of cedar panelling, and answer that his father judged the cause of the poor and needy: Is not this to know me?

And the last words are the hardest: to all his people. Not only the tribes that turned out at Hebron or the men who came to Ziklag while it cost something. Justice that stops at the people who deserve it from you is gratitude with a gavel. The God who saved David wherever he went is the one who asks his people to deal like this.

The prophet who saw furthest put the two words in the mouth of a child not yet born, whose government would have no end, and said he would uphold his kingdom with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. Israel got a taste of it under David. The rest came with the child Isaiah foresaw: Jesus, the son of David, who brings justice to the nations without breaking a bruised reed (Matthew 12:18–21), and whose kingdom is the one place where justice reaches all his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder; and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests; and Shavsha was secretary; and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David's sons were the chief officials in the service of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the cabinet a settled kingdom has: Joab over the army, Jehoshaphat the recorder, Zadok and Ahimelech as priests, Shavsha running the correspondence of a state that now has correspondence.

Benaiah is over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, professional soldiers from the Philistine coast, from the nation David spent his life fighting, trusted with his life at close quarters. He had lived among them as a fugitive and learned who could be relied on.

And the last clause quietly declines to repeat something. The account in Samuel says David's sons were priests. This book will not write that.

Only Levites may carry the ark; only the sons of Aaron may offer; a man died on a cart track for putting out his hand. The care over one word at the end of a list is the care that runs through the whole book.

Abiathar was Ahimelech’s son (1 Samuel 22:20), and Abiathar seems to have had a son named Ahimelech; the lists name the son here.

18.theology:
The Chronicler is less interested in the battles than in where the metal went (vv. 8, 11). A king told he would never build the house spent his wars supplying it.

And verse 14 is where the fighting was aimed. Justice and equity to all his people is the standard for every later king of Judah, and Isaiah used the same two words of the true son of David, whose government has no end. Under him, and by his Spirit in his people, justice that reaches everyone is no longer only an ideal.
18.examples: A man who cannot do what he most wants can still spend years making it possible for somebody else. Solomon's priests washed in a basin his father had captured.

19.title: The Ammonite Humiliation and the Wars That Follow
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after this Nahash the king of the Ammonites died, and his son reigned in his place.<sup>2</sup>And David said, "I will deal kindly with Hanun the son of Nahash, for his father dealt kindly with me." So David sent messengers to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came to the land of the Ammonites to Hanun to console him.<sup>3</sup>But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Have not his servants come to you to search and to overthrow and to spy out the land?"<sup>4</sup>So Hanun took David's servants and shaved them and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away;<sup>5</sup>and they departed. When David was told concerning the men, he sent messengers to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."<sup>6</sup>When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, Hanun and the Ammonites sent 1,000 talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, from Aram-maacah, and from Zobah.<sup>7</sup>They hired 32,000 chariots and the king of Maacah with his army, who came and encamped before Medeba. And the Ammonites were mustered from their cities and came to battle.<sup>8</sup>When David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the army of the mighty men.<sup>9</sup>And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the city, and the kings who had come were by themselves in the open country.<sup>10</sup>When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians.<sup>11</sup>The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and they were arrayed against the Ammonites.<sup>12</sup>And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will help you.<sup>13</sup>Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him."<sup>14</sup>So Joab and the people who were with him drew near before the Syrians for battle, and they fled before him.<sup>15</sup>And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai, Joab's brother, and entered the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem.<sup>16</sup>But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they sent messengers and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates, with Shophach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head.<sup>17</sup>And when it was told to David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to them and drew up his forces against them. And when David set the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him.<sup>18</sup>And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 7,000 chariots and 40,000 foot soldiers, and put to death also Shophach the commander of their army.<sup>19</sup>And when the servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him. So the Syrians were not willing to save the Ammonites anymore.
19.overview: David sends condolences to Hanun of Ammon, whose father had been good to him; Hanun's counsellors call the envoys spies, and he shames them and sends them home (vv. 1-5). Ammon hires Syrian armies (vv. 6-7); Joab, caught between two forces, splits his army with Abishai and charges them to be strong and leave the outcome to God, and both enemy lines break (vv. 8-15). Syria escalates, David crosses the Jordan himself, and the coalition sues for peace (vv. 16-19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Kindness Repaid with an Outrage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nahash of Ammon dies and David sends condolences (vv. 1-2). Hanun's advisers call the comforters spies, and he has them shaved and half-stripped (vv. 3-4). David sends to meet them on the road and keeps them at Jericho until their beards grow (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: David repays a kindness he received from a pagan king when he was nobody, years after anyone could have claimed it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 is the measure of the man: he lets the shamed envoys recover out of sight, and sets no date.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after this Nahash the king of the Ammonites died, and his son reigned in his place. And David said, "I will deal kindly with Hanun the son of Nahash, for his father dealt kindly with me." So David sent messengers to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came to the land of the Ammonites to Hanun to console him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nahash king of the Ammonites is probably not a stranger to this story. He is most likely the man who besieged Jabesh-gilead a lifetime ago and offered the town surrender terms of one gouged-out right eye per man, as a disgrace on all Israel. Saul's first act as king was to rout him for it.

Which is very likely why he was good to David: the Ammonite king across the river had a use for anyone Saul wanted dead. The Chronicler does not say what the kindness was.

What he records is that David remembered it. Years have passed, the debt is unenforceable and the creditor is in his grave, and the king of Israel sends an embassy across the Jordan to sit with a bereaved son.

The word for dealing kindly is the covenant word, the steadfast love the choir at the ark had just sung. That is the logic of a man who has understood what he has received: treated better than he deserved, he goes looking for someone to treat better than they deserve.

verseByVerse.quote: But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Have not his servants come to you to search and to overthrow and to spy out the land?" So Hanun took David's servants and shaved them and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away; and they departed. When David was told concerning the men, he sent messengers to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The suspicion is plausible. David has been swallowing kingdoms for years, and a hard-headed Ammonite counsellor has reason to wonder what Israelites are really doing near his capital.

But it takes the one thing that cannot be faked without cost, men sent to sit with a young king whose father has just died, and reads it as reconnaissance. Cynicism explains everything and can be checked by nothing. Once Hanun accepted it, kindness itself became evidence against David.

A beard was a man's standing, and shaving one off by force was a punishment for criminals; cutting the robes at the hip left them exposed. Men on an errand of sympathy were sent home past every village that way.

David does not summon them to the palace. He sends riders to catch them before the city, so they never have to be seen, gives them a town to stay in, and sets no date: until your beards have grown, however long it takes.

The king took their humiliation seriously. He did not tell them it was only hair, or that the honour of the mission covered it, or that a soldier should be above such things. He assumed that what had been done to them would take time to get over, and arranged the time. Men who have been shamed are usually told to be reasonable about it by people who were not there.

A greater King went further than Jericho. Jesus went out himself to people whom shame had driven to the edges, and then, despising the shame, was stripped and mocked in public (Hebrews 12:2), so that people disgraced by others or by their own sin could be covered and brought home. The patience David showed his envoys is a small picture of the welcome waiting for every ashamed person who comes to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ammonites hire chariots from three Syrian states (vv. 6-7). Joab finds the battle set against him in front and behind (vv. 8-10), splits the army with Abishai, each pledged to help the other (vv. 10-12), and gives his charge (v. 13). The Syrians break, then the Ammonites, and Joab goes home (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Joab's charge (v. 13) holds both halves without strain: use your strength, and leave the outcome with the LORD. Neither clause is an excuse for dropping the other, and the man who said it was surrounded at the time.
verseByVerse.examples: Trusting God with the verdict did not stop Joab making a plan for losing (v. 12).

verseByVerse.quote: When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, Hanun and the Ammonites sent 1,000 talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, from Aram-maacah, and from Zobah. They hired 32,000 chariots and the king of Maacah with his army, who came and encamped before Medeba. And the Ammonites were mustered from their cities and came to battle. When David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the army of the mighty men. And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the city, and the kings who had come were by themselves in the open country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A stench to David: the word is used of something rotting. The Ammonites now understand what they have done, and they start buying an army.

A thousand talents of silver, chariots from three states, a whole force camped at Medeba: one of the largest mobilisations in the Old Testament, the direct result of a young man unable to say he had made a mistake.

Joab arrives with the mighty men and finds the trap already set: Ammonites drawn up at the city gate in front of him, and the hired kings out in the open country behind.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations; and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Here, for instance, verse 18 has seven thousand chariot crews where 2 Samuel 10:18 has seven hundred chariots, and the thirty-two thousand chariots of verse 7 may mean chariotry with its crews and runners rather than vehicles. Neither touches what the passage teaches; this commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error.
verseByVerse.note: A thousand talents was about 37 tons of silver (a talent was about 75 pounds, ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians. The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and they were arrayed against the Ammonites. And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will help you. Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surrounded, Joab does two things, and they are the two things that have to be done in that order.

First a plan. The best troops face the Syrians, the professionals; his brother Abishai holds the Ammonites at the gate.

Two commanders, back to back, each promising to break off his own battle to save the other. Neither of them pretends the plan will certainly work. They have agreed in advance what to do when one of them starts losing, which is a kind of foresight that only comes from men who have lost before.

Then the charge. Be strong, and use the strength: no passivity, no suggestion that trusting God means doing less. For our people and the cities of our God: he names what they fight for, and calls Israel's towns God's property. And the last clause hands the result away: may the LORD do what seems good to him. Joab does not tell his men God is obliged to win, nor that the outcome does not matter. Fight with everything for a cause that belongs to God, and leave the verdict with the one whose cause it is.

And it comes from Joab, who knifed Abner in a gateway and Amasa on a road and put spears through Absalom against the king's order. That man says the truest sentence about courage and providence in the book, and Scripture records it without comment.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joab and the people who were with him drew near before the Syrians for battle, and they fled before him. And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai, Joab's brother, and entered the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Syrians break first: hired troops with no stake in the quarrel take one charge from Israel's best and run.

And the Ammonites, watching their expensive allies disappear, run too. Not one of them has been beaten in a fight; the line collapses because the men beside them left.

Then Joab came to Jerusalem. No siege, no sack, no pursuit. He has scattered the field army and he goes home, and the Chronicler offers no explanation. Rabbah is still standing, and it will take another spring and another campaign to bring it down — which is where the next chapter opens, and what David was doing while it happened.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — The Syrians Sue for Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Syria sends for troops from beyond the Euphrates under Shophach (v. 16). David comes out himself and crosses the Jordan (v. 17). The army falls, Shophach with it (v. 18), and Hadadezer's vassals make peace and will not help Ammon again (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter began with one young king taking bad advice about an embassy of sympathy. It ends with a coalition broken, a commander dead, and a whole region changing sides.
verseByVerse.examples: Hanun still had the Ammonite army, and no friends left in the world (v. 19).

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they sent messengers and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates, with Shophach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head. And when it was told to David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to them and drew up his forces against them. And when David set the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him. And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 7,000 chariots and 40,000 foot soldiers, and put to death also Shophach the commander of their army. And when the servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him. So the Syrians were not willing to save the Ammonites anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is no longer about Ammon; it is Aram deciding whether it can live with an Israelite kingdom on its southern border.

And this time David comes out himself. He had sent Joab to the first battle; for the second he calls up the nation, because the scale has changed.

Seven thousand chariot crews, forty thousand foot, Shophach dead on the field, and Hadadezer's servants become subject to David.

The last line is the epitaph on Hanun's decision. He had bought an alliance with a thousand talents, and when the silver was spent the allies found other commitments. Loyalty that was purchased behaves like a purchase.

All of it began with a delegation sent to sit with a grieving young man, and a room full of clever advisers who could not believe that anybody meant it.

19.theology:
Verse 13 holds two things most people hold one at a time: fight with everything you have, and the verdict is not yours. Joab neither promises victory nor excuses anyone from the battle. For a Christian the strength is not only his own: the Spirit who lives in believers is the power for the fight, and the outcome rests with a Father who has already given his Son.

That the words are Joab's does not make them less true. God's truth is not confined to the mouths of people whose lives commend it.
19.examples:
David repaid a dead foreign king's favour, though the debt was unenforceable, because being kindly treated had made him kind. And with his shamed envoys he did not minimise what had been done or hurry them through it: shame takes as long as it takes, and the king budgeted for it.

One message admitting he had listened to bad advice would have saved Hanun a thousand talents of silver, two armies and every ally he had. The cost of an apology is always quoted before it is paid, and never afterwards.

20.title: The Siege of Rabbah and the Giants: Completing the Conquest
20.text: <sup>1</sup>In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, Joab led out the army and ravaged the country of the Ammonites and came and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem. And Joab struck down Rabbah and overthrew it.<sup>2</sup>And David took the crown of their king from his head. He found that it weighed a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone. And it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount.<sup>3</sup>And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and axes. And thus David did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.<sup>4</sup>And after this there arose war with the Philistines at Gezer. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Sippai, who was one of the descendants of the giants, and the Philistines were subdued.<sup>5</sup>And there was again war with the Philistines, and Elhanan the son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.<sup>6</sup>And there was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was descended from the giants.<sup>7</sup>And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea, David's brother, struck him down.<sup>8</sup>These were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
20.overview:
Joab takes Rabbah in the spring while David stays in Jerusalem; the Ammonite crown is lifted onto David's head (vv. 1-3). Then three notices of Philistine war, each ending with a dead giant, all of whom fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants (vv. 4-8).

Verse 1 is almost word for word the setting of 2 Samuel 11, and this book does not tell what happened next: the Chronicler is writing the story of the throne rather than the story of the man.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Rabbah, and What Is Not Here
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the season when kings go out to battle, Joab ravages Ammon and besieges Rabbah while David stays at Jerusalem (v. 1). The city falls, its king's crown is lifted onto David's head (v. 2), and the population is put to forced labour (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The book keeps the opening sentence of David's worst episode and nothing more. The reader who knows 2 Samuel finds the scene set, the king at home and the army away, and then the fall of a city, with the whole spring in between left blank.
verseByVerse.examples: In the other account this moment comes after a prophet has told the king a story about a lamb. Here it comes after nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, Joab led out the army and ravaged the country of the Ammonites and came and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem. And Joab struck down Rabbah and overthrew it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who has read Samuel will stop at the last five words, because there the other account turns to a man who could not sleep, walked on his roof in the evening, and saw something.

The Chronicler writes the setting and not the scene. Bathsheba appears in this book only as Bath-shua, Solomon's mother (3:5); Uriah's death, Nathan and the lamb, Amnon and Absalom are not here.

It is the largest deliberate omission in Chronicles and readers have argued about it for a very long time. Some have called it whitewash. It cannot be, and the reason is nine chapters back: in the roll of David's mighty men this same writer prints the name Uriah the Hittite (11:41) and passes on without a word. A man concealing what David did to Uriah does not put Uriah in the honour roll.

What he is doing is something else. He is writing for people who have no king, no army and no independence, and who need to know what God promised to David's house and what that house was for. So he tells the story of the throne rather than the story of the man: how Israel got a king, a city, an ark, a covenant, a site and a temple. The private ruin of David, and the mercy that met his confession (Psalm 51), is not his subject, and he assumes his readers know it, because he leaves the door of verse 1 standing open and walks past it.

For a reader who knows both books, the silence after the sentence is the loudest thing in the chapter.
verseByVerse.note: The full story is told in 2 Samuel 11–12.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took the crown of their king from his head. He found that it weighed a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone. And it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount. And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and axes. And thus David did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Hebrew can be read their king or, with the Greek translation, Milcom, the Ammonite god, so it may well have been the crown of the god's statue, held over the king of Israel for as long as the ceremony took.

Then the spoil, and the population set to work in every town of Ammon. It is the harsh end of an ancient war, reported without softening and without relish: a nation that hired armies rather than admit a mistake is quarrying stone.

A king who stayed at home has a foreign crown lifted onto his head while the men who took the city are still in the breach: a coronation with a hole in the middle of it.

Did David torture the Ammonites? The Hebrew most likely means he set them to work with saws and picks, as forced labour, not that he killed them with tools. It is recorded, not commended. The KJV reads that he cut them with saws; the Hebrew here says literally that he sawed with the saw, while 2 Samuel 12:31 says he set them to the saws, and many think one letter has slipped between the two.
verseByVerse.note: The crown weighed a talent, about 75 pounds (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — The Sons of the Giants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three short notices of Philistine war, each ending with a giant dead: Sippai at Gezer (v. 4), Lahmi the brother of Goliath (v. 5), and a six-fingered taunter at Gath struck down by David's nephew (vv. 6-7). All of them fell by the hand of David and his servants (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The champion in the valley was David's; the champion's family were finished off over years by other men, in his name, and the record puts it all down to the king.
verseByVerse.examples: Sibbecai of Hushah, Elhanan son of Jair, Jonathan son of Shimea: each has a name, a home town and one sentence in Scripture, and God did not forget them.

verseByVerse.quote: And after this there arose war with the Philistines at Gezer. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Sippai, who was one of the descendants of the giants, and the Philistines were subdued. And there was again war with the Philistines, and Elhanan the son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first is at Gezer, where Sibbecai the Hushathite strikes down Sippai, one of the descendants of the giants. Sibbecai was in the roll of the mighty men in chapter 11, one line among thirty. Here he kills a giant, in one sentence, and disappears.

The second verse raises a real difficulty. This text says Elhanan struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath; the corresponding verse in 2 Samuel says Elhanan struck down Goliath himself.

The oldest explanation, and still the most likely, is that a copyist's eye slipped in the Samuel verse, whose Hebrew has a recognised awkwardness at exactly that point, and that Chronicles preserves the original. Others suppose two men or two names. The KJV, following this verse, prints the brother of in italics in 2 Samuel 21:19. The question is real, and it need not trouble anyone: the killing of Goliath is told at length in 1 Samuel 17, and one damaged line in a list does not touch it.

The spear like a weaver's beam is the description of Goliath's spear, and of the Egyptian's that Benaiah faced with a staff. It runs in the family, and so does what happens to them.

The descendants of the giants were the Rephaim, a people of great stature in Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:10–11), and the word here is not the one used of the Nephilim of Genesis 6.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was descended from the giants. And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea, David's brother, struck him down. These were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Gath the Chronicler counts: twenty-four in number, as though he wants the reader to have the figure and not just the impression.

The giant taunts, in the same posture as the first one, and somebody comes out: David's nephew, son of one of the brothers who had stood in that valley years before doing nothing.

David killed none of these three. He was in Jerusalem, by the account in Samuel no longer allowed near a battlefield. The text credits him anyway, because they were won in his name, by his men, against the family of the champion he had already beaten.

That is the shape of the whole thing. One decisive fight in a valley, settled by one man with a sling while everyone else watched; and then a long, unglamorous mopping-up carried out over years by men whose names nobody remembers, against opponents who were already beaten in principle and still had to be faced one at a time. The victory was the king's. The clearing of the field was given to his servants to do, and it went down on his record. Christians have long heard the gospel’s shape in that. The decisive battle was fought by David’s greater Son alone, who disarmed the powers and triumphed over them at the cross (Colossians 2:15); his people still face what taunts them one at a time, with the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17), and every victory goes down to his name. There is a giant somewhere still taunting, and the church is at Gath and at Gezer with a sword in its hand, and every one of them falls by the hand of David’s Son.

20.theology:
Chronicles omits David's great sin but does not conceal it (see on v. 1). It answers a different question from Samuel: not what David was like, but what God promised to his house and what it was for. Its readers, who had no king at all, needed the second.

Verse 8 states the principle the honour roll has been working towards since chapter 11: a victory won in the king's name, in the king's manner, by men the king trained, is counted as the king's.
20.examples:
None of these three fought the famous giant; they fought his relatives, years after the story everyone tells was over. Most faithful work is the clearing up after somebody else's decisive victory, and it still has to be done a giant at a time.

Rabbah fell in the spring the king stayed home. The chapter records the crown coming to him anyway. Success arriving on schedule is no evidence at all about how a man has spent the season.

21.title: The Census, the Plague, and the Altar: Where the Temple Will Stand
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel.<sup>2</sup>So David said to Joab and the commanders of the army, "Go, number Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, and bring me a report, that I may know their number."<sup>3</sup>But Joab said, "May the LORD add to his people a hundred times as many as they are! Are they not, my lord the king, all of them my lord's servants? Why then should my lord require this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?"<sup>4</sup>But the king's word prevailed against Joab. So Joab departed and went throughout all Israel and came back to Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>And Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to David. In all Israel there were 1,100,000 men who drew the sword, and in Judah 470,000 who drew the sword.<sup>6</sup>But he did not include Levi and Benjamin in the numbering, for the king's command was abhorrent to Joab.<sup>7</sup>But God was displeased with this thing, and he struck Israel.<sup>8</sup>And David said to God, "I have sinned greatly in that I have done this thing. But now, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly."<sup>9</sup>And the LORD spoke to Gad, David's seer, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD, Three things I offer you; choose one of them, that I may do it to you.'"<sup>11</sup>So Gad came to David and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Choose what you will:<sup>12</sup>either three years of famine, or three months of devastation by your foes while the sword of your enemies overtakes you, or else three days of the sword of the LORD, pestilence on the land, with the angel of the LORD destroying throughout all the territory of Israel.' Now decide what answer I shall return to him who sent me."<sup>13</sup>Then David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great, but do not let me fall into the hand of man."<sup>14</sup>So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel, and 70,000 men of Israel fell.<sup>15</sup>And God sent the angel to Jerusalem to destroy it, but as he was about to destroy it, the LORD saw, and he relented from the calamity. And he said to the angel who was working destruction, "It is enough; now stay your hand." And the angel of the LORD was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.<sup>16</sup>And David lifted his eyes and saw the angel of the LORD standing between earth and heaven, and in his hand a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces.<sup>17</sup>And David said to God, "Was it not I who gave command to number the people? It is I who have sinned and done great evil. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand, O LORD my God, be against me and against my father's house. But do not let the plague be on your people."<sup>18</sup>Now the angel of the LORD had commanded Gad to say to David that David should go up and raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.<sup>19</sup>So David went up at Gad's word, which he had spoken in the name of the LORD.<sup>20</sup>Now Ornan was threshing wheat. He turned and saw the angel, and his four sons who were with him hid themselves.<sup>21</sup>As David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David and went out from the threshing floor and paid homage to David with his face to the ground.<sup>22</sup>And David said to Ornan, "Give me the site of the threshing floor that I may build on it an altar to the LORD—give it to me at its full price—that the plague may be averted from the people."<sup>23</sup>Then Ornan said to David, "Take it, and let my lord the king do what seems good to him. See, I give the oxen for burnt offerings and the threshing sledges for the wood and the wheat for a grain offering; I give it all."<sup>24</sup>But King David said to Ornan, "No, but I will buy them for the full price. I will not take for the LORD what is yours, nor offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing."<sup>25</sup>So David paid Ornan 600 shekels of gold by weight for the site.<sup>26</sup>And David built there an altar to the LORD and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings and called on the LORD, and the LORD answered him with fire from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering.<sup>27</sup>Then the LORD commanded the angel, and he put his sword back into its sheath.<sup>28</sup>At that time, when David saw that the LORD had answered him at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he sacrificed there.<sup>29</sup>For the tabernacle of the LORD, which Moses had made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering were at that time in the high place at Gibeon,<sup>30</sup>but David could not go before it to inquire of God, for he was afraid of the sword of the angel of the LORD.
21.overview:
David orders a census against Joab's protest (vv. 1-6). God strikes Israel; David confesses, and Gad brings three punishments to choose from (vv. 7-12). David chooses to fall into God's hand, and the plague is stopped at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (vv. 13-15), where David asks to be struck instead of the people (vv. 16-17). He buys the site at full price, God answers with fire from heaven, and the angel sheathes his sword (vv. 18-27). The chapter ends by explaining why the sacrifice was not made at Gibeon (vv. 28-30).

This is the hinge of the book: the temple site is found here, at the place where a plague stopped.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A King Who Wanted a Number
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Satan incites David to number Israel (vv. 1-2). Joab objects that it will bring guilt on Israel and is overruled (vv. 3-4). The totals come back with two tribes quietly missing, for the king's command was abhorrent to Joab (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Whoever incited him, neither account reduces David's guilt by a syllable: he will say twice, in his own words, that the sin was his.
verseByVerse.examples: Joab said the right thing, was overruled, and could not stop what he saw coming. Being right in the council room does not always mean being able to prevent the harm.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel. So David said to Joab and the commanders of the army, "Go, number Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, and bring me a report, that I may know their number."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same episode is told in 2 Samuel 24, and it opens: the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them. One book names God as the mover; this one names Satan. It is the plainest example in Scripture of two writers assigning the same action to different agents, and it should not be smoothed over.

Two things need saying. The first is language. The Hebrew word here has no article, and elsewhere the same word plainly means an adversary: the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon, a man called Hadad. Some read this verse as a hostile power or human enemy. Most English versions read it as the accuser of Job and the tempter of the Gospels, and that may well be right; the verse alone will not settle it.

The second is larger. Scripture repeatedly puts two causes behind one event and refuses to choose. Satan strips Job, and Job says the LORD has taken away, without sin. A lying spirit deceives Ahab's prophets, and God sends him. Lawless men crucify Jesus by the definite plan of God, and Peter charges them with murder in the same sentence.

So the older account looks at the census from above and says God was behind it; this one looks from below and names the adversary who pushed. Neither writer thought he was correcting the other, and the Chronicler almost certainly had 2 Samuel in front of him.

What neither writer does is excuse David. Twice the king says the sin was his (vv. 8, 17), and nobody mentions the tempter again. A man who has been incited is not a man who has been excused.

And the order is revealing: not to raise a levy or plan a campaign, but that I may know their number. He wants the figure for its own sake, the king who has been told twice in three chapters that the LORD saved him wherever he went.
verseByVerse.note: God was sovereign over what Satan intended, as in Job 1–2.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joab said, "May the LORD add to his people a hundred times as many as they are! Are they not, my lord the king, all of them my lord's servants? Why then should my lord require this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?" But the king's word prevailed against Joab. So Joab departed and went throughout all Israel and came back to Jerusalem. And Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to David. In all Israel there were 1,100,000 men who drew the sword, and in Judah 470,000 who drew the sword. But he did not include Levi and Benjamin in the numbering, for the king's command was abhorrent to Joab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab objects, and the objection is better than anything the king says in this chapter.

Three arguments in four lines. The first is that numbers are God's business to give, not the king's to audit. The second is that they already belong to him, so the count adds nothing. And the third is the one Joab alone seems to see: this will not stop with David. It will be a cause of guilt for Israel, and seventy thousand men are going to find out how right he was.

The law had already said why. When a census was taken in Israel, every man counted had to pay a ransom for his life, and the reason given was that there be no plague among them when you number them. A head that is counted is a life that must be redeemed. Nothing in this chapter mentions the ransom money, and the plague comes exactly as promised, which is as close to an explanation as the text offers.

The king's word prevailed. Told he was wrong by the most experienced man in his kingdom, he used his authority to end the conversation, the one power no adviser can answer.

The figures do not match the totals in the parallel account. What this book adds is the footnote: Levi and Benjamin were left out. Levi was exempt from a military census by law. Benjamin was not, and Joab simply left it out.

It is neither obedience nor refusal. He carried out an order he believed was a sin, under protest, and quietly falsified the return, and Scripture reports it without telling us what to make of it.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations; and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Here Samuel has 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah; some think one total includes the standing army of chapter 27 and the other does not. Likewise the three years of famine in verse 12 stand where the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 24:13 has seven, though the Greek of Samuel also has three.
