Neither touches what the passage teaches; this commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–17 — Three Days, and a Drawn Sword
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God strikes Israel and David confesses at once (vv. 7-8). Gad brings three options, and David chooses the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great (vv. 9-13). Seventy thousand die before the LORD says It is enough, and the angel halts at Ornan's threshing floor (vv. 14-15). David sees the drawn sword and prays to be struck instead (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The sword in this section is real, and so is the word that stops it. Judgment and mercy meet over the same threshing floor.
verseByVerse.examples: A guilty man appealing to mercy is not asking God to pretend. David names his sin, accepts that judgment is coming, and still trusts the one who judges.

verseByVerse.quote: But God was displeased with this thing, and he struck Israel. And David said to God, "I have sinned greatly in that I have done this thing. But now, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Displeased is a mild word in English for what follows. The Hebrew says the thing was evil in God's eyes, and the response is immediate.

No prophet has spoken yet. Nobody has told a story about a lamb, and the king is not defending himself or asking what exactly was wrong. He says he sinned greatly, asks for the guilt to be taken away, and calls himself a fool.

Three sentences, and every one of them concedes something. That capacity was in him from the beginning and it is the reason God calls this man a man after his own heart — not because he sinned less than Saul, but because when he was caught he did not manage the situation. Saul, confronted about the Amalekite cattle, explained that the people had kept the best animals to sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Gad, David's seer, saying, "Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD, Three things I offer you; choose one of them, that I may do it to you.'" So Gad came to David and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Choose what you will: either three years of famine, or three months of devastation by your foes while the sword of your enemies overtakes you, or else three days of the sword of the LORD, pestilence on the land, with the angel of the LORD destroying throughout all the territory of Israel.' Now decide what answer I shall return to him who sent me." Then David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great, but do not let me fall into the hand of man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gad is called David's seer — a prophet attached to the court, whose job was to bring the king words he had not asked for. He arrives with three.

The duration shrinks (years, months, days), the intensity climbs to meet it, and the agency changes: famine works through weather, defeat through enemy armies, and the third is God himself with no intermediary.

Then comes his answer, the sentence that a hundred readings of this chapter will not wear out. He is not choosing the shortest option, though it happens to be the shortest. He says why he chooses it, and the reason has nothing to do with duration: he is picking his judge. He would rather be dealt with directly by the God he has just offended than handed over to people, and the ground he gives is God's character. His mercy is very great.

The plague has not begun. The third option means an angel with orders to destroy, and he chooses it, having concluded from a lifetime with this God that even his wrath is safer than human kindness. Men are capricious, and cruel by turns, and their mercy runs out on a schedule of its own. God's does not.

It is the same judgment any sinner has to make in the end, and the alternatives have not changed. There is nowhere to fall except into somebody's hands. David had learned enough about whose they were to choose the ones holding a sword.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel, and 70,000 men of Israel fell. And God sent the angel to Jerusalem to destroy it, but as he was about to destroy it, the LORD saw, and he relented from the calamity. And he said to the angel who was working destruction, "It is enough; now stay your hand." And the angel of the LORD was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab came back from a tour of the country (nine months long, Samuel says) with a figure of one and a half million fighting men. David now has a second figure, seventy thousand, and the Chronicler puts the two nine verses apart without joining them. A king asked how many men he had, and God answered in a way that could not be filed.

The LORD saw, and something in the sight of the city stopped the judgment in mid-stroke, and what he says to the angel is a handful of words in Hebrew and one of the great mercies of the Old Testament: It is enough; now stay your hand.

Relented is the language of a man changing his mind, and Scripture uses it because that is how the moment looked from below; it also says God is not a man, that he should change his mind (Numbers 23:19). Enough is a judgment too. It means that the punishment had a measure and the measure was known, and that the one setting it was not carried along by his own anger. Wrath that can be told to stop is not the wrath of a temper. It is the settled response of a holy God who has decided in advance where it ends.

And where it stopped is dropped in as though it were geography: the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Everything left in this book happens on that piece of ground.

Why did 70,000 die for David’s sin? Second Samuel says God’s anger was already against Israel (2 Samuel 24:1); the nation shared the pride, and the plague judged king and people together. David offered himself in their place (v. 17), a picture of the King who would.

verseByVerse.quote: And David lifted his eyes and saw the angel of the LORD standing between earth and heaven, and in his hand a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces. And David said to God, "Was it not I who gave command to number the people? It is I who have sinned and done great evil. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand, O LORD my God, be against me and against my father's house. But do not let the plague be on your people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between earth and heaven, over the city, the blade out. The king and the elders put on sackcloth and go down on their faces in the open, at the top of the hill.

And then David prays, the finest thing he says in this book.

Was it not I who gave command to number the people? Three moves, and each one costs him something. He takes the whole blame and states the chain of command out loud: the order was mine. He calls the dying people sheep — the flock God had told him, as Israel reminded him at Hebron, to shepherd (11:2). And then he asks to be struck in their place, and to have his own house struck with him.

That is a shepherd offering to die for the flock, and it is refused. It had to be. David was the one man in Israel who could not stand in for anybody, because he was the one man in Israel who had actually done it. A substitute has to be innocent, and there was no such person on that hill.

So the offer hangs there unaccepted, and God answers it a different way, which is what the rest of the chapter is about. And the hill it was made on is named at the start of the second book of Chronicles: Mount Moriah, where the temple was built on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Abraham had been sent to the land of Moriah to offer his son (Genesis 22:2), and Jews and Christians have long taken it to be this same ridge, where a father climbed with his son and a knife and was stopped by a voice and shown a ram in a thicket. Substitution had been asked for on that hill before, and it had been provided. On a day still a thousand years off, outside the wall of the same city, a shepherd would make the offer David made here, and would not be refused (John 10:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The Threshing Floor Bought at Full Price
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gad tells David to raise an altar on the threshing floor (vv. 18-19). Ornan sees the angel, and offers floor, oxen, sledges and wheat for nothing (vv. 20-23). David refuses to offer what cost him nothing and pays 600 shekels of gold (vv. 24-25). God answers with fire from heaven, and the angel sheathes his sword (vv. 26-27).
verseByVerse.theology: Fire from heaven is how God signs for a place, and here it settles where the house of God is to stand: on the spot where the sword stopped.
verseByVerse.examples: The first generosity in this section comes from an outsider: a Jebusite farmer who offered everything he had on the spot.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the angel of the LORD had commanded Gad to say to David that David should go up and raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. So David went up at Gad's word, which he had spoken in the name of the LORD. Now Ornan was threshing wheat. He turned and saw the angel, and his four sons who were with him hid themselves. As David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David and went out from the threshing floor and paid homage to David with his face to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The instruction comes back through Gad, and David goes at once, up the hill towards the angel with the sword.

Ornan is threshing wheat at harvest with his four sons, doing the most ordinary thing a man can do in that country in that season.

He saw it too, a detail no other account gives. This is not a private vision granted to a king: a Jebusite farmer and his boys looked up from the wheat and saw a figure with a sword over the city, and the sons hid, which is the only sane response.

He was a Jebusite. His people had held that ridge against Israel for centuries until David took the stronghold, and he is still there, farming, on the high ground north of the city, when the king of Israel comes up the path towards him. He gets down with his face to the ground.
verseByVerse.note: Ornan is another form of Araunah.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said to Ornan, "Give me the site of the threshing floor that I may build on it an altar to the LORD—give it to me at its full price—that the plague may be averted from the people." Then Ornan said to David, "Take it, and let my lord the king do what seems good to him. See, I give the oxen for burnt offerings and the threshing sledges for the wood and the wheat for a grain offering; I give it all." But King David said to Ornan, "No, but I will buy them for the full price. I will not take for the LORD what is yours, nor offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing." So David paid Ornan 600 shekels of gold by weight for the site.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is offering the floor, the oxen for the burnt offering, the sledges for firewood and the wheat for the grain offering: his entire working capital, on the spot, to a king he has just met under an angel's sword.

And David says no. The first half of his answer is about Ornan: it would be his sacrifice with the king's name attached. The second half is about David, and people have carried it away from this chapter for three thousand years. A burnt offering that cost him nothing would have been a gesture performed with someone else's oxen.

Six hundred shekels of gold changes hands, where the other account has fifty shekels of silver; the likeliest explanation is in the note below, though it cannot be proved. What both accounts agree on is that David insisted on paying and said why.

The costliest offering ever made was not made by David and did not cost the one who brought it nothing. It cost him everything he had, and he had said in advance that no one was taking it from him.
verseByVerse.note: Samuel’s fifty shekels probably bought the threshing floor and oxen, and Chronicles’ 600 shekels of gold the whole site.

verseByVerse.quote: And David built there an altar to the LORD and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings and called on the LORD, and the LORD answered him with fire from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering. Then the LORD commanded the angel, and he put his sword back into its sheath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fire from heaven: only this account has it. God lit the altar himself at the tabernacle's dedication, on Carmel, and will again when Solomon finishes his prayer on this very hill.

Each time, it settles something. Here it settles a place. David has offered on a threshing floor because he could not reach the lawful altar, and God comes down on it in front of witnesses and accepts what has been offered there, and that is how Israel learns where the temple goes.

Both kinds of offering are made: the burnt offering that goes up entirely, and the peace offering that ends in a meal. Judgment satisfied and fellowship restored, in that order, on the same fire.

The blade that had been out over Jerusalem goes away, and what put it away was blood on an altar. The sword did not blunt itself and it was not talked down. Something died in the place where it was pointing, and the sword went home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–30 — Why the Altar Had to Be Here
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes by explaining the irregularity. The lawful altar was at Gibeon (v. 29), but David could not go before it, for fear of the angel's sword (v. 30), so he sacrificed where God had answered him (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Chapter 16 left Israel's worship split between two hills: the ark and the singing in Jerusalem, the altar and the daily offering at Gibeon. This is where the split begins to close, and it closes at the place where a plague was stopped.
verseByVerse.examples: God did not send David on a journey to the lawful altar. He gave him one on the ground where he stood, and lit it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time, when David saw that the LORD had answered him at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he sacrificed there. For the tabernacle of the LORD, which Moses had made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering were at that time in the high place at Gibeon, but David could not go before it to inquire of God, for he was afraid of the sword of the angel of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last three verses are the Chronicler explaining himself, and they close a gap he opened five chapters ago.

So David has just sacrificed in the wrong place, and this book, which cares more than any other about who may do what and where, accounts for it.

The lawful altar was a day's business away, with a sword over the city behind him and the plague killing people while he travelled. God sent a prophet to say build here and lit the fire himself, and the irregular altar on a Jebusite's floor turned out to be the one God had been aiming at all along.

That is where the second half of this book comes from. Everything after this chapter — the gold, the plans, the courses of priests, the charge to Solomon, the last prayer of David's life — is about a building that will stand on this floor and gather the two halves of Israel's worship into one house at last.

And the site was found at the lowest point of David's life. He wanted a number, seventy thousand people died, and the place where the sword stopped is the place where God chose to live. The ground was bought at full price by a man who refused to give God anything that had cost him nothing, and it was paid for out of a disaster he had caused himself. God has never yet been reduced to working with untainted material, and the mercy seat would stand at the exact spot where judgment halted.

21.theology:
Verse 1 names Satan and 2 Samuel 24:1 names the LORD (see on vv. 1-2), but no account allows the excuse: David says I have sinned greatly (v. 8), and the tempter is never mentioned again.

Verse 13 is the chapter's centre. Offered three judgments, David picks his judge rather than his sentence: let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great. And verse 15 shows he was right — the judgment had a measure, and the one who set it said it is enough while the angel's arm was still raised.
21.examples:
David confessed before any prophet arrived, and ran towards the God whose mercy is very great. That road is still open: the one who confesses is met by a God who is faithful to forgive (1 John 1:9), because the shepherd David could not be has already been struck for the flock.

I will not take for the LORD what is yours, nor offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing. An offering that costs the giver nothing has not been given; it has been arranged.

22.title: David Prepares for the Temple: The Man of War and the Man of Peace
22.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David said, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God and here the altar of burnt offering for Israel."<sup>2</sup>David commanded to gather together the resident aliens who were in the land of Israel, and he set stonecutters to prepare dressed stones for building the house of God.<sup>3</sup>David also provided great quantities of iron for nails for the doors of the gates and for clamps, as well as bronze in quantities beyond weighing,<sup>4</sup>and cedar timbers without number, for the Sidonians and Tyrians brought great quantities of cedar to David.<sup>5</sup>For David said, "Solomon my son is young and inexperienced, and the house that is to be built for the LORD must be exceedingly magnificent, of fame and glory throughout all lands. I will therefore make preparation for it." So David provided materials in great quantity before his death.<sup>6</sup>Then he called for Solomon his son and charged him to build a house for the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>7</sup>David said to Solomon, "My son, I had it in my heart to build a house to the name of the LORD my God.<sup>8</sup>But the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 'You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed so much blood before me on the earth.<sup>9</sup>Behold, a son shall be born to you who shall be a man of rest. I will give him rest from all his surrounding enemies. For his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quiet to Israel in his days.<sup>10</sup>He shall build a house for my name. He shall be my son, and I will be his father, and I will establish his royal throne in Israel forever.'<sup>11</sup>"Now, my son, the LORD be with you, so that you may succeed in building the house of the LORD your God, as he has spoken concerning you.<sup>12</sup>Only, may the LORD grant you discretion and understanding, that when he gives you charge over Israel you may keep the law of the LORD your God.<sup>13</sup>Then you will prosper if you are careful to observe the statutes and the rules that the LORD commanded Moses for Israel. Be strong and courageous. Fear not; do not be dismayed.<sup>14</sup>With great pains I have provided for the house of the LORD 100,000 talents of gold, a million talents of silver, and bronze and iron beyond weighing, for there is so much of it; timber and stone, too, I have provided. To these you must add.<sup>15</sup>You have an abundance of workmen: stonecutters, masons, carpenters, and all kinds of craftsmen without number, skilled in working<sup>16</sup>gold, silver, bronze, and iron. Arise and work! The LORD be with you!"<sup>17</sup>David also commanded all the leaders of Israel to help Solomon his son, saying,<sup>18</sup>"Is not the LORD your God with you? And has he not given you peace on every side? For he has delivered the inhabitants of the land into my hand, and the land is subdued before the LORD and his people.<sup>19</sup>Now set your mind and heart to seek the LORD your God. Arise and build the sanctuary of the LORD God, so that the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy vessels of God may be brought into a house built for the name of the LORD."
22.overview:
Standing on the threshing floor, David names the temple site (v. 1) and begins stockpiling, for Solomon my son is young and inexperienced (vv. 2-5). He charges Solomon privately, explaining why he himself was refused the work, repeating the covenant, praying for wisdom to keep the law, and handing over an immense store (vv. 6-16). Then he charges the leaders to help: Arise and build (vv. 17-19).

Everything from here to the end of the book is preparation for a building David will not live to see, on ground he had refused to accept as a gift.
22.theology:
The refusal at verses 7-8 is not called a punishment (see on vv. 6-10). Being right and being the wrong man are not alternatives.

Verse 19 puts the book's governing word into an imperative with a job attached: set your mind and heart to seek the LORD your God. Arise and build. Its purpose clause closes the split of 16:37-42.
22.examples:
Most of what is done for God is ironmongery for somebody else's building, and David was content to supply it.

He said out loud why he was doing it: his son was young and inexperienced and the work was enormous. He saw the gap without contempt, spent what was left of his life closing it from his own end, and then told the boy to these you must add.

Solomon later asked for the wisdom his father had prayed for and received it, and it is not hard to see which half of his father's prayer he eventually stopped praying. No son of David kept that law whole but one, and his obedience is counted to all who are his; that is what lets a believer take up the same charge without fear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Here Shall Be the House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the threshing floor, with the fire barely out, David names the site of the house and the altar (v. 1). Then the stockpiling begins: stone dressed by resident aliens, iron for nails, bronze and cedar beyond counting (vv. 2-4), because his son is young and the house must be magnificent (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The site was fixed where the plague stopped, and fixed by God's fire rather than by David's preference.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithfulness often looks like the least memorable item in the inventory: an old king stockpiling nails (v. 3).

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God and here the altar of burnt offering for Israel." David commanded to gather together the resident aliens who were in the land of Israel, and he set stonecutters to prepare dressed stones for building the house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is still on the threshing floor. The angel has put up his sword, seventy thousand are dead, the wheat is still lying where Ornan left it, and the king looks at the ground under his feet and says: here.

Here the house, and here the altar. He is not proposing a site but identifying one, because God has just answered by fire on this exact patch of rock. Second Chronicles names it in the same terms: Mount Moriah, the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

The gerim were foreigners settled in Israel, and by Solomon's day the census of them runs to more than a hundred and fifty thousand men on the works. It was conscription and the Chronicler does not dress it up. The stones of the house of Israel's God were cut and squared by men who could not have gone into it — and the prophets, looking at the same building centuries later, would hear God call it a house of prayer for all peoples, and promise the foreigner who held to the covenant a name inside the walls better than sons and daughters.

verseByVerse.quote: David also provided great quantities of iron for nails for the doors of the gates and for clamps, as well as bronze in quantities beyond weighing, and cedar timbers without number, for the Sidonians and Tyrians brought great quantities of cedar to David. For David said, "Solomon my son is young and inexperienced, and the house that is to be built for the LORD must be exceedingly magnificent, of fame and glory throughout all lands. I will therefore make preparation for it." So David provided materials in great quantity before his death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first item on the inventory is nails: not gold, not anything anyone would look at, but ironmongery in quantity for hinges and the cramps that hold dressed blocks together. An old man is buying fixings for a building he will never walk into.

Then bronze beyond weighing, and cedar brought down the coast by the same trade route that had built David his own house.

Verse 5 gives the reason in David's own words: his son is not yet up to it, an unusual thing for a father to say about his heir, said without contempt.

Before his death. The clause is flat and it is the point: he worked at it until he died, for a son he knew was not ready.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–16 — A Charge to a Young Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David tells Solomon why he could not build: he had shed much blood (vv. 7-8). The task goes to a man of rest, and the covenant of chapter 17 is repeated to him (vv. 9-10). Then the charge: wisdom to keep the law, and be strong and courageous (vv. 11-13). The inventory follows, ending in Arise and work! (vv. 14-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 10 hands the son the covenant of chapter 17 almost word for word. Solomon begins his work already inside a promise he did nothing to earn, and the charge that follows is built on it.
verseByVerse.examples: A father's best prayer for a gifted son (v. 12) is that his gifts will be spent on obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he called for Solomon his son and charged him to build a house for the LORD, the God of Israel. David said to Solomon, "My son, I had it in my heart to build a house to the name of the LORD my God. But the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 'You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed so much blood before me on the earth. Behold, a son shall be born to you who shall be a man of rest. I will give him rest from all his surrounding enemies. For his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quiet to Israel in his days. He shall build a house for my name. He shall be my son, and I will be his father, and I will establish his royal throne in Israel forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is easy to hear this as a punishment, and the text does not say so. These are the wars of chapters 18 to 20, of which the Chronicler's verdict was that the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went. When David tells the story again he puts it in five words: you are a man of war.

What the blood did was disqualify him for one particular task. A house of rest cannot be raised by the man whose calling was fighting, and that says nothing about whether he did his calling well. He was right, and he was the wrong man, which is harder to accept than a rebuke, because there is nothing to repent of and nothing to appeal. Some readers think Uriah’s blood is in view as well, and David certainly had that to repent of; but the words given name wars, and they describe a calling rather than a charge.

Then the alternative. Behold, a son shall be born to you who shall be a man of rest. I will give him rest from all his surrounding enemies. For his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quiet to Israel in his days. The name and the promise sound alike — Shelomoh, shalom — so that every time anybody called the boy in for supper they were saying what God intended to do with the country.

And rest is the exact thing a temple is for. The ark had been carried from tent to tent for four hundred years and the psalm says of this hill, this is my resting place forever. A man of rest builds a house of rest for a God who had never had one. The pattern does not end with Solomon: a greater than Solomon has come (Matthew 12:42), who calls the weary to himself and gives them rest (Matthew 11:28), and whose house, Hebrews says, is his people (Hebrews 3:6).

How was the throne established for ever when Solomon’s line ended? The promise rests on the Son of David who reigns now (Luke 1:32–33).
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s name sounds like shalom, “peace.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, my son, the LORD be with you, so that you may succeed in building the house of the LORD your God, as he has spoken concerning you. Only, may the LORD grant you discretion and understanding, that when he gives you charge over Israel you may keep the law of the LORD your God. Then you will prosper if you are careful to observe the statutes and the rules that the LORD commanded Moses for Israel. Be strong and courageous. Fear not; do not be dismayed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge is three short sentences and a prayer, and the prayer is the surprising part.

David asks God to make his son wise, and says what for: not to govern shrewdly or design a building of fame, but that ... you may keep the law. In his father's prayer, intelligence is a tool for obedience.

Solomon will one day be offered anything he wants and will ask for exactly this. The father asked for it first.

Then commands lifted straight out of another handover: the words spoken to Joshua when Moses died and the river had to be crossed. David lays them on a boy who has to build a temple.

Building is treated as a campaign, and the resources issued are the ones Joshua got: the law, courage commanded, and the promise that God goes with you. For the Christian that presence is the Spirit given to every believer, who supplies the strength the command calls for.

verseByVerse.quote: With great pains I have provided for the house of the LORD 100,000 talents of gold, a million talents of silver, and bronze and iron beyond weighing, for there is so much of it; timber and stone, too, I have provided. To these you must add. You have an abundance of workmen: stonecutters, masons, carpenters, and all kinds of craftsmen without number, skilled in working gold, silver, bronze, and iron. Arise and work! The LORD be with you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Figures on this scale (see the note) have been discussed for a very long time, and part of the answer may be that the Hebrew word for thousand is also the word for a unit or a company, so that ancient totals do not always mean what a modern ledger would mean by them. Nobody can settle it. What the sentence is plainly doing is saying that the store was past counting, and that a man who could not build had spent everything he had on making it possible.

With great pains is a single word meaning in my affliction. He gathered it out of wars and long campaigns, over decades, while his family fell apart around him.

And then: To these you must add. He does not hand over a finished endowment and take the credit.

The charge ends at a shout, from a man near the end of his life to a young one at the beginning of the only job that mattered.
verseByVerse.note: A talent was about 75 pounds (ESV note): 100,000 talents of gold is some 3,750 tons.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–19 — A Charge to the Leaders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A public charge follows. David tells the leaders to help Solomon, grounding it in two questions: is not the LORD with you, and has he not given you peace? (v. 18). Then the command: seek the LORD and build, so that the ark and the holy vessels may be brought into one house (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: David's two questions come before his command. God's presence and the peace he has given are the ground of the work; the work is the answer to them, never the price of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Peace is a gift to be used. David's leaders were told to spend theirs on God's house rather than on their own comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: David also commanded all the leaders of Israel to help Solomon his son, saying, "Is not the LORD your God with you? And has he not given you peace on every side? For he has delivered the inhabitants of the land into my hand, and the land is subdued before the LORD and his people. Now set your mind and heart to seek the LORD your God. Arise and build the sanctuary of the LORD God, so that the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy vessels of God may be brought into a house built for the name of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last verses turn to the men who will serve Solomon, and David opens with questions rather than an order.

Is not the LORD your God with you? He is establishing the ground before he asks for anything: God is with you; God has given you rest. And he treats the rest as working capital. The wars were not fought so that Israel could sit down. The quiet that has been won is the condition in which something can finally be built, and a nation that mistakes the rest for the point will spend it on itself.

Seek is the word the whole book has been carrying since Saul's obituary, and here it arrives with a job attached. Set your mind and heart to seek him — and the way you seek him, this year, in this generation, is to quarry stone and haul cedar and organise labour. Nobody is being told to choose between devotion and work. They are being told which work is the devotion.

And the purpose clause closes a wound that has been open since chapter 16. So that the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy vessels of God may be brought into a house built for the name of the LORD. The ark has been in a tent on one hill and the altar and the vessels on another for a generation, and every day the daily sacrifice has been offered six miles from the throne of God. One house, at last, with both in it.

That is what the old man wanted, and he did not get it. He bought the ground, cut the stone, weighed out the gold, hired the masons, prayed for his son and told the nation to get up and build, and then died before the foundations were dug. The house he never entered stood for nearly four hundred years and came down. The one it was pointing at is still being built, out of living stones, and the Bible's closing vision says there is no temple in the city at all, because the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.

23.title: The Levitical Orders: Every Ministry Has Its Place
23.text: <sup>1</sup>When David was old and full of days, he made Solomon his son king over Israel.<sup>2</sup>David assembled all the leaders of Israel and the priests and the Levites.<sup>3</sup>The Levites, thirty years old and upward, were numbered, and the total was 38,000 men.<sup>4</sup>"Twenty-four thousand of these," David said, "shall have charge of the work in the house of the LORD, 6,000 shall be officers and judges,<sup>5</sup>4,000 gatekeepers, and 4,000 shall offer praises to the LORD with the instruments that I have made for praise."<sup>6</sup>And David organized them in divisions corresponding to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Gershon were Ladan and Shimei.<sup>8</sup>The sons of Ladan: Jehiel the chief, and Zetham, and Joel, three.<sup>9</sup>The sons of Shimei: Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran, three. These were the heads of the fathers' houses of Ladan.<sup>10</sup>And the sons of Shimei: Jahath, Zina, and Jeush and Beriah. These four were the sons of Shimei.<sup>11</sup>Jahath was the chief, and Zizah the second; but Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, therefore they became counted as a single father's house.<sup>12</sup>The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, four.<sup>13</sup>The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart to dedicate the most holy things, that he and his sons forever should make offerings before the LORD and minister to him and pronounce blessings in his name forever.<sup>14</sup>But the sons of Moses the man of God were named among the tribe of Levi.<sup>15</sup>The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer.<sup>16</sup>The sons of Gershom: Shebuel the chief.<sup>17</sup>The sons of Eliezer: Rehabiah the chief. Eliezer had no other sons, but the sons of Rehabiah were very many.<sup>18</sup>The sons of Izhar: Shelomith the chief.<sup>19</sup>The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.<sup>20</sup>The sons of Uzziel: Micah the chief and Isshiah the second.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Mahli: Eleazar and Kish.<sup>22</sup>Eleazar died having no sons, but only daughters; their kinsmen, the sons of Kish, married them.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth, three.<sup>24</sup>These were the sons of Levi by their fathers' houses, the heads of fathers' houses as they were listed according to the number of the names of the individuals from twenty years old and upward who were to do the work for the service of the house of the LORD.<sup>25</sup>For David said, "The LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to his people, and he dwells in Jerusalem forever.<sup>26</sup>And so the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle or any of the things for its service."<sup>27</sup>For by the last words of David the sons of Levi were numbered from twenty years old and upward.<sup>28</sup>For their duty was to assist the sons of Aaron for the service of the house of the LORD, having the care of the courts and the chambers, the cleansing of all that is holy, and any work for the service of the house of God.<sup>29</sup>Their duty was also to assist with the showbread, the flour for the grain offering, the wafers of unleavened bread, the baked offering, the offering mixed with oil, and all measures of quantity or size.<sup>30</sup>And they were to stand every morning, thanking and praising the LORD, and likewise at evening,<sup>31</sup>and whenever burnt offerings were offered to the LORD on Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days, according to the number required of them, regularly before the LORD.<sup>32</sup>Thus they were to keep charge of the tent of meeting and the sanctuary, and to attend the sons of Aaron, their brothers, for the service of the house of the LORD.
23.overview:
Old and full of days, David makes Solomon king and assembles the nation (vv. 1-2). The Levites are counted and divided into four orders (vv. 3-6) and the three clans set out house by house, with Aaron given the altar forever and the sons of Moses entered as ordinary Levites (vv. 7-23). The enrolment age drops to twenty and the duties are restated for a settled sanctuary (vv. 24-32).

The chapter's argument is in the arithmetic and the job titles. The tribe's oldest duty has been abolished, and what replaces it is daily.

Why is this here? The Chronicler's first readers had come back from Babylon to a humbler, rebuilt temple, and they needed to know that its staff and duties were not improvised but went back to David, and through him to Moses, so that their worship stood in an unbroken line with the worship God had appointed. Lists that look dull to us were their title deeds.
23.theology:
Verses 25-26 give the reason the whole order changed: the LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to his people, and he dwells in Jerusalem forever. Carrying was the shape of Levitical service for four centuries because God was travelling. He has stopped, and so the shoulder-work ends and the daily work begins.

And verses 13-14 put two brothers side by side (see on vv. 13-17): no greatness of a father transfers. The book that spends nine chapters on descent is the book that says descent from the greatest man in Israel conferred nothing at all.
23.examples:
Six thousand Levites were sent out as officers and judges, and four thousand were put on instruments the king had provided. A tribe set apart for God supplied the magistrates as well as the choir, and neither posting was a demotion from the other.

The duties in verses 28-29 run from the cleansing of everything holy to checking weights and measures. Somebody had to make sure a measure was honest, and Scripture files that between the showbread and the morning thanksgiving without a change of tone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — An Old King Numbers the Levites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Old and full of days, David makes Solomon king and calls an assembly (vv. 1-2). The Levites from thirty upward are counted (v. 3) and divided into four orders, including officers and judges and four thousand musicians (vv. 4-5), under the three sons of Levi (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Most of the tribe now serves the house itself; the rest keep its doors, lead its music and judge in the towns.
verseByVerse.examples: A king who could not build the house provided the instruments for its praise (v. 5). What we are refused is rarely the end of what we can give.

verseByVerse.quote: When David was old and full of days, he made Solomon his son king over Israel. David assembled all the leaders of Israel and the priests and the Levites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence for the succession. Kings gives it a whole unpeaceful chapter: an older son proclaiming himself at a spring, Joab and Abiathar going over to him, Nathan and Bathsheba at the bedside of a man too cold to get warm, a coronation arranged to beat a coup. None of it is here.

What is here is the phrase old and full of days, which is the description given to Abraham and to Isaac and to Job at the end. It means a life that reached its own measure, and it will be said of David once more, six chapters on, in almost the same words.

Then he assembles everybody, because what he has left to do is administrative, and it will take the rest of the book.

verseByVerse.quote: The Levites, thirty years old and upward, were numbered, and the total was 38,000 men. "Twenty-four thousand of these," David said, "shall have charge of the work in the house of the LORD, 6,000 shall be officers and judges, 4,000 gatekeepers, and 4,000 shall offer praises to the LORD with the instruments that I have made for praise." And David organized them in divisions corresponding to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The four figures repay the trouble of adding up: 24,000, 6,000, 4,000 and 4,000 make exactly the thirty-eight thousand of verse 3.

Two orders are surprising. Six thousand Levites are out in the towns as magistrates, a sixth of the tribe set apart for God supplied to the civil courts. And four thousand are on music, with instruments David provided. Long after his death reforming kings brought out what the record still called the instruments of David.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–23 — The Three Houses of Levi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The clans are set out one at a time: Gershon (vv. 7-11); Kohath (v. 12), where Aaron is set apart forever (v. 13) and the sons of Moses entered simply among the tribe of Levi (vv. 14-17); the rest of Kohath (vv. 18-20); and Merari, closing with a family that survived because cousins married the daughters (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Moses is called the man of God in the same breath that his sons are entered as rank and file (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.examples: Even a list of names shows God's care for the household nobody else would remember: his law kept a family with only daughters from vanishing (v. 22).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Gershon were Ladan and Shimei. The sons of Ladan: Jehiel the chief, and Zetham, and Joel, three. The sons of Shimei: Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran, three. These were the heads of the fathers' houses of Ladan. And the sons of Shimei: Jahath, Zina, and Jeush and Beriah. These four were the sons of Shimei. Jahath was the chief, and Zizah the second; but Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, therefore they became counted as a single father's house. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, four.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gershon divides into Ladan and Shimei, the chief of each house marked out. One small note gets in: two small families were merged into one father's house so that neither vanished off the roster.

Then Kohath, the branch charged with the holy things, on which the next verses turn.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart to dedicate the most holy things, that he and his sons forever should make offerings before the LORD and minister to him and pronounce blessings in his name forever. But the sons of Moses the man of God were named among the tribe of Levi. The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer. The sons of Gershom: Shebuel the chief. The sons of Eliezer: Rehabiah the chief. Eliezer had no other sons, but the sons of Rehabiah were very many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses.

Two brothers in one line of a genealogy, and what the chapter says about each of them cuts.

Aaron first: three functions and two forevers. His descendants get the altar, the sanctuary and the blessing, permanently, by God's appointment.

Then Moses' sons, named among the tribe, and that is all. The man who spoke with God face to face and wrote the law this book is trying to keep has sons on a staff list, ordinary Levites in the same columns as everybody else.

Nobody in Israel had a better claim than Moses, and it bought his family nothing; the priesthood went to the line of the brother who made the golden calf. Standing before God is not inherited from a great father. It is given.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Izhar: Shelomith the chief. The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth. The sons of Uzziel: Micah the chief and Isshiah the second. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Mahli: Eleazar and Kish. Eleazar died having no sons, but only daughters; their kinsmen, the sons of Kish, married them. The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth, three.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The remaining Kohathite houses go past quickly — Shelomith of Izhar; Jeriah, Amariah, Jahaziel and Jekameam of Hebron, numbered first to fourth; Micah and Isshiah of Uzziel.

Then Merari, and in the middle of the list a family that nearly ended: Eleazar had only daughters, and their kinsmen married them.

That is a law of Moses working four hundred years on. Five sisters had once asked why their father's name should be taken away for want of a son, and God told Moses they were right, and that they should marry within their clan so the inheritance stayed put. A man died leaving daughters, and the law God gave kept his household's land, its place on the roll and its name in Scripture.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The enrolment age drops to twenty (v. 24), because God has given rest and the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle (vv. 25-27). The new duties follow: assisting the priests, cleansing the holy things, the showbread, all measures (vv. 28-29), thanks every morning and evening (v. 30), the appointed offerings (v. 31), and the keeping of the sanctuary (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The tribe's oldest and most dangerous duty, carrying the holy things on the shoulder, has just been abolished: God has stopped moving, and there is nothing left to lift.
verseByVerse.examples: A settled God does not need fewer servants than a travelling one. He needs different ones, and more of them.

verseByVerse.quote: These were the sons of Levi by their fathers' houses, the heads of fathers' houses as they were listed according to the number of the names of the individuals from twenty years old and upward who were to do the work for the service of the house of the LORD. For David said, "The LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to his people, and he dwells in Jerusalem forever. And so the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle or any of the things for its service." For by the last words of David the sons of Levi were numbered from twenty years old and upward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Numbers counts Levites for service from thirty (Numbers 4:3) and also from twenty-five (Numbers 8:24); after the exile they served from twenty, as here (Ezra 3:8).

The Kohathites' whole identity was carrying. No wagons were issued to them because the holy things went on the shoulder, and men had died for handling them wrongly. All of that is now over, not because the rules relaxed but because God has stopped moving.

And because the load is gone, a twenty-year-old can sweep a court and stack the showbread. The tribe whose ancestors had died for touching a holy thing now handle holy things every day, because God had come to stay.

verseByVerse.quote: For their duty was to assist the sons of Aaron for the service of the house of the LORD, having the care of the courts and the chambers, the cleansing of all that is holy, and any work for the service of the house of God. Their duty was also to assist with the showbread, the flour for the grain offering, the wafers of unleavened bread, the baked offering, the offering mixed with oil, and all measures of quantity or size. And they were to stand every morning, thanking and praising the LORD, and likewise at evening, and whenever burnt offerings were offered to the LORD on Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days, according to the number required of them, regularly before the LORD. Thus they were to keep charge of the tent of meeting and the sanctuary, and to attend the sons of Aaron, their brothers, for the service of the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new job description is startlingly ordinary.

And in the same sentence as the sacred bread, all measures of quantity or size. God had said a just weight and a just measure were his, and here they are, kept by Levites between the wafers and the morning praise.

Then the standing order the whole tribe lived by: thanks every morning and evening.

Every morning and every evening, in winter, when the court was empty and nobody was listening, somebody stood there saying thank you, and it went on for four hundred years.

That is what a settled God does to a tribe. He takes away the heroic duty and gives them the daily one, and the daily one turns out to be the harder and the better of the two.

The New Testament carries both halves of this to Christ. The God who came to dwell in Jerusalem has come nearer still: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). And the morning and evening thanks has passed to his people, who through him continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God (Hebrews 13:15), not to earn a place in the house but because he has given them one, and by the Spirit who now lives in them. Every Christian now has a shift at dawn.

24.title: The Priestly Divisions: Order in the House of God
24.text: <sup>1</sup>The divisions of the sons of Aaron were these. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.<sup>2</sup>But Nadab and Abihu died before their father and had no children, so Eleazar and Ithamar became the priests.<sup>3</sup>With the help of Zadok of the sons of Eleazar, and Ahimelech of the sons of Ithamar, David organized them according to the appointed duties in their service.<sup>4</sup>Since more chief men were found among the Jekameam the fourth.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Uzziel, Micah; of the sons of Micah, Shamir.<sup>25</sup>The brother of Micah, Isshiah; of the sons of Isshiah, Zechariah.<sup>26</sup>The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Jaaziah: Beno.<sup>27</sup>The sons of Merari: of Jaaziah, Beno, Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri.<sup>28</sup>Of Mahli: Eleazar, who had no sons.<sup>29</sup>Of Kish, the sons of Kish: Jerahmeel.<sup>30</sup>The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jerimoth. These were the sons of the Levites according to their fathers' houses.<sup>31</sup>These also, the head of each father's house and his younger brother alike, cast lots, just as their brothers the sons of Aaron, in the presence of King David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of fathers' houses of the priests and of the Levites.
24.overview:
With Nadab and Abihu dead, David organises the priesthood through Eleazar and Ithamar, sixteen houses and eight (vv. 1-4). The order of service is drawn by lot and recorded before witnesses (vv. 5-6), and the twenty-four courses are listed as the lots came out (vv. 7-18), each serving by Aaron's procedure (v. 19). The remaining Levite houses draw lots on the same terms (vv. 20-31).

The eighth lot fell to Abijah, and that course was still in operation when Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, came up for his week of duty.
24.theology:
Verse 19 marks a line David keeps everywhere: he arranged the timetable and did not touch the service (see on vv. 13-19).

And the appointments were made by lot, in public, with a written record, even inside each family: the head of each father's house and his younger brother alike.
24.examples:
A rota is how anything outlasts the enthusiasm of the people who begin it. Twenty-four courses serving a week at a time were still running after the exile, the return, and centuries of foreign rule.

Eleazar of Mahli (not Aaron's son of the same name) had no sons, and childlessness did not take him off the record of God's people. Nothing else is known about him, but somebody thought it worth writing down that he had been there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Two Families Left, and a Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nadab and Abihu died childless, so Eleazar and Ithamar became the priests (vv. 1-2). With Zadok and Ahimelech representing the two lines, David organises twenty-four heads of houses in proportion to their numbers (vv. 3-4). The order is settled by lot, all alike and written down before witnesses (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: God's instructions for worship are not formalities, and the first sentence of an administrative list says so.
verseByVerse.examples: Fairness that can be seen is a kindness to everyone who has to live with the result.

verseByVerse.quote: The divisions of the sons of Aaron were these. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. But Nadab and Abihu died before their father and had no children, so Eleazar and Ithamar became the priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter opens with a family list and a bereavement. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. But Nadab and Abihu died before their father and had no children, so Eleazar and Ithamar became the priests.

Anyone reading Leviticus knows what that means. On the day the tabernacle was dedicated, when fire had just come out from the LORD and consumed the offering and the whole nation shouted and fell on their faces, Aaron's two eldest took their censers and offered unauthorised fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them. Fire came out again, and they died in front of the tent, and their father was told not to mourn.

So every course in this chapter, every priest at Solomon's altar and in the second temple, comes down through Eleazar or Ithamar because the other two improvised.

It is the lesson of the cart on the road to Jerusalem, filed without comment at the head of a list. God said how, and how is not a formality.

verseByVerse.quote: With the help of Zadok of the sons of Eleazar, and Ahimelech of the sons of Ithamar, David organized them according to the appointed duties in their service. Since more chief men were found among the sons of Eleazar than among the sons of Ithamar, they organized them under sixteen heads of fathers' houses of the sons of Eleazar, and eight of the sons of Ithamar. They divided them by lot, all alike, for there were sacred officers and officers of God among both the sons of Eleazar and the sons of Ithamar. And the scribe Shemaiah, the son of Nethanel, a Levite, recorded them in the presence of the king and the princes and Zadok the priest and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar and the heads of the fathers' houses of the priests and of the Levites, one father's house being chosen for Eleazar and one chosen for Ithamar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both high priests stand with David, Zadok from Eleazar's line and Ahimelech from Ithamar's. Neither family is managed by the other.

The division is proportional: the larger house gets sixteen slots because it has more men, not more influence.

Then the order of service is settled, and it is settled in the one way that cannot be lobbied. They divided them by lot, all alike. No priest could arrange to be on duty in the best weeks; no family could be quietly kept out of the good weeks. Proverbs says the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD, and that is precisely why it was used here — to take the rota out of human hands and put it in God's.

Then it was minuted: a named Levite clerk, both high priests watching, the houses drawn alternately. It was fair, seen to be fair, and on paper.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The draw is recorded in order, first to twenty-fourth, with the eighth to Abijah (vv. 7-18). Each course served by Aaron's procedure, as God had commanded (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The rota was David's idea; the procedure inside the house was Aaron's, and Aaron's had come from God. New arrangements, old obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithful routine can carry God's purposes further than anyone who set it up could see (see on vv. 7-12).

verseByVerse.quote: The first lot fell to Jehoiarib, the second to Jedaiah, the third to Harim, the fourth to Seorim, the fifth to Malchijah, the sixth to Mijamin, the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah, the ninth to Jeshua, the tenth to Shecaniah, the eleventh to Eliashib, the twelfth to Jakim,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The names come in the order the lots came out, and then the eighth.

Nearly a thousand years later these words are still in force. Luke opens his Gospel with a priest named Zechariah, and the first thing he tells us is his course: of the division of Abijah. Only four priestly families came back from Babylon (Ezra 2:36–39), and by later Jewish tradition they were divided again into twenty-four courses under the old names, so the arrangement outlived even the loss of most of its families. The draw made before David and Zadok was still deciding, after the Greeks and the Romans, which week an old priest from the hill country came up to Jerusalem.

And it was in that week, on his one turn at the incense, that he went into the temple and found somebody standing at the right side of the altar.

It was the kind of page a reader skips. The Chronicler wrote it anyway, and the arrangement outlasted the building it was made for.
verseByVerse.note: Zechariah's division is named in Luke 1:5.

verseByVerse.quote: the thirteenth to Huppah, the fourteenth to Jeshebeab, the fifteenth to Bilgah, the sixteenth to Immer, the seventeenth to Hezir, the eighteenth to Happizzez, the nineteenth to Pethahiah, the twentieth to Jehezkel, the twenty-first to Jachin, the twenty-second to Gamul, the twenty-third to Delaiah, the twenty-fourth to Maaziah. These had as their appointed duty in their service to come into the house of the LORD according to the procedure established for them by Aaron their father, as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The remaining names go by at the same pace — Huppah, Jeshebeab, Bilgah, Immer, Hezir, Happizzez, Pethahiah, Jehezkel, Jachin, Gamul, Delaiah, and last of all Maaziah.

Twenty-four courses, each serving (as later practice shows) a week at a time, twice a year, with everyone present at the three great feasts. One family serving continuously would have been exhausted inside a generation.

Verse 19 says where the pattern for the service came from: Aaron, as God had commanded him.

Two authorities, carefully distinguished. The rota is David's — nothing in the law of Moses says anything about twenty-four courses drawn by lot. But what a priest did once he was through the door was Aaron's procedure, and Aaron's procedure had come from God. David arranged the timetable and did not touch the service.

That is the same line he drew over the ark and over the music. The manner of carrying was commanded and he obeyed it to the letter; the choir was not commanded and he invented it. Knowing which is which is most of the art of ordering the worship of God.

The rota also says something about the priests themselves. They served a week and went home, and their sons took their places when they died. Hebrews draws the contrast: the former priests were many, because death prevented them from continuing in office, but Jesus holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever and always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:23–25). His course is never off duty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–31 — The Levites Draw on the Same Terms
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the tribe is listed house by house (vv. 20-30), Eleazar again noted as having no sons (v. 28). Then they draw lots too, senior and younger alike, before the same witnesses (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The last verse is the point of the chapter: function was divided; standing was not.
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody in the court was too senior, or too junior, to be sent wherever the lot fell.

verseByVerse.quote: And of the rest of the sons of Levi: of the sons of Amram, Shubael; of the sons of Shubael, Jehdeiah. Of Rehabiah: of the sons of Rehabiah, Isshiah the chief. Of the Izharites, Shelomoth; of the sons of Shelomoth, Jahath. The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, Jekameam the fourth. The sons of Uzziel, Micah; of the sons of Micah, Shamir. The brother of Micah, Isshiah; of the sons of Isshiah, Zechariah. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Jaaziah: Beno.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites who are not priests are listed as a second register, the names of chapter 23 with the next generation added under each.

It is a working document rather than a history, kept because it is how the house of God was actually staffed.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Merari: of Jaaziah, Beno, Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri. Of Mahli: Eleazar, who had no sons. Of Kish, the sons of Kish: Jerahmeel. The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jerimoth. These were the sons of the Levites according to their fathers' houses. These also, the head of each father's house and his younger brother alike, cast lots, just as their brothers the sons of Aaron, in the presence of King David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of fathers' houses of the priests and of the Levites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Merari's line is set out, and then verse 28 repeats something the last chapter already said. Of Mahli: Eleazar, who had no sons.

A man whose family stopped with him is written into the record of the tribe in two consecutive chapters, with the same note both times, and nothing else is said about him.

Then the last verse, and it is where the chapter has been going.

Two things are being said and both matter. The Levites drew on exactly the same terms as the priests — the man who would never touch the altar put his hand in the bag beside the man who would. And within each family, the head of the house and his younger brother drew alike, which means being the eldest bought nothing at all.

Every man in that court had a different job and precisely the same claim on it, which was none, because the assignments were coming from somewhere outside the room.

25.title: The Temple Musicians: Prophecy Through Song
25.text: <sup>1</sup>David and the chiefs of the service also set apart for the service the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals. The list of those who did the work and of their duties was:<sup>2</sup>Of the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asharelah, sons of Asaph, under the direction of Asaph, who prophesied under the direction of the king.<sup>3</sup>Of Jeduthun, the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the direction of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre in thanksgiving and praise to the LORD.<sup>4</sup>Of Heman, the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel and Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, and Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, Mahazioth.<sup>5</sup>All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer, according to the promise of God to exalt him, for God had given Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.<sup>6</sup>They were all under the direction of their father in the music in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres for the service of the house of God. Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman were under the order of the king.<sup>7</sup>The number of them along with their brothers, who were trained in singing to the LORD, all who were skillful, was 288.<sup>8</sup>And they cast lots for their duties, small and great, teacher and pupil alike.<sup>9</sup>The first lot fell for Asaph to Joseph; the second to Gedaliah, to him and his brothers and his sons, twelve;<sup>10</sup>the third to Zaccur, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>11</sup>the fourth to Izri, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>12</sup>the fifth to Nethaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>13</sup>the sixth to Bukkiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>14</sup>the seventh to Jesharelah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>15</sup>the eighth to Jeshaiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>16</sup>the ninth to Mattaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>17</sup>the tenth to Shimei, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>18</sup>the eleventh to Azarel, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>19</sup>the twelfth to Hashabiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>20</sup>to the thirteenth, Shubael, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>21</sup>to the fourteenth, Mattithiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>22</sup>to the fifteenth, to Jeremoth, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>23</sup>to the sixteenth, to Hananiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>24</sup>to the seventeenth, to Joshbekashah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>25</sup>to the eighteenth, to Hanani, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>26</sup>to the nineteenth, to Mallothi, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>27</sup>to the twentieth, to Eliathah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>28</sup>to the twenty-first, to Hothir, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>29</sup>to the twenty-second, to Giddalti, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>30</sup>to the twenty-third, to Mahazioth, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>31</sup>to the twenty-fourth, to Romamti-ezer, his sons and his brothers, twelve.
25.overview:
The temple musicians are set apart, and their work is called prophecy three times in three verses (vv. 1-3). Heman is given seventeen children as God's way of exalting him (vv. 4-6). Two hundred and eighty-eight trained singers are divided into twenty-four courses of twelve by lot, small and great, teacher and pupil alike (vv. 7-8), and the draw is recorded in full (vv. 9-31).

The list balances, and it is written out at length because the working document is part of what the Chronicler wants his readers to hold.
25.theology:
Singing is called prophecy, and the usage is not loose (see on vv. 1-3). The Bible's longest book by chapters is a hymn book, and the men in this chapter took what God had said and set it where a nation could carry it.

And the same chapter insists the singers were trained and skillful (v. 7). Nothing here treats craft as a rival to inspiration. It hands the prophetic office to men who had been apprenticed and could play.

The New Testament gives this ministry to the whole church. Believers are to let the word of Christ dwell in them richly, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Colossians 3:16), and Hebrews hears Christ himself say, in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise (Hebrews 2:12). Some of these men's songs became Scripture (Psalms 50 and 73–83 bear Asaph's name). This commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that such inspired prophecy ended with the closed canon, while respecting brothers who see it otherwise; what has not ended is the task of setting God's word where a people can carry it, and singing it with the Son who leads the song.
25.examples:
The lots were cast small and great, teacher and pupil alike, and master and pupil both had to live with the result.

God's promise to exalt Heman arrived as seventeen children, and fourteen of the twenty-four musical courses carried his sons' names.

Most of these men are named once in Scripture and never again. A rota is duller and more durable than enthusiasm.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David and the officers set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, who prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals (vv. 1-3). Heman the king's seer had seventeen children (vv. 4-6). The 288 trained singers cast lots for their duties, small and great alike (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: To sing what God has said is to speak for him to his people, which is why these musicians can be said to prophesy.
verseByVerse.examples: Gift and practice are not rivals: the men who prophesied with lyres had also learned to play them (v. 7).

verseByVerse.quote: David and the chiefs of the service also set apart for the service the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals. The list of those who did the work and of their duties was: Of the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asharelah, sons of Asaph, under the direction of Asaph, who prophesied under the direction of the king. Of Jeduthun, the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the direction of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre in thanksgiving and praise to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word nobody would predict for temple musicians is prophesied.

And the verb comes again in verse 2, of Asaph's sons, and again in verse 3, of Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre in thanksgiving and praise to the LORD. Three times in three verses, of men with instruments in their hands.

It is not a loose way of speaking. Samuel told Saul he would meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute and lyre before them, prophesying. Elisha, asked for a word from God, called for a musician, and while the man played the hand of the LORD came upon him. Music and the word of God have been standing next to each other in Israel from the beginning.

The singers took what God had said and gave it back to the people set to music, so that a truth could get into a nation's memory in a way a sermon cannot. Israel learned much of its theology by singing it.

Verse 2 adds that Asaph prophesied under the direction of the king, which sounds alarming until it is clear what it can and cannot mean. David set the rota, appointed the men and made the instruments. Nobody in this chapter is telling a prophet what God says.

verseByVerse.quote: Of Heman, the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel and Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, and Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, Mahazioth. All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer, according to the promise of God to exalt him, for God had given Heman fourteen sons and three daughters. They were all under the direction of their father in the music in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres for the service of the house of God. Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman were under the order of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heman's household is a large one, and the text says why: it was the promise of God to exalt him.

The exalting arrived as children. Not office, not land, not a name in the chronicle of the kings: a full house, and fourteen of the twenty-four musical courses his own boys.

The three daughters are named in the same breath as God's gift. Verse 6 most naturally reaches back to the sons, and should not be pressed further. What can be said plainly is that women did sing in Israel's worship: the returning exiles counted two hundred singers, men and women, and a psalm puts young women with tambourines in the middle of a procession into the sanctuary.

One curiosity. The last nine names in verse 4 are odd as names and ordinary as Hebrew words, and read in order they make a petition: be gracious to me, LORD, be gracious to me; you are my God; I have magnified and exalted help; sitting in trouble, I said, give visions abundantly. It cannot be proved. If it is right, a prayer has been standing inside a staff list for three thousand years, and a father named his sons one line at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: The number of them along with their brothers, who were trained in singing to the LORD, all who were skillful, was 288. And they cast lots for their duties, small and great, teacher and pupil alike.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two hundred and eighty-eight is twenty-four courses of twelve. Two words do the work: trained, taught, apprenticed, and skillful. Somebody spent years on these men, and they were good.

Chenaniah got the conductor's post because he understood music.

The master and the student put their hands in the same bag. A man who had given a lifetime to his instrument might draw a bad week while the boy he taught last spring drew the Passover. Nothing in the system rewarded seniority, and nothing protected reputation, because the appointments were not being made by anyone in the room.

Small and great. The phrase is used elsewhere of God taking no account of a man's standing, and here it has been built into a duty roster.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lots are recorded one at a time, first to twenty-fourth, and almost every line closes with the same phrase: his sons and his brothers, twelve (vv. 9-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty-four courses of twelve is exactly the figure verse 7 gave. The Chronicler has set out a rota that balances, and written it out in full.
verseByVerse.examples: The repetition is the design and not a fault in the writing: a rota reads like this because a rota works like this, and somebody was willing to be dull on paper.

verseByVerse.quote: The first lot fell for Asaph to Joseph; the second to Gedaliah, to him and his brothers and his sons, twelve; the third to Zaccur, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the fourth to Izri, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the fifth to Nethaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the sixth to Bukkiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the seventh to Jesharelah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the eighth to Jeshaiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the ninth to Mattaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the tenth to Shimei, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the eleventh to Azarel, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the twelfth to Hashabiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on it goes — Bukkiah, Jesharelah, Jeshaiah, Mattaniah, Shimei, Azarel, Hashabiah — the same clause every time, the same number every time.

The three families are shuffled together by the lot rather than kept in blocks. In these first lots the sons of Asaph, Jeduthun and Heman come up mixed together; nobody chose the order.

verseByVerse.quote: to the thirteenth, Shubael, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the fourteenth, Mattithiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the fifteenth, to Jeremoth, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the sixteenth, to Hananiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the seventeenth, to Joshbekashah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the eighteenth, to Hanani, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the nineteenth, to Mallothi, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twentieth, to Eliathah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-first, to Hothir, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-second, to Giddalti, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-third, to Mahazioth, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-fourth, to Romamti-ezer, his sons and his brothers, twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second half of the list falls mostly to Heman's sons, down to Romamti-ezer at the twenty-fourth.

Every week of the year twelve trained men turned up and sang, and were replaced the next week by twelve more. The men in the ninth course never had the feast-day crowds, and nobody in the country could have named more than a handful of them.

The house they sang in was burned to the ground nearly four hundred years later and the rota was carried into exile and brought back and started again. Two hundred and eighty-eight names on a page, drawn by lot, small and great alike, teacher and pupil, twelve at a time — and God has never once needed his praise to be interesting to be worth having.

26.title: Gatekeepers and Administrators: Guarding the Holy and Serving the Community
26.text: <sup>1</sup>As for the divisions of the gatekeepers: of the Korahites, Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph.<sup>2</sup>And Meshelemiah had sons: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth,<sup>3</sup>Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Eliehoenai the seventh.<sup>4</sup>And Obed-edom had sons: Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sachar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth,<sup>5</sup>Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, Peullethai the eighth, for God blessed him.<sup>6</sup>Also to his son Shemaiah were sons born who were rulers in their fathers' houses, for they were men of great ability.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Shemaiah: Othni, Rephael, Obed and Elzabad, whose brothers were able men, Elihu and Semachiah.<sup>8</sup>All these were of the sons of Obed-edom with their sons and brothers, able men qualified for the service; sixty-two of Obed-edom.<sup>9</sup>And Meshelemiah had sons and brothers, able men, eighteen.<sup>10</sup>And Hosah, of the sons of Merari, had sons: Shimri the chief (for though he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief),<sup>11</sup>Hilkiah the second, Tebaliah the third, Zechariah the fourth: all the sons and brothers of Hosah were thirteen.<sup>12</sup>These divisions of the gatekeepers, corresponding to their chief men, had duties, just as their brothers did, ministering in the house of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And they cast lots by fathers' houses, small and great alike, for their gates.<sup>14</sup>The lot for the east fell to Shelemiah. They cast lots also for his son Zechariah, a shrewd counselor, and his lot came out for the north.<sup>15</sup>Obed-edom's came out for the south, and to his sons was allotted the gatehouse.<sup>16</sup>For Shuppim and Hosah it came out for the west, at the gate of Shallecheth on the road that goes up. Watch corresponded to watch.<sup>17</sup>On the east there were six each day, on the north four each day, on the south four each day, as well as two and two at the gatehouse.<sup>18</sup>And for the colonnade on the west there were four at the road and two at the colonnade.<sup>19</sup>These were the divisions of the gatekeepers among the Korahites and the sons of Merari.<sup>20</sup>And of the Levites, Ahijah had charge of the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated gifts.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Ladan, the sons of the Gershonites belonging to Ladan, the heads of the fathers' houses belonging to Ladan the Gershonite: Jehieli.<sup>22</sup>The sons of Jehieli, Zetham, and Joel his brother, were in charge of the treasuries of the house of the LORD.<sup>23</sup>Of the Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites—<sup>24</sup>and Shebuel the son of Gershom, son of Moses, was chief officer in charge of the treasuries.<sup>25</sup>His brothers:
