from Eliezer were his son Rehabiah, and his son Jeshaiah, and his son Joram, and his son Zichri, and his son Shelomoth.<sup>26</sup>This Shelomoth and his brothers were in charge of all the treasuries of the dedicated gifts that David the king and the heads of the fathers' houses and the officers of the thousands and the hundreds and the commanders of the army had dedicated.<sup>27</sup>From spoil won in battles they dedicated gifts for the maintenance of the house of the LORD.<sup>28</sup>Also all that Samuel the seer and Saul the son of Kish and Abner the son of Ner and Joab the son of Zeruiah had dedicated—all dedicated gifts were in the care of Shelomoth and his brothers.<sup>29</sup>Of the Izharites, Chenaniah and his sons were appointed to external duties for Israel, as officers and judges.<sup>30</sup>Of the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his brothers, 1,700 men of ability, had the oversight of Israel westward of the Jordan for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king.<sup>31</sup>Of the Hebronites, Jerijah was chief of the Hebronites of whatever genealogy or fathers' houses. (In the fortieth year of David's reign search was made and men of great ability among them were found at Jazer in Gilead.)<sup>32</sup>King David appointed him and his brothers, 2,700 men of ability, heads of fathers' houses, to have the oversight of the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of the Manassites for everything pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king.
26.overview:
The gatekeepers are organised by family and described throughout as able men (vv. 1-12). The gates are drawn by lot, small and great alike, and the daily watch is set (vv. 13-19). Then the treasuries, kept by a descendant of Moses (vv. 20-24) and holding gifts dedicated from the spoil of war by David, Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab (vv. 25-28). Finally Levites are posted outside the sanctuary as officers and judges on both sides of the Jordan (vv. 29-32).

The figures for the watch add to twenty-four men on duty every day, with the most of them on the east, which is the front.
26.theology:
The doorkeepers are Korah's descendants, a rebel's line kept alive by mercy (see on vv. 1-5), and they are the family who sang of being glad to keep a door in the house of God.

And verse 28 keeps Saul's dedicated gifts in the treasury beside Samuel's. His obituary stands: he broke faith and did not seek the LORD. What he gave was not thrown out with him.

The gates were guarded because the house was holy and the wrong person could not simply walk in. The New Testament announces that the way has been opened: through the blood of Jesus believers may enter the holy places with confidence, by the new and living way he opened through the curtain (Hebrews 10:19–20). The sons of Korah stood at the threshold, glad to be there at all; the children of God, rebels by nature like their ancestor, are now welcomed all the way in.
26.examples:
The house was guarded for nearly four hundred years by people nobody can name, chosen by lot and described only as able men.

A descendant of Moses kept the accounts of the storerooms (v. 24): real, necessary, unglamorous work, and Scripture records his name.

In the fortieth and last year of his reign, David sent men over the Jordan to find capable administrators for a temple that had not been begun. He knew he would not see it. He was still hiring.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The doorkeepers are organised by family: the Korahites under Meshelemiah (vv. 1-3), Obed-edom's large household, for God blessed him (vv. 4-8), Meshelemiah's eighteen (v. 9) and Hosah's thirteen, headed by a son who was not the firstborn (vv. 10-11). The gates are drawn by lot, small and great alike (vv. 12-16), and the daily watch numbered (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Mercy runs through this list: a rebel's line kept alive, and a family blessed for sheltering the ark, both now trusted with the doors.
verseByVerse.examples: If he is the same man, as seems likely, Obed-edom is here for the fourth time. He took the ark into his yard when the king was frightened of it, walked to Jerusalem beside it as a doorkeeper, stood on the permanent staff with sixty-eight brothers, and now heads a family of sixty-two on the gates.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the divisions of the gatekeepers: of the Korahites, Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph. And Meshelemiah had sons: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth, Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Eliehoenai the seventh. And Obed-edom had sons: Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sachar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth, Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, Peullethai the eighth, for God blessed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first name in the list has a history in it: a Korahite.

Korah stood up in the wilderness with two hundred and fifty men and told Moses and Aaron they had taken too much on themselves. He wanted the priesthood. The ground swallowed him and his household, and fire took the two hundred and fifty with their censers.

And then, buried in a census ten chapters later, one sentence: the sons of Korah did not die. The line survived, and here they are, four hundred years on, appointed to the doors of the house of God.

Eleven psalms carry their name, and one of them says: a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere; I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness. The family that grasped at the altar and lost everything wrote the song about being content at the threshold, and was kept alive by mercy to sing it.

Then Obed-edom, and against his eighth son a clause that explains all of them: for God blessed him. That is the sentence from chapter 13, when the ark stood in his house for three months. Years later the clerk keeping the register still knows why that family is large.

This Obed-edom, a Levite of the Korahite gatekeepers, is probably the man who kept the ark (13:13), called a Gittite because he had lived in Gath-rimmon, a Levitical town (Joshua 21:24–25).

verseByVerse.quote: Also to his son Shemaiah were sons born who were rulers in their fathers' houses, for they were men of great ability. The sons of Shemaiah: Othni, Rephael, Obed and Elzabad, whose brothers were able men, Elihu and Semachiah. All these were of the sons of Obed-edom with their sons and brothers, able men qualified for the service; sixty-two of Obed-edom. And Meshelemiah had sons and brothers, able men, eighteen. And Hosah, of the sons of Merari, had sons: Shimri the chief (for though he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief), Hilkiah the second, Tebaliah the third, Zechariah the fourth: all the sons and brothers of Hosah were thirteen. These divisions of the gatekeepers, corresponding to their chief men, had duties, just as their brothers did, ministering in the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men of great ability: the word is the one used of soldiers and fighting strength, again and again in this chapter. Somebody had to stop the wrong people going in, hold the doors against festival crowds, and be awake all night on the north side.

Of Hosah's sons there is a note dropped in without explanation: though he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief.

The Chronicler does not say whether it was wisdom or favouritism. He has already noted that the sons of Moses were ordinary Levites and that a younger brother drew lots with the head of the house, and here again the expected order does not hold.

verseByVerse.quote: And they cast lots by fathers' houses, small and great alike, for their gates. The lot for the east fell to Shelemiah. They cast lots also for his son Zechariah, a shrewd counselor, and his lot came out for the north. Obed-edom's came out for the south, and to his sons was allotted the gatehouse. For Shuppim and Hosah it came out for the west, at the gate of Shallecheth on the road that goes up. Watch corresponded to watch. On the east there were six each day, on the north four each day, on the south four each day, as well as two and two at the gatehouse. And for the colonnade on the west there were four at the road and two at the colonnade. These were the divisions of the gatekeepers among the Korahites and the sons of Merari.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is the third time in three chapters: priests, head of house and younger brother alike; singers, teacher and pupil alike; doorkeepers, small and great alike. Nobody in the service of that house got a posting because of who he was.

The gates come out one by one. North went to Zechariah, a shrewd counselor: a man with judgment was put on a door. And a small clause about how it fitted together: Watch corresponded to watch.

The east has the most, and the east is the front, the way the sanctuary faced and a king would come. Six men stood there every morning, and nobody has heard of any of them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the treasuries, with a descendant of Moses as chief officer (vv. 20-24). Shelomoth keeps the gifts dedicated from spoil won in battle (vv. 25-27), including those of Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab (v. 28). Others are posted outside as officers and judges, west and east of the Jordan (vv. 29-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The treasury belongs to holiness as much as the altar does: what is given to God has to be kept honestly and recorded.
verseByVerse.examples: A Levite settling a boundary dispute in Gilead was as much in God's service as one standing at the temple door (v. 30).

verseByVerse.quote: And of the Levites, Ahijah had charge of the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated gifts. The sons of Ladan, the sons of the Gershonites belonging to Ladan, the heads of the fathers' houses belonging to Ladan the Gershonite: Jehieli. The sons of Jehieli, Zetham, and Joel his brother, were in charge of the treasuries of the house of the LORD. Of the Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites— and Shebuel the son of Gershom, son of Moses, was chief officer in charge of the treasuries. His brothers: from Eliezer were his son Rehabiah, and his son Jeshaiah, and his son Joram, and his son Zichri, and his son Shelomoth. This Shelomoth and his brothers were in charge of all the treasuries of the dedicated gifts that David the king and the heads of the fathers' houses and the officers of the thousands and the hundreds and the commanders of the army had dedicated. From spoil won in battles they dedicated gifts for the maintenance of the house of the LORD. Also all that Samuel the seer and Saul the son of Kish and Abner the son of Ner and Joab the son of Zeruiah had dedicated—all dedicated gifts were in the care of Shelomoth and his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are two kinds of treasury, the stores of the house and the stores of dedicated gifts, and both need accounts.

Moses' descendant is the treasurer (son of in such lists can leap generations). Three chapters ago the sons of Moses were entered among ordinary Levites, and here is what that meant in practice: the descendant of the man who spoke with God face to face kept the accounts of the storerooms.

The stores hold spoil won in battle, given by David, the heads of houses and the commanders, for the maintenance of the house. Everything brought back from Edom, Moab, Ammon and Philistia is in there.

Saul is on that list. The king whose obituary in chapter 10 says he died for breaking faith with the LORD and for not seeking him had, at some point in his forty years, brought things to God and set them apart. They were still there. Nobody had melted them down or quietly removed his name from the ledger. Beside them sit gifts from Abner and from Joab, two generals who spent years killing each other's men and who both died by violence, filed on the same shelf as Samuel's.

God kept what Saul gave him. That does not undo chapter 10 and the Chronicler does not pretend it does. It simply stands there in an inventory, and it speaks to anyone who has wondered whether the good they did before they went wrong was wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the Izharites, Chenaniah and his sons were appointed to external duties for Israel, as officers and judges. Of the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his brothers, 1,700 men of ability, had the oversight of Israel westward of the Jordan for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king. Of the Hebronites, Jerijah was chief of the Hebronites of whatever genealogy or fathers' houses. (In the fortieth year of David's reign search was made and men of great ability among them were found at Jazer in Gilead.) King David appointed him and his brothers, 2,700 men of ability, heads of fathers' houses, to have the oversight of the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of the Manassites for everything pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chenaniah and his sons go out as officers and judges, and Hashabiah and Jerijah, with thousands of able men, have the oversight of Israel west and east of the Jordan.

And the terms refuse to split: for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king, one commission with no seam.

A note in verse 31 is easy to miss: in the fortieth year of David's reign search was made for able men at Jazer in Gilead.

The fortieth year is the last one: an old man who has handed the throne to his son is still combing the far side of the Jordan for capable men to staff a building that has not been started.

27.title: The Civic Order of David's Kingdom: Twelve Months, Twelve Tribes, One King
27.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the number of the people of Israel, the heads of fathers' houses, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and their officers who served the king in all matters concerning the divisions that came and went, month after month throughout the year, each division numbering 24,000:<sup>2</sup>Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel was in charge of the first division in the first month; in his division were 24,000.<sup>3</sup>He was a descendant of Perez and was chief of all the commanders. He served for the first month.<sup>4</sup>Dodai the Ahohite was in charge of the division of the second month; in his division were 24,000.<sup>5</sup>The third commander, for the third month, was Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada the chief priest; in his division were 24,000.<sup>6</sup>This is the Benaiah who was a mighty man of the thirty and in command of the thirty; Ammizabad his son was in charge of his division.<sup>7</sup>Asahel the brother of Joab was fourth, for the fourth month, and his son Zebadiah after him; in his division were 24,000.<sup>8</sup>The fifth commander, for the fifth month, was Shamhuth the Izrahite; in his division were 24,000.<sup>9</sup>Sixth, for the sixth month, was Ira, the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite; in his division were 24,000.<sup>10</sup>Seventh, for the seventh month, was Helez the Pelonite, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000.<sup>11</sup>Eighth, for the eighth month, was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000.<sup>12</sup>Ninth, for the ninth month, was Abiezer of Anathoth, a Benjaminite; in his division were 24,000.<sup>13</sup>Tenth, for the tenth month, was Maharai of Netophah, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000.<sup>14</sup>Eleventh, for the eleventh month, was Benaiah of Pirathon, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000.<sup>15</sup>Twelfth, for the twelfth month, was Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel; in his division were 24,000.<sup>16</sup>Over the tribes of Israel, for the Reubenites, Eliezer the son of Zichri was chief officer; for the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maacah;<sup>17</sup>for Levi, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel; for Aaron, Zadok;<sup>18</sup>for Judah, Elihu, one of David's brothers; for Issachar, Omri the son of Michael;<sup>19</sup>for Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah; for Naphtali, Jeremoth the son of Azriel;<sup>20</sup>for the Ephraimites, Hoshea the son of Azaziah; for the half-tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah;<sup>21</sup>for the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah; for Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner;<sup>22</sup>for Dan, Azarel the son of Jeroham. These were the leaders of the tribes of Israel.<sup>23</sup>David did not count those below twenty years of age, for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven.<sup>24</sup>Joab the son of Zeruiah began to count, but did not finish. Yet wrath came upon Israel for this, and the number was not entered in the chronicles of King David.<sup>25</sup>Over the king's treasuries was Azmaveth the son of Adiel; and over the treasuries in the country, in the cities, in the villages, and in the towers, was Jonathan the son of Uzziah;<sup>26</sup>and over those who did the work of the field for tilling the soil was Ezri the son of Chelub;<sup>27</sup>and over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite; and over the produce of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite.<sup>28</sup>Over the olive and sycamore trees in the Shephelah was Baal-hanan the Gederite; and over the stores of oil was Joash.<sup>29</sup>Over the herds that pastured in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite; over the herds in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai.<sup>30</sup>Over the camels was Obil the Ishmaelite; and over the donkeys was Jehdeiah the Meronothite.<sup>31</sup>Over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagrite. All these were stewards of King David's property.<sup>32</sup>Jonathan, David's uncle, was a counselor, being a man of understanding and a scribe. He and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni attended the king's sons.<sup>33</sup>Ahithophel was the king's counselor, and Hushai the Archite was the king's friend.<sup>34</sup>Ahithophel was succeeded by Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar. Joab was commander of the king's army.
27.overview: Israel's fighting strength is set out as a rota of twelve monthly divisions, commanded almost entirely by men from the roll of the mighty men (vv. 1-15). Then a chief officer for each tribe, with Gad and Asher absent and Abner's son over Benjamin (vv. 16-22). Two verses return to the census, giving a reason chapter 21 never gave (vv. 23-24). Twelve stewards run the crown estates, and the household staff closes the list (vv. 25-34).
27.theology:
Verse 23 supplies what chapter 21 left out: the young were not counted for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven (see on vv. 23-24).

And verse 24 says the total was never entered in the annals, while the sin and its confession were.
27.examples:
David put the men who understood the animals in charge of them, wherever they came from (vv. 30-31).

Asahel had been dead for years and his name still heads the fourth division, with his son entered after him. An organisation can honour the man who began a thing while getting on with the work he left.

Abner's son holds royal office over Saul's own tribe (v. 21). Old enmities between two houses did not have to pass to the next generation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Twelve Divisions, One a Month
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The standing army is a rota: twelve divisions of 24,000, each serving one month in twelve (v. 1). The commanders are named month by month: Jashobeam, chief of all the commanders; Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; Asahel, with his son after him; and on through the twelve (vv. 2-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The defence of the kingdom was spread across the whole year and the whole people, so that no one carried all of it and no one was excused.
verseByVerse.examples: The men who were there at the beginning ended up running the timetable (see on vv. 7-15).

verseByVerse.quote: This is the number of the people of Israel, the heads of fathers' houses, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and their officers who served the king in all matters concerning the divisions that came and went, month after month throughout the year, each division numbering 24,000: Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel was in charge of the first division in the first month; in his division were 24,000. He was a descendant of Perez and was chief of all the commanders. He served for the first month. Dodai the Ahohite was in charge of the division of the second month; in his division were 24,000. The third commander, for the third month, was Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada the chief priest; in his division were 24,000. This is the Benaiah who was a mighty man of the thirty and in command of the thirty; Ammizabad his son was in charge of his division.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The army is a rota, and the arithmetic is the point: every soldier served one month in twelve and spent the other eleven on his own land.

It is a militia rather than a standing army, and it keeps the kingdom out of two traps at once. A nation with no force is at everybody's mercy; a nation with a permanent professional army under a king tends to find out what that costs. David built neither. He built a timetable.

Twelve times twenty-four thousand is 288,000; the singers came to 288, the priests to twenty-four courses, the doorkeepers to twenty-four a day. The match may be no more than the tidiness of twelves, but it is there.

The first commander is Jashobeam, described as a descendant of Perez and chief of all the commanders. Perez was Judah's son by Tamar, and the line runs through Boaz and Obed and Jesse to David, and on, as the first page of Matthew records, to Jesus (Matthew 1:3–16).

And the third month belongs to Benaiah, a priest's son, the man who killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day. He would command Solomon's army in the end.

verseByVerse.quote: Asahel the brother of Joab was fourth, for the fourth month, and his son Zebadiah after him; in his division were 24,000. The fifth commander, for the fifth month, was Shamhuth the Izrahite; in his division were 24,000. Sixth, for the sixth month, was Ira, the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite; in his division were 24,000. Seventh, for the seventh month, was Helez the Pelonite, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000. Eighth, for the eighth month, was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000. Ninth, for the ninth month, was Abiezer of Anathoth, a Benjaminite; in his division were 24,000. Tenth, for the tenth month, was Maharai of Netophah, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000. Eleventh, for the eleventh month, was Benaiah of Pirathon, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000. Twelfth, for the twelfth month, was Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel; in his division were 24,000.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the fourth month, and a name that stops a careful reader: Asahel.

Asahel was dead. He had been killed years before this list was drawn up, run through with the butt of a spear by Abner in the retreat from Gibeon after being told twice to turn aside. His name still heads the division, with his son entered after him. Either the list keeps an arrangement first made in the Hebron years, before his death, or the division kept his name after he fell; the text does not say which.

The rest of the twelve read like a page from chapter 11, because that is what they are. Shamhuth, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Helez the Pelonite, Sibbecai the Hushathite who killed a giant at Gezer, Abiezer of Anathoth, Maharai of Netophah, Benaiah of Pirathon, Heldai the Netophathite. Almost every one of them is in the roll of the mighty men.

Men who walked into a Philistine border town to join a wanted man, or stood in a barley field when everyone else ran, are now running a duty roster. That is what usually becomes of the people who were there at the beginning, and it is not a comedown.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — The Tribal Officers, and the Number That Was Not Entered
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Each tribe has a chief officer named, including one of David's brothers for Judah and Abner's son for Benjamin (vv. 16-22). Then two verses return to the census: the young were not counted, because of the promise to make Israel as the stars (v. 23), and Joab's unfinished total brought wrath and was never entered in the chronicles (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: A people God has promised to make beyond counting is not a resource for a king to total.
verseByVerse.examples: A confessed sin stays in the record so that it can be learned from, not so that it can go on accusing.

verseByVerse.quote: Over the tribes of Israel, for the Reubenites, Eliezer the son of Zichri was chief officer; for the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maacah; for Levi, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel; for Aaron, Zadok; for Judah, Elihu, one of David's brothers; for Issachar, Omri the son of Michael; for Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah; for Naphtali, Jeremoth the son of Azriel; for the Ephraimites, Hoshea the son of Azaziah; for the half-tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah; for the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah; for Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner; for Dan, Azarel the son of Jeroham. These were the leaders of the tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each tribe gets a chief officer, named.

Two are missing. Gad and Asher have no officer in this list, and nobody knows why. It may be damage to the text, or an administrative arrangement lost to us. The gap is there and it should not be papered over.

Two entries carry a story. Judah's officer, one of David's brothers, is most likely Eliab, the eldest, who stood in the valley of Elah while a shepherd boy went out to the giant.

Abner was Saul's general, who put Ish-bosheth on a throne against David, killed Asahel, and was murdered by Joab in the gateway at Hebron. His son is a royal officer over Saul's own tribe. Whatever settlement was reached between the houses of David and Saul, it is recorded in one line of a staff list.

verseByVerse.quote: David did not count those below twenty years of age, for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven. Joab the son of Zeruiah began to count, but did not finish. Yet wrath came upon Israel for this, and the number was not entered in the chronicles of King David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is a reason chapter 21 never gave, and it goes to the heart of what was wrong. God had told Abraham to count the stars if he could. A man who totals a people God has promised to make uncountable has already contradicted the promise. The boys belonged to a number nobody was ever meant to have.

Verse 24 adds that Joab began and did not finish, and that the number was never entered in the chronicles.

Somebody had the figure (chapter 21 prints it), and it was kept out of the official annals, so the one thing David wanted from the exercise was the one thing the record would not preserve, which is a strange and merciful way to keep a chronicle.

The wrath is in the chronicle; the sin is there, told twice, with the king's own confession. What was struck out was the total he had sinned to obtain. Scripture keeps what a man needs to remember and loses what he wanted, and the confessed sin is answered by mercy, not by a ledger.

Nor did the census cancel the promise it contradicted. Those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29), and John saw before the throne and before the Lamb a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation (Revelation 7:9). The people no king was allowed to total have become countless because the Son of David has been gathering them from the whole earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–34 — Stewards, Counsellors, and a Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Twelve stewards run the crown estates, field, vine, olive, herd and flock, with an Ishmaelite over the camels and a Hagrite over the flocks (vv. 25-31). Then the household: a tutor for the king's sons, Ahithophel the counsellor and Hushai the friend, and Joab still commanding the army (vv. 32-34).
verseByVerse.theology: Farming and herding take their place in Scripture beside the army and the priesthood as part of the kingdom's order.
verseByVerse.examples: The Chronicler gives Ahithophel and Hushai their job titles and moves on (v. 33); 2 Samuel tells how that pair ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Over the king's treasuries was Azmaveth the son of Adiel; and over the treasuries in the country, in the cities, in the villages, and in the towers, was Jonathan the son of Uzziah; and over those who did the work of the field for tilling the soil was Ezri the son of Chelub; and over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite; and over the produce of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite. Over the olive and sycamore trees in the Shephelah was Baal-hanan the Gederite; and over the stores of oil was Joash. Over the herds that pastured in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite; over the herds in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai. Over the camels was Obil the Ishmaelite; and over the donkeys was Jehdeiah the Meronothite. Over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagrite. All these were stewards of King David's property.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve men, and only one of them looks after money. The wealth of Israel was soil, trees and animals, and the administration reflects it: separate officials for vineyards and wine cellars, for upland and lowland herds.

Ishmaelites and Hagrites were desert peoples, and camels and flocks are what desert peoples know. David put the men who understood the animals in charge of the animals, and the fact that they came from outside Israel does not appear to have entered into it. He had Philistines guarding his own body and an Ishmaelite running his camels.

verseByVerse.quote: Jonathan, David's uncle, was a counselor, being a man of understanding and a scribe. He and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni attended the king's sons. Ahithophel was the king's counselor, and Hushai the Archite was the king's friend. Ahithophel was succeeded by Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar. Joab was commander of the king's army.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The household comes last: David's uncle Jonathan as tutor to the princes, described first as a man of understanding and second as literate.

Then two names in one sentence, with nothing said.

Anyone who has read the other account knows them differently. Ahithophel went over to Absalom; David, walking up the Mount of Olives barefoot and weeping, prayed the LORD would turn his counsel to foolishness, and sent Hushai back into the city to do it. It worked, and Ahithophel went home, set his house in order and hanged himself. Verse 34 names his successors without saying why the post fell vacant.

Still there. He had been first up into Jebus and won the command with one act of nerve, and he had murdered Abner in a gateway and Amasa on a road and killed Absalom against a direct order. He had told David the census was wrong and been overruled, and he had said the finest sentence about courage and providence in the book. Nobody could remove him, and the register of David's kingdom closes with his name and his rank.

28.title: David's Final Charge: The Blueprint from the Spirit and the Call to Seek
28.text: <sup>1</sup>David assembled at Jerusalem all the officials of Israel, the officials of the tribes, the officers of the divisions that served the king, the commanders of thousands, the commanders of hundreds, the stewards of all the property and livestock of the king and his sons, together with the palace officials, the mighty men and all the seasoned warriors.<sup>2</sup>Then King David rose to his feet and said: "Hear me, my brothers and my people. I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and for the footstool of our God, and I made preparations for building.<sup>3</sup>But God said to me, 'You may not build a house for my name, for you are a man of war and have shed blood.'<sup>4</sup>Yet the LORD God of Israel chose me from all my father's house to be king over Israel forever. For he chose Judah as leader, and in the house of Judah my father's house, and among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel.<sup>5</sup>And of all my sons (for the LORD has given me many sons) he has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel.<sup>6</sup>He said to me, 'It is Solomon your son who shall build my house and my courts, for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father.<sup>7</sup>I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues strong in keeping my commandments and my rules, as he is today.'<sup>8</sup>Now therefore in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the LORD, and in the hearing of our God, observe and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, that you may possess this good land and leave it for an inheritance to your children after you forever.<sup>9</sup>"And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.<sup>10</sup>Be careful now, for the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it."<sup>11</sup>Then David gave Solomon his son the plan of the vestibule of the temple, and of its houses, its treasuries, its upper rooms, and its inner chambers, and of the room for the mercy seat;<sup>12</sup>and the plan of all that he had in mind for the courts of the house of the LORD, all the surrounding chambers, the treasuries of the house of God, and the treasuries for dedicated gifts;<sup>13</sup>for the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, and all the work of the service in the house of the LORD; for all the vessels for the service in the house of the LORD,<sup>14</sup>the weight of gold for all golden vessels for each service, the weight of silver vessels for each service,<sup>15</sup>the weight of the golden lampstands and their lamps, the weight of gold for each lampstand and its lamps, the weight of silver for a lampstand and its lamps, according to the use of each lampstand in the service,<sup>16</sup>the weight of gold for each table for the showbread, the silver for the silver tables,<sup>17</sup>and pure gold for the forks, the basins and the cups; for the golden bowls and the weight of each; for the silver bowls and the weight of each;<sup>18</sup>for the altar of incense made of refined gold, and its weight; also his plan for the golden chariot of the cherubim that spread their wings and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD.<sup>19</sup>"All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD, all the work to be done according to the plan."<sup>20</sup>Then David said to Solomon his son, "Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you, until all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished.<sup>21</sup>And behold the divisions of the priests and the Levites for all the service of the house of God; and with you in all the work will be every willing man who has skill for any kind of service; also the officers and all the people will be wholly at your command."
28.overview:
David assembles every officer in the kingdom and stands to speak (vv. 1-2). He explains the refusal (v. 3), traces the choosing that narrowed from Judah to Solomon, who will sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD (vv. 4-7), and charges the assembly and his son to seek God (vv. 8-10). Then he hands over the plans, down to the weight of gold for the forks, in writing from the hand of the LORD (vv. 11-19), and ends with Joshua's words and a promise that runs to completion (vv. 20-21).

Verse 9 is the sentence the whole book has been travelling towards, and verse 19 says where the building came from: not an architect, but a pattern.
28.theology:
Verses 4-6 set out election as a funnel, in David's own mouth, about his own throne (see on vv. 4-7). And the throne is called the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel, which is why its loss centuries later did not cancel the promise attached to it.

Verse 7's if stands beside chapter 17's unconditional word, and history shows how the two worked: each generation's enjoyment of the covenant hung on that generation, and the covenant itself did not. Solomon did not continue strong, and the promise ran on underneath the wreckage until the Son of David came who did, whose obedience is counted to all who trust him. That is why a reader who has not continued strong is not cast off for it: the way back is confession, and the God who searches hearts is found by those who seek him.

And verse 19 names the temple's origin with the word used of the pattern Moses was shown on the mountain (see on vv. 16-19).
28.examples:
A dying man who could not be kept warm under blankets rose to his feet to make the speech. Nothing in the chapter required him to stand, and the record says he did.

Parents can point their children to the God they have known, but they cannot know him on their children's behalf (v. 9).

The king who once put the ark on a cart handed his son a plan with the forks itemised. Care in the house of God has no lower limit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David assembles every officer in the kingdom and rises to his feet (vv. 1-2). He had meant to build a house of rest for the ark, and was refused as a man of war (v. 3). He traces the choosing that put him and his son where they are, on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel (vv. 4-6), with a condition attached (v. 7). He charges the assembly (v. 8), and then his son: seek him, and he will be found (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Four times in three verses the verb is chose, and it narrows each time — the tribe, then the family, then the man, then the son. David is standing in front of the nation explaining his own throne, and not one clause of the explanation is about him.
verseByVerse.examples: David's first words to the whole kingdom are about his own refusal (v. 3), and he says them without complaint.

verseByVerse.quote: David assembled at Jerusalem all the officials of Israel, the officials of the tribes, the officers of the divisions that served the king, the commanders of thousands, the commanders of hundreds, the stewards of all the property and livestock of the king and his sons, together with the palace officials, the mighty men and all the seasoned warriors. Then King David rose to his feet and said: "Hear me, my brothers and my people. I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and for the footstool of our God, and I made preparations for building. But God said to me, 'You may not build a house for my name, for you are a man of war and have shed blood.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everybody is called in: officials, commanders, stewards, palace staff, the mighty men. The whole apparatus of chapters 23 to 27 is standing in one place.

He rises to his feet near the end. The other account describes a man so cold no bedclothes could warm him, with his sons already circling the throne. Whatever it cost him, the speech is delivered standing, and the Chronicler thought the detail belonged in the record.

The footstool. That is what he calls the ark, and the psalms call it that too — worship at his footstool, for he is holy. It is a startling way to describe the most sacred object in Israel, and it puts the scale right. The gold-covered box between the cherubim is the stool under the feet of a God whose throne is heaven and whose footstool, on his own account, is the earth. The building David wanted to raise, with its cedar and its bronze sea and its hundred thousand talents of gold, was a room for a footrest.

Then the refusal, in God's own words and blunter than anywhere else.

Not you have sinned. Not you are disqualified by guilt. You are a man of war — a description of what he was, given by the God who had made him it and given him the victories the blood came from. And he says it out loud in front of the entire kingdom, standing on his feet, without a word of complaint.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet the LORD God of Israel chose me from all my father's house to be king over Israel forever. For he chose Judah as leader, and in the house of Judah my father's house, and among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel. And of all my sons (for the LORD has given me many sons) he has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel. He said to me, 'It is Solomon your son who shall build my house and my courts, for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father. I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues strong in keeping my commandments and my rules, as he is today.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the clearest things Scripture says about how God works, and David says it about himself. Follow the funnel. Out of twelve tribes, Judah. Out of Judah, a farmer's household in Bethlehem. Out of that household, the youngest (1 Samuel 16 implies eight; the list at 2:13–15 names seven, perhaps because one died without heirs), who was not even called in from the sheep. Each stage narrows, each is God's doing, and the verb is the same every time.

There is no reason supplied, not Judah's faithfulness or Jesse's piety or David's courage. The nearest thing is he took pleasure in me, which explains nothing and is meant to. Moses had told Israel that God set his love on them not because they were many, but simply because he loved them.

And the last phrase: not the throne of Israel. The throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel. That is what this book said in chapter 17, where God called it my house and my kingdom, and it is what the next chapter will say when Solomon sits down on the throne of the LORD as king. Israel's monarchy was a tenancy, and the chair belonged to somebody else.

And then verse 7, which does not sit easily beside chapter 17.

An if. The promise made to David through Nathan had no condition on it; this one does. Both are Scripture and both are true, and history shows how they fit (see the theology of this chapter). Solomon did not continue strong, and the kingdom was torn in half in his son's lifetime — and the promise ran on underneath the wreckage for century after century, until a son of David was born who did continue strong, and in whom the word forever finally meant what it said.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the LORD, and in the hearing of our God, observe and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, that you may possess this good land and leave it for an inheritance to your children after you forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he turns to his son, David turns to the room.

Two sets of witnesses are named — the assembly, and God. This is being said on the record and under oath, which is how a dying man speaks when he will not get another chance.

And the verb is the book's own word again: seek out all the commandments. Not merely obey the ones you already know. Go looking for what God has said, which is exactly what David himself had failed to do the first time he went for the ark, and had done in the three months afterwards.

The promise attached is the land, held and handed on. Now think about who was reading this. The Chronicler's first readers were people whose grandparents had watched that land taken away, who lived on a fraction of it under a foreign governor, and who could remember exactly which commandments had been ignored while it happened. The sentence was not nostalgia to them. It was a diagnosis.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever. Be careful now, for the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the old man turns to his son in front of everybody, and says the sentence this whole book has been travelling towards.

Know the God of your father. He does not say know about him. And he calls him the God of your father, which is doing two things at once: pointing to a life the boy has watched from the inside — the ark, the plague, the threshing floor, the years of running and the years of building — and saying that none of it transfers. Solomon has to know him for himself. A father's religion is evidence, not inheritance.

Serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind. The whole heart is the thing this book keeps asking for; the men came to Hebron with a whole heart and Zebulun with no double heart. And the second phrase is stronger than it looks in English: it is a delighting soul, service a man actually wants to give. God is not asking to be served by somebody who would rather be elsewhere and has decided to be dutiful about it. The prophets would promise that God himself would give that new heart and put his Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:26–27), and he does so in everyone who belongs to Christ.

For the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. There is the reason wholeness is demanded rather than suggested. A divided heart works perfectly well in front of people, and there is no one it works on here. The God who told Samuel that man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart is the God being served, and every intention is already open in front of him.

If you seek him, he will be found by you. The book began with a king who did not seek and died; it went on through a king who sought the wrong thing, then sought the right thing the wrong way, then learned to seek God's face and told the nation to keep seeking it after the ark was found. Here it arrives as a bare promise with nothing between the two halves. Seek, and found. Moses had said it to a people facing exile: you will seek him and you will find him if you search after him with all your heart. Jeremiah would say it to people already in Babylon. And the Son of God said it in five words on a hillside — seek, and you will find.

But if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever. David does not soften it for his own child in public. And the hardest thing about the sentence is what happened next: the boy who received this charge built the house, saw the glory fill it, heard God speak to him twice, and ended his life with altars to Chemosh and Molech on the hill east of Jerusalem. He had been warned by his father, in front of the nation, in words nobody could misunderstand.

Then the last word, and it is practical: be strong and do it. The theology has been laid out and the charge ends in a verb. Do it.

Can a believer be cast off forever? The warning is real, and it describes those who forsake God for good, who show they never truly knew him (1 John 2:19). Those who truly seek God find him (Jeremiah 29:13), and he keeps them (John 10:28). A troubled believer who fears this verse is about him is usually showing, by the fear itself, that he still wants God; the one who forsakes God for good does not lie awake over it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then David hands over the plans in astonishing detail: rooms, courts, the room for the mercy seat (vv. 11-12), the divisions of priests and Levites (v. 13), the weight of gold and silver for every object down to the forks, and the golden chariot of the cherubim (vv. 14-18). And the source is named: in writing from the hand of the LORD (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The temple was given, not designed: a king received it in writing and handed it on.
verseByVerse.examples: A God who specifies the forks has not overlooked the smallest part of anyone's service.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David gave Solomon his son the plan of the vestibule of the temple, and of its houses, its treasuries, its upper rooms, and its inner chambers, and of the room for the mercy seat; and the plan of all that he had in mind for the courts of the house of the LORD, all the surrounding chambers, the treasuries of the house of God, and the treasuries for dedicated gifts; for the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, and all the work of the service in the house of the LORD; for all the vessels for the service in the house of the LORD, the weight of gold for all golden vessels for each service, the weight of silver vessels for each service, the weight of the golden lampstands and their lamps, the weight of gold for each lampstand and its lamps, the weight of silver for a lampstand and its lamps, according to the use of each lampstand in the service,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 13 is not architecture at all. The rotas of the last five chapters are inside the plan, filed between the chambers and the vessels: who would work there was part of the design, not bolted on once the roof was up.

Somebody had specified how much gold went into a lamp, a figure for each item according to its use. It is the same care that would not let the ark travel on a cart.

verseByVerse.quote: the weight of gold for each table for the showbread, the silver for the silver tables, and pure gold for the forks, the basins and the cups; for the golden bowls and the weight of each; for the silver bowls and the weight of each; for the altar of incense made of refined gold, and its weight; also his plan for the golden chariot of the cherubim that spread their wings and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD. "All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD, all the work to be done according to the plan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list of weights runs on, and it gets smaller as it goes. Tables, forks, basins, cups, bowls, the altar of incense, each by weight.

Forks. The plan given to David included the specification for the forks. Whatever else this tells us, it tells us that God is not indifferent to the small fittings of the place where he is worshipped, and that there is no line in that house below which it stops mattering.

And then the last item, and it is the greatest: his plan for the golden chariot of the cherubim that spread their wings and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD. The two enormous figures that would stand in the Most Holy Place, wings touching wall to wall over the box, are described as a chariot — the thing a king rides. It is the same picture Ezekiel would see by a canal in Babylon and David sang in a psalm, of God riding on a cherub and flying.

The word translated plan is the word used of the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain, when he told him to make the tabernacle and everything in it according to the pattern he had been shown. So the temple is not David's design and not a magnificent building commissioned by a rich king. It is a copy, and the copying is the whole point of it. Its rooms and its weights and its forks were given.

Centuries later a letter to Hebrew Christians explains what the copying was of. The priests who serve there, it says, serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, and quotes the very instruction to Moses about the pattern. Every measurement in this chapter is a measurement of something that already existed somewhere else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–21 — Be Strong and Do It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The charge ends where Joshua's began: be strong and courageous, for God will not leave you until the work is finished (v. 20). And the help is already in place: priests, Levites, every willing and skilled man, and all the people (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise has a terminus, and the terminus is not Solomon's death or his best effort. God will not leave him until all the work ... is finished — which means the finishing is part of what is being promised.
verseByVerse.examples: The men who will help are described twice over: willing, and skilled. Neither on its own was thought sufficient to build a house for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to Solomon his son, "Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you, until all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished. And behold the divisions of the priests and the Levites for all the service of the house of God; and with you in all the work will be every willing man who has skill for any kind of service; also the officers and all the people will be wholly at your command."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those are, very nearly, the words Moses spoke to Joshua before the Jordan crossing (Deuteronomy 31:6–8), and David has been using them on Solomon since chapter 22. But he puts something of his own in the middle of them: the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He cannot resist the personal pronoun. Forty years of being carried by this God are compressed into the words even my God, inserted into a promise, and they are the only credential the old man offers.

Hebrews quotes the promise to tell frightened people God will never leave them nor forsake them (Hebrews 13:5), and Paul voices the same confidence, that the one who began a good work will bring it to its finish (Philippians 1:6).

And the last verse answers a young man's obvious fear: you are not doing this alone. The rotas are drawn up, the staff in post, every willing man with skill beside him, and the people at his command.

So the old king sits down. He has told the nation why he was refused, traced his own throne back to a choice he had no part in, warned his son in front of everybody, handed over a pattern he received in writing, and promised a God who does not leave the work half-built.

29.title: The Offering of All Things: Generosity, Prayer, and the Passing of the Kingdom
29.text: <sup>1</sup>And David the king said to all the assembly, "Solomon my son, whom alone God has chosen, is young and inexperienced, and the work is great, for the palace will not be for man but for the LORD God.<sup>2</sup>So I have provided for the house of my God, so far as I was able, the gold for the things of gold, the silver for the things of silver, and the bronze for the things of bronze, the iron for the things of iron, and wood for the things of wood, besides great quantities of onyx and stones for setting, antimony, colored stones, all sorts of precious stones and marble.<sup>3</sup>Moreover, in addition to all that I have provided for the holy house, I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and because of my devotion to the house of my God I give it to the house of my God:<sup>4</sup>3,000 talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and 7,000 talents of refined silver, for overlaying the walls of the house,<sup>5</sup>and for all the work to be done by craftsmen, gold for the things of gold and silver for the things of silver. Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the LORD?"<sup>6</sup>Then the leaders of fathers' houses made their freewill offerings, as did also the leaders of the tribes, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the officers over the king's work.<sup>7</sup>They gave for the service of the house of God 5,000 talents and 10,000 darics of gold, 10,000 talents of silver, 18,000 talents of bronze and 100,000 talents of iron.<sup>8</sup>And whoever had precious stones gave them to the treasury of the house of the LORD, in the care of Jehiel the Gershonite.<sup>9</sup>Then the people rejoiced because they had given willingly, for with a whole heart they had offered freely to the LORD. David the king also rejoiced greatly.<sup>10</sup>Therefore David blessed the LORD in the presence of all the assembly. And David said: "Blessed are you, O LORD, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever.<sup>11</sup>Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, O LORD, and you are exalted as head above all.<sup>12</sup>Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all. In your hand are power and might, and in your hand it is to make great and to give strength to all.<sup>13</sup>And now we thank you, our God, and praise your glorious name.<sup>14</sup>"But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you.<sup>15</sup>For we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding.<sup>16</sup>O LORD our God, all this abundance that we have provided for building you a house for your holy name comes from your hand and is all your own.<sup>17</sup>I know, my God, that you test the heart and have pleasure in uprightness. In the uprightness of my heart I have freely offered all these things, and now I have seen your people, who are present here, offering freely and joyously to you.<sup>18</sup>O LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you.<sup>19</sup>Grant to Solomon my son a whole heart that he may keep your commandments, your testimonies, and your statutes, performing all, and that he may build the palace for which I have made provision."<sup>20</sup>Then David said to all the assembly, "Bless the LORD your God." And all the assembly blessed the LORD, the God of their fathers, and bowed their heads and paid homage to the LORD and to the king.<sup>21</sup>And they offered sacrifices to the LORD, and on the next day offered burnt offerings to the LORD, 1,000 bulls, 1,000 rams, and 1,000 lambs, with their drink offerings, and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel.<sup>22</sup>And they ate and drank before the LORD on that day with great gladness. And they made Solomon the son of David king the second time, and they anointed him as prince for the LORD, and Zadok as priest.<sup>23</sup>Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of David his father. And he prospered, and all Israel obeyed him.<sup>24</sup>All the leaders and the mighty men, and also all the sons of King David, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon.<sup>25</sup>And the LORD made Solomon very great in the sight of all Israel and bestowed on him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.<sup>26</sup>Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel.<sup>27</sup>The time that he reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.<sup>28</sup>Then he died at a good age, full of days, riches, and honor. And Solomon his son reigned in his place.<sup>29</sup>Now the acts of King David, from first to last, are written in the Chronicles of Samuel the seer, and in the Chronicles of Nathan the prophet, and in the Chronicles of Gad the seer,<sup>30</sup>with accounts of all his rule and his might and of the circumstances that came upon him and upon Israel and upon all the kingdoms of the countries.
29.overview:
David tells the assembly the work is great, lists what he has provided, and gives his own fortune on top of it (vv. 1-4). He asks who else will offer willingly, the leaders answer with an avalanche, and the people rejoice because they had given willingly (vv. 5-9). Then his last prayer: of your own have we given you, our days are a shadow, and two petitions for his people's hearts and his son's (vv. 10-19). Sacrifices, a feast, and Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD (vv. 20-25). Then David dies, full of days (vv. 26-30).

The obituary is written to be read against Saul's in chapter 10, and the whole book stands between the two.
29.theology:
Verse 14 is the theology of giving in one line: all things come from you, and of your own have we given you. Nobody has handed God anything he did not supply first, including the willingness, which is why David's next petition is that God would keep it in place (v. 18). Hearts do not hold themselves steady; holding them is the work God has now given his Spirit to do in his people.

And verse 23 finishes what 17:14 began: Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD (see on vv. 23-25).

It is also why the New Testament can preach this verse's throne as Christ's. Peter told Jerusalem that God had sworn to seat one of David's descendants on his throne, and that he had done it by raising Jesus and exalting him to his right hand (Acts 2:30–36). And the giving that opens the chapter has its own answer in him: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). Every willing gift since is a small echo of that one.
29.examples:
After forty years of having his victories written down, David chose to disappear into the plating of a room (vv. 3-4).

Parents who have prayed for a child's whole heart and watched the child go astray have not prayed wrongly. David's request for Solomon was still the right one, and God answered it in the end in a greater Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Who Then Will Offer Willingly?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David tells the assembly that Solomon is young and the work great, for the palace is for the LORD God (v. 1). He lists what he has provided as king (v. 2), then gives his own treasure for overlaying the walls (vv. 3-4), and asks who else will offer willingly (v. 5). The leaders answer with an avalanche (vv. 6-8), and the people rejoice because they had given willingly (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Bringing a gift to this house is described in the language of ordination (see on vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.examples: They were glad because they had given, not the other way round (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: And David the king said to all the assembly, "Solomon my son, whom alone God has chosen, is young and inexperienced, and the work is great, for the palace will not be for man but for the LORD God. So I have provided for the house of my God, so far as I was able, the gold for the things of gold, the silver for the things of silver, and the bronze for the things of bronze, the iron for the things of iron, and wood for the things of wood, besides great quantities of onyx and stones for setting, antimony, colored stones, all sorts of precious stones and marble. Moreover, in addition to all that I have provided for the holy house, I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and because of my devotion to the house of my God I give it to the house of my God:
verseByVerse.commentary:
He tells the entire kingdom that the new king is not ready. It is not a betrayal; it is the argument he is about to build on, because if the boy is not equal to it and the work is enormous, then everyone in the room has something to do about it. And the standard is set in the last clause: the building is not for a man. That is why the young king's inexperience matters and why the cost cannot be trimmed.

Then he lists what he has already provided as king — gold for the gold work, silver for the silver, bronze, iron, timber, onyx, antimony, coloured stones, marble. Everything matched to its purpose. That is the state provision, gathered out of forty years of tribute and war.

And then verse 3 turns the chapter: his own money, the private fortune of an old man, given on top of everything he had arranged as king. The reason is not duty or example. It is my devotion, a word meaning delight. He wanted to.

verseByVerse.quote: 3,000 talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and 7,000 talents of refined silver, for overlaying the walls of the house, and for all the work to be done by craftsmen, gold for the things of gold and silver for the things of silver. Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three thousand talents of the gold of Ophir, the finest known, and seven thousand of refined silver, for overlaying the walls: not a vessel with his name on it, but the walls, where nobody would know whose it was.

The Hebrew behind the question of verse 5 is a fixed expression: who will fill his hand today for the LORD. It is the language used when a priest is ordained — Moses is told to fill the hands of Aaron and his sons, and the filled hand is the sign that a man has been set apart for God's service.

So David does not ask for a subscription. He asks who will be ordained today, and the way a man answers is by putting something in his own hand and holding it out. Giving is being described as consecration, and the two are not being compared. They are the same act.

Does David’s freewill offering teach tithing? It teaches willing, generous giving to God from what he first gave (v. 14).

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.
verseByVerse.note: A talent was about 75 pounds (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the leaders of fathers' houses made their freewill offerings, as did also the leaders of the tribes, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the officers over the king's work. They gave for the service of the house of God 5,000 talents and 10,000 darics of gold, 10,000 talents of silver, 18,000 talents of bronze and 100,000 talents of iron. And whoever had precious stones gave them to the treasury of the house of the LORD, in the care of Jehiel the Gershonite. Then the people rejoiced because they had given willingly, for with a whole heart they had offered freely to the LORD. David the king also rejoiced greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The response is enormous: thousands of talents of gold, silver, bronze and iron, and every man's precious stones handed in for the treasury.

One curiosity: the text counts ten thousand darics, a Persian coin that did not exist for nearly five hundred years more. Most think the Chronicler has converted an ancient sum into money his readers used, as a writer today might give a medieval price in modern currency. It is not a slip but a man making sure his readers understand what was given.

Three separate words for willingness are piled into one sentence — willingly, whole heart, freely — and then the joy is placed carefully on the far side of the act. They did not give because they were in a good mood. They rejoiced because they had given, which is an order of events most people never test and every generous person knows.

The final clause is recorded separately, as though the writer wanted it to stand on its own. The old king, who had been refused the one thing he wanted to do, watched other people fund it and was gladder than any of them.

Can the totals be real? Three thousand talents is over a hundred tons of gold, and with chapter 22's figures the sums are larger than any known treasury of the age. Some think they are rounded or enlarged in copying; others note that ancient kings did boast of enormous hoards. Nobody can now check them. What the text plainly teaches does not hang on the arithmetic: the gifts were vast, willing and gladly given.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David blesses God before everybody: Yours is the kingdom (vv. 10-13). Then the turn: But who am I, and what is my people? For all things come from God (v. 14), and our days are a shadow (v. 15). He appeals to the God who tests hearts (vv. 16-17), and asks that God would keep his people's hearts and give Solomon a whole one (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Forty years of answers have not made chapter 17's question smaller: who am I? (v. 14).
verseByVerse.examples: The prayer hands everything back to God before it asks for anything. Asking comes best from open hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore David blessed the LORD in the presence of all the assembly. And David said: "Blessed are you, O LORD, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever. Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, O LORD, and you are exalted as head above all. Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all. In your hand are power and might, and in your hand it is to make great and to give strength to all. And now we thank you, our God, and praise your glorious name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the last great prayer of his life. Five nouns, and every one of them is the sort of thing a king is congratulated on. Greatness, power, glory, victory, majesty. David has all five by any human measure — he took Jerusalem, beat the Philistines twice, broke the Syrian coalition, and is standing in front of a kingdom that runs from Egypt to the Euphrates. He hands the entire list over in one breath and says none of it is his.

Then yours is the kingdom, which in this book is not a figure of speech. He has just told the nation that his son will sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD.

Christians have long finished the Lord's Prayer with those words (see the note), and wherever the church first put them there, they plainly echo this prayer. An old man at the end of his reign gave the church the words it uses to hand everything back.

Riches and honour. Hold those two words, because they come back. Sixteen verses later the chronicle will close the reign by saying that David died at a good age, full of days, riches and honour — the very pair he has just said belong to God and come out of his hand. The obituary is written in the vocabulary of the prayer, which means the writer wants nobody to mistake where the old man's wealth and standing had come from.

And there is a phrase in the middle of the verse that no king says lightly: in your hand it is to make great. Greatness is something God does to people. David had been told exactly that at the start, when the word came through Nathan promising to make his name like the name of the great ones of the earth, and years later he repeats it back as doctrine.

And the paragraph ends in the plainest way possible: And now we thank you, our God, and praise your glorious name. After the greatness and the majesty and the dominion over all things — thank you.
verseByVerse.note: The closing words added to the Lord’s Prayer in later manuscripts (“yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory”) closely echo v. 11.

verseByVerse.quote: "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you. For we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has asked that before. Standing in front of the ark after Nathan brought him the covenant, he sat down and said: who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house. Decades have passed. He has taken a capital, buried a son, buried the men who died in a plague he caused, handed over a kingdom. And the question comes back unchanged except that it has got wider — not my house now, but my people.

What he cannot get over is not that God gave him a throne. It is that the assembly has just been able to give something away. He treats the capacity for generosity as the astonishing thing, and then explains why.

Every talent in that pile had been mined, transported, taxed or captured, and every stage of it had run through God's hands before it reached theirs. So the offering was not a transfer of wealth from Israel to God. It was Israel handing back a fraction of what it was holding, and being thanked for it.

Then verse 15, and it is said by a man standing beside storehouses full of gold and iron.

Strangers and sojourners are resident foreigners — people with no title to the ground they stand on, living somewhere at the owner's pleasure. God had used exactly those words about Israel and the land: the land is mine, and you are strangers and sojourners with me. David is not being morbid and he is not disparaging what he has. He is stating the terms of the tenancy.

And the last clause has no comfort in it at all. Our days are a shadow, and there is nothing here to hold. The comfort is not in the clause but in the one he is speaking to. The men who wrote the letter to the Hebrews said the same of Abraham and the rest: they confessed they were strangers and exiles on the earth, and people who talk like that are looking for a country. David is about to die, and he says it in a prayer, in public, on the best day of his old age. For anyone who feels how quickly life runs out, that is the right way round: the shortness is said to God, and the same letter says God has prepared for them a city (Hebrews 11:16).

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD our God, all this abundance that we have provided for building you a house for your holy name comes from your hand and is all your own. I know, my God, that you test the heart and have pleasure in uprightness. In the uprightness of my heart I have freely offered all these things, and now I have seen your people, who are present here, offering freely and joyously to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD our God, all this abundance that we have provided for building you a house for your holy name comes from your hand and is all your own. He says it again, in case the first time was mistaken for modesty. The pile in the courtyard is God's property and always was.

He is claiming a clean motive, out loud, to the God who examines motives. That would be intolerable from most men and it is not a claim to a clean life — this is the king of the census and of the roof at evening. It is a claim about one act. He knows why he gave the gold, he knows God is testing exactly that, and he is willing to say what he found when he looked.

And the part he plainly enjoyed most: he has seen the people offering freely and joyously. An old leader's last public satisfaction was not that the fund was full. It was that he had seen their faces while they gave.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you. Grant to Solomon my son a whole heart that he may keep your commandments, your testimonies, and your statutes, performing all, and that he may build the palace for which I have made provision."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the two petitions the prayer has been travelling towards, and both ask God to do something inside people.

Looking at gold given gladly, he asks God to make it last, because it will not last by itself. He had seen a nation dance the ark up a hill and forget it for decades, and felt his own heart go where it should not. There is no mechanism inside a man for holding it steady, so he asks God to.

Not a long reign, wealth or sons: a whole heart, the thing he asked for in chapter 22 and pressed in chapter 28, and the last prayer this book records him praying.

The son did not keep the whole heart; he ended with shrines to Chemosh and Molech facing the house he had raised. That does not make the prayer wrong. A father asked God for the one thing worth having for his child, at the end of his life, and its answer came a thousand years later out of the same family, in a son whose heart was never divided for an instant, and whose whole-hearted obedience now stands for every divided heart that trusts him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — Solomon on the Throne of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The assembly blesses God (v. 20), the sacrifices are enormous, and they eat and drink before the LORD with great gladness (vv. 21-22). Solomon is made king a second time, and sat on the throne of the LORD (v. 23). All David's sons pledge allegiance (v. 24), and God makes Solomon great (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The kingdom is handed on with worship, sacrifice and a shared meal: the throne is received before the LORD, not seized.
verseByVerse.examples: Feasting before God is part of worship, not a break from it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to all the assembly, "Bless the LORD your God." And all the assembly blessed the LORD, the God of their fathers, and bowed their heads and paid homage to the LORD and to the king. And they offered sacrifices to the LORD, and on the next day offered burnt offerings to the LORD, 1,000 bulls, 1,000 rams, and 1,000 lambs, with their drink offerings, and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel. And they ate and drank before the LORD on that day with great gladness. And they made Solomon the son of David king the second time, and they anointed him as prince for the LORD, and Zadok as priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then David said to all the assembly, Bless the LORD your God. He has just spent ten verses doing it and now he turns and tells them to. And they do — the whole assembly blessing the God of their fathers, bowing their heads and paying homage to the LORD and to the king.

The next day the sacrifices are enormous, and then a sentence this book keeps arriving at: they ate and drank before the LORD with great gladness.

It ended at a table. So did the day the tribes made him king at Hebron, when they stayed three days and the far northern tribes brought the food. So did the day the ark came home, when every man and woman in the crowd went away with bread and meat and a cake of raisins. Whenever this kingdom gets something right, the record closes with people eating.

Then Solomon is made king the second time, anointed as prince for the LORD, with Zadok anointed priest beside him. The first time is probably the brief notice in 23:1; readers of Kings will also remember the hurried anointing at the Gihon spring while Adonijah was claiming the throne (1 Kings 1). This one is done properly, in daylight, in front of the nation, with the priest and the prince anointed together.

Why does Chronicles leave out the bedridden David and Adonijah's bid for the crown? Not because it denies them: its readers had Kings, and it alludes to the rival brothers in verse 24. Its purpose is to show the handover of God's kingdom from one chosen king to the next, and it tells that side of a day Kings tells from the palace. Both are true accounts of one succession, written for different ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of David his father. And he prospered, and all Israel obeyed him. All the leaders and the mighty men, and also all the sons of King David, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon. And the LORD made Solomon very great in the sight of all Israel and bestowed on him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The throne of the LORD. Not the throne of Israel, not the throne of David — and this is the third time the book has said it. God had called it my house and my kingdom when the covenant was made through Nathan. David had called it the throne of the kingdom of the LORD when he presented his son to the assembly. Now a man sits down on it, and the chronicle records whose chair it was.
