That is the sentence that let this book be written at all. Its first readers had no king and no independence, and if the throne had ever belonged to David it was gone. It never did. The kingdom was the LORD's, held in tenancy by a family he had chosen, and losing the tenant did not put the kingdom on the market.

Then the succession is secured in the way that matters: All the leaders and the mighty men, and also all the sons of King David, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon. All the sons — including the older brothers, one of whom had tried to take the throne.

Verse 25 answers the prayer of the day before in a way nobody in the courtyard can have missed.

Majesty is the word David had just handed over — yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty. He gave it away in the prayer and God put it on his son within the day. That is what the whole prayer said would happen: in your hand it is to make great, and what is handed back to God is never lost.

Does generous giving make a person rich? No. This is God honouring a king he had chosen, not a rule that gifts come back as money. The New Testament promises that God will supply what the generous need, so that they can go on giving (2 Corinthians 9:8–11), and some of the most generous people in Scripture stayed poor.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The obituary is a handful of sentences: forty years, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem (vv. 26-27); a good age, full of days, riches and honour (v. 28); and the prophetic sources named (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: What separates the two obituaries in this book (10:13-14 and here) is not talent or success but whether the king sought the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: A name once used as an insult becomes a title of honour when God writes the record.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel. The time that he reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. Then he died at a good age, full of days, riches, and honor. And Solomon his son reigned in his place. Now the acts of King David, from first to last, are written in the Chronicles of Samuel the seer, and in the Chronicles of Nathan the prophet, and in the Chronicles of Gad the seer, with accounts of all his rule and his might and of the circumstances that came upon him and upon Israel and upon all the kingdoms of the countries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turn back nineteen chapters: Saul died for his breach of faith, because he did not seek guidance from the LORD.

Two kings, two paragraphs, and the whole book standing between them. One died on a hill with his armour in a Philistine temple because he did not seek the LORD. The other died at a good age, full of days, having spent his last years buying a threshing floor, weighing out gold and praying for his son's heart. Everything in between is the difference between those two sentences.

And the epitaph calls him the son of Jesse. Saul used that phrase when he could not bear to say the name. Nabal used it to refuse a man food. A rebel raised the northern tribes with it. And in a stronghold in the wilderness, before any of this, the Spirit came on a man called Amasai and he took the insult and made it his oath: we are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse. The official chronicle of the kingdom of Israel uses the sneer as his name.

The sources are then named: the chronicles of Samuel the seer, of Nathan the prophet, and of Gad the seer. Three prophets, and every one of them is remembered for bringing this king or the last one a word he did not want to hear. Samuel told Saul the kingdom was torn from him. Nathan told David the house would be built by somebody else, and later told him a story about a lamb. Gad brought him three punishments and made him choose. The record of the reign was kept by the men who had stood in front of it and said no.

The closing verse says what those records contained: his rule, his might, and ... the circumstances that came upon him and upon Israel and upon all the kingdoms of the countries. The word behind circumstances is simply the times — what happened to him. The chronicle of a reign is not only what a king did. It is also everything that was done to him, and the prophets who kept the record wrote down both.

So the book closes. A shepherd from Bethlehem, a fugitive at Ziklag, a king who got the ark wrong and then got it right, a man who counted his soldiers and buried seventy thousand of his people, who bought a threshing floor at full price because he would not offer what cost him nothing, and who died having never laid a stone of the house he gave his life to. The house was built and filled with glory and burned to the ground nearly four hundred years later. The throne it stood beside was the LORD's, and he had promised it to this family forever, and nearly six hundred years after the last of David's sons was dragged in chains out of a broken city an angel stood in a village in Galilee and said that the Lord God would give a child the throne of his father David, and that of his kingdom there would be no end.

Are these lost books Scripture? They were the prophets’ records and royal annals the inspired writer drew on, as Luke drew on earlier accounts (Luke 1:1–3). Not every writing of a prophet was given to be Scripture; God has preserved all of his word that he meant the church to have (2 Timothy 3:16–17).
